name: Bigfoot
region: Pacific Northwest, Appalachia, the Great Lakes and the South; reported in every US state but Hawaii, and across Canada
first: Indigenous names such as Sasq'ets (Halkomelem) long predate the 1958 "Bigfoot" headline from Bluff Creek, California
summary: A huge, hair-covered, upright ape said to roam North American forests.
body: Bigfoot is the best-known cryptid in North America: a bipedal primate usually described as 7 to 9 feet tall, heavily built, and covered in dark brown, black or reddish hair. Witnesses describe a cone-shaped head, no visible neck, long arms and a smooth, gliding walk.

The name took off in 1958, when a road crew at Bluff Creek, California found giant footprints around their equipment and the Humboldt Times ran the story. In 1967 Roger Patterson and Bob Gimlin filmed a large, dark figure walking along the same creek. The Patterson-Gimlin film is still argued over today.
Reports cluster where there is dense forest, water and few people: the Cascades, northern California, the Ozarks, East Texas, Ohio's Appalachian counties and the Pacific coast of British Columbia.
signs: Footprints 14 to 18 inches long, often with a mid-foot flex
Wood knocks and rock clacks at night
Whoops, howls and "Samurai chatter" vocalizations
Tree breaks and teepee-style stick structures
A strong skunk-like or wet-dog smell
Eyeshine well above the height of a deer

name: Yeti
region: Himalaya: Nepal, Tibet, Bhutan and Sikkim
first: Sherpa and Tibetan tradition; "Abominable Snowman" coined after a 1921 Everest expedition
summary: The ape-like snow creature of the Himalaya, known to Sherpas long before climbers arrived.
body: The Yeti belongs to Himalayan folklore, where the meh-teh is a wild creature of the high valleys. Western interest exploded after Charles Howard-Bury's 1921 Everest reconnaissance reported tracks in the snow, and a newspaper mistranslation gave the world the "Abominable Snowman".

In 1951 Eric Shipton photographed a large footprint on the Menlung Glacier, the most famous Yeti image ever taken. Later expeditions collected scalps, hair and bones from monasteries; DNA studies in 2014 and 2017 traced most samples to bears, but the legend lives on in the mountains.
signs: Large tracks crossing snowfields at altitude
High-pitched whistles or cries
Glimpses of a reddish or grey upright figure
size: Described from child-sized to over 8 ft
habitat: High valleys and glaciers, 12,000 ft and up

name: Yowie
region: Eastern Australia: the Blue Mountains, Queensland's Gold Coast hinterland and the Great Dividing Range
first: Aboriginal stories; settler reports of "hairy men" from the 1800s
summary: Australia's hairy wild man of the bush, a close cousin of Bigfoot.
body: The Yowie is Australia's answer to Bigfoot: a tall, hairy, upright creature reported from the eastern bush. Aboriginal groups across the region tell of hairy men of the hills, and 19th-century colonial newspapers carried accounts of "yahoos" seen by stockmen and timber-getters.
Modern reports come from the Blue Mountains west of Sydney, the Springbrook and Lamington areas of south-east Queensland, and the forests along the Great Dividing Range.
signs: Large human-like tracks
Deep grunts and screams in the bush
Rocks thrown at campers
Strong rotten smell
habitat: Rainforest gullies and dry sclerophyll forest

name: Skunk Ape
region: Florida: the Everglades, Big Cypress and the Panhandle swamps
first: Reports climbed through the 1960s and 70s
summary: Florida's swamp-dwelling Bigfoot, famous for a smell you won't forget.
body: The Skunk Ape is the Bigfoot of the Florida swamps, named for the overpowering odour witnesses describe. It is usually said to be smaller and leaner than its northern cousin, with reddish or dark hair.

In 2000 an anonymous woman mailed two photos of an ape-like animal in her backyard to the Sarasota County Sheriff's Office. The "Myakka photos" remain the most famous Skunk Ape evidence, and the Skunk Ape Research Headquarters in Ochopee still welcomes visitors on the Tamiami Trail.
signs: Overwhelming rotten-egg or skunk smell
Tracks in swamp mud
Shapes crossing roads at night in Big Cypress

name: Fouke Monster
region: Fouke and Boggy Creek, Miller County, Arkansas
first: 1971 attack report; earlier local sightings back to the 1940s
summary: The hairy creature of Boggy Creek, Arkansas, made famous by a 1972 drive-in hit.
body: In May 1971 the Ford family reported that a large, hairy creature reached through a window of their rented house near Fouke and later attacked Bobby Ford on the porch. Three-toed tracks were found in a nearby field.

The story inspired Charles B. Pierce's docudrama The Legend of Boggy Creek (1972), one of the most successful independent films of its decade. Fouke still has a monster mart and draws curious visitors every year.
signs: Three-toed tracks
Glowing eyes along the creek bottoms
Screams at night

name: Honey Island Swamp Monster
region: Honey Island Swamp, St. Tammany Parish, Louisiana
first: Harlan Ford's 1963 sighting
summary: A grey-haired, yellow-eyed swamp giant from the bayous of Louisiana.
body: Retired air-traffic controller Harlan Ford said he saw a tall, grey-haired creature with yellow eyes in the Honey Island Swamp in 1963. He later found webbed, four-toed tracks and made casts, which became the centre of the legend.
Swamp-tour guides around Slidell still tell the story, and the creature is now part of Louisiana's rich mix of bayou folklore alongside the rougarou.
signs: Four-toed tracks
Yellow or amber eyes
Grey, matted hair

name: Momo
region: Louisiana, Pike County, Missouri
first: July 1972
summary: A hairy, pumpkin-headed creature behind the summer scare of 1972 in Missouri.
body: In July 1972 three children in Louisiana, Missouri said they saw a hairy, dark creature with a large, pumpkin-shaped head carrying a dead dog along the edge of the woods. Over the next weeks dozens of residents reported odd smells, screams and sightings, and the press dubbed it Momo.
Momo reports faded by the end of the summer, but the case is a classic example of a short, intense local "flap".
signs: Hair covering the face
Strong, foul odour
Screams from the woods

name: Almas
region: Caucasus Mountains, Central Asia and Mongolia
first: Old Mongolian and Caucasian folklore
summary: A shy, human-sized wild man of the Caucasus and Central Asian steppes.
body: The Almas is described as more human than ape: a hairy, man-sized wild person living in remote mountains. Russian researchers, notably Marie-Jeanne Koffmann, collected hundreds of eyewitness accounts in the Caucasus from the 1960s onward.
The legend of Zana, a "wild woman" said to have been captured in Abkhazia in the 1800s, is often linked to the Almas.
signs: Small, human-like tracks
Glimpses near orchards and mills at night

name: Yeren
region: Shennongjia, Hubei Province, China
first: Ancient Chinese texts; modern reports from the 1970s
summary: The red-haired wild man of China's Shennongjia forests.
body: Shennongjia's mountain forests are the heartland of the Yeren, a tall, reddish-haired creature that walks upright. Reports in the 1970s led the Chinese Academy of Sciences to send several expeditions into the region.
The searches found hair and footprints but no conclusive evidence. Today Shennongjia is a UNESCO World Heritage site and the Yeren is part of its tourist identity.
signs: Reddish hair caught on branches
Large tracks on forest trails

name: Orang Pendek
region: Kerinci Seblat National Park, Sumatra, Indonesia
first: Colonial-era reports from the 1910s
summary: A small, upright ape of Sumatra that some researchers think may be a real undiscovered primate.
body: Orang pendek means "short person" in Indonesian. It is described as a powerfully built ape, about the height of a child, that walks on two legs. Local villagers, Dutch colonists and modern researchers have all reported it.
Unlike many cryptids, the Orang Pendek is taken seriously by some primatologists, because Sumatra's forests are vast and still produce new species.
signs: Small, human-like footprints
Dark hair, long mane

name: Dogman
region: Michigan's Lower Peninsula and Wisconsin, with reports across the Midwest and South
first: Folklore in Wexford County, Michigan; popularised by a 1987 radio song
summary: A tall, upright, dog-headed creature with glowing eyes, the Midwest's favourite monster.
body: The Dogman is described as a muscular canine that can stand and walk on its hind legs, often 6 to 7 feet tall, with a wolf-like head and pointed ears. Witnesses frequently mention amber or red eyeshine and a feeling of intense dread.

In 1987 DJ Steve Cook of WTCM radio in Traverse City aired a song called The Legend as an April Fools' joke. Listeners began calling in with their own sightings, and the Michigan Dogman legend grew from there. Wisconsin's related Beast of Bray Road made headlines in 1991 near Elkhorn.
signs: Upright canine silhouette on hind legs
Amber or red eyeshine at head height
Growls and howls that sound wrong
Large canine tracks with deep heel prints
habitat: Rural woods, farmland edges and back roads

name: Rougarou
region: South Louisiana: Acadiana and the bayou country
first: French Canadian loup-garou tradition, carried south by the Acadians
summary: The Cajun werewolf said to stalk the bayous, especially during Lent.
body: The Rougarou comes from the French loup-garou, a person cursed to take the form of a wolf. In Cajun and Creole tradition it hunts the swamps at night, and parents used it to keep children in line. Some versions say the curse passes to anyone who draws its blood.
Houma, Louisiana hosts an annual Rougarou Fest each October, celebrating the legend and raising money for coastal restoration.
signs: Wolf-like head on a human body
Red eyes in the cypress
Howls across the marsh

name: Chupacabra
region: Puerto Rico, Mexico, Central America and the southern US, especially Texas
first: Puerto Rico, 1995
summary: The goat-sucker: a spiny creature blamed for draining livestock of blood.
body: In 1995 farmers in Puerto Rico began finding goats and chickens dead with small puncture wounds. Witness Madelyne Tolentino described a spiny, bipedal creature with large dark eyes, and comedian Silverio Pérez coined the name chupacabras.

As reports spread to Mexico and Texas, the Chupacabra changed shape: in the US it is usually a hairless, dog-like animal. Most of those carcasses have turned out to be coyotes or foxes with severe mange, but the original Puerto Rican version remains a mystery.
signs: Livestock with neat puncture wounds
Spines or quills down the back
Hairless, grey-blue dog-like animal (US version)

name: Mothman
region: Point Pleasant, West Virginia
first: November 15, 1966
summary: A winged figure with glowing red eyes seen around Point Pleasant in 1966 and 1967.
body: On November 15, 1966, two young couples driving near the abandoned TNT area outside Point Pleasant, West Virginia said a tall, grey, winged figure with glowing red eyes chased their car at high speed. Dozens of similar reports followed over the next year.

On December 15, 1967 the Silver Bridge over the Ohio River collapsed, killing 46 people, and the sightings were soon tied to the disaster. John Keel's book The Mothman Prophecies (1975) and the 2002 film made Mothman a pop-culture icon. Point Pleasant now has a Mothman Museum, a shiny steel statue and a Mothman Festival every September.
signs: Large red eyes that glow in headlights
Wingspan of 10 ft or more
Flies without flapping, at high speed
habitat: The TNT area wetlands and the Ohio River valley

name: Thunderbird
region: Great Plains, Pennsylvania and the American Southwest
first: A sacred figure in many Indigenous nations' traditions; modern "giant bird" reports since the 1800s
summary: Giant birds with impossible wingspans reported across North America.
body: The Thunderbird is a powerful spirit being in the traditions of many Indigenous peoples, from the Pacific Northwest to the Great Lakes. Separately, settlers and modern witnesses have reported enormous birds, far larger than any condor.

The best-known modern case came in July 1977, when 10-year-old Marlon Lowe said a huge bird tried to carry him off in his backyard in Lawndale, Illinois. Pennsylvania has its own long list of thunderbird sightings.
signs: Wingspan of 15 to 20 ft
Shadow over open fields
Livestock or pets carried off
habitat: Open plains, ridges and river valleys

name: Jersey Devil
region: The Pine Barrens of southern New Jersey
first: Legend of Mother Leeds, 1735; the great sighting wave of January 1909
summary: A hooved, winged devil said to haunt the New Jersey Pine Barrens since 1735.
body: According to legend, Mother Leeds of the Pine Barrens cursed her 13th child in 1735, and the baby turned into a winged, horse-headed creature that flew up the chimney. It has haunted the pines ever since.

In the week of January 16 to 23, 1909, thousands of people across New Jersey and Pennsylvania reported strange tracks and sightings. Schools and mills closed, and the Philadelphia Zoo offered a reward. New Jersey's NHL team is named after the creature.
signs: Hoof prints on rooftops and in snow
Blood-curdling screams in the pines
Bat-like wings and a forked tail
habitat: Pine forest, cedar swamps and bogs

name: Owlman
region: Mawnan, Cornwall, England
first: April 1976
summary: A feathered, owl-like figure seen over a Cornish churchyard in 1976.
body: In April 1976 two young sisters on holiday said they saw a large, feathered, man-like figure hovering over the tower of St Mawnan's church in Cornwall. More sightings followed that summer and in 1978.
The Owlman is often compared to Mothman: both are winged humanoids with glowing eyes, seen in a short burst of activity.
signs: Pointed ears, red or glowing eyes
Grey feathers, black pincer-like claws

name: Kongamato
region: Jiundu Swamp, northwest Zambia, and neighbouring Angola and DR Congo
first: Frank Melland's book In Witch-bound Africa (1923)
summary: A leathery-winged flyer from Zambia's swamps, sometimes called a living pterosaur.
body: In 1923 British colonial official Frank Melland wrote that people in the Jiundu Swamp described a reddish, featherless flying creature with leathery wings and teeth, which they called kongamato. When shown a drawing of a pterosaur, witnesses reportedly picked it out.
Most zoologists suspect large fruit bats or storks, but the Kongamato remains a favourite of the "living dinosaur" corner of cryptozoology.
signs: Leathery, featherless wings
Long beak with teeth

name: Loch Ness Monster
region: Loch Ness, Scottish Highlands
first: St Columba's encounter with a "water beast" in 565 AD; the modern legend from 1933
summary: Scotland's long-necked lake monster, the world's most famous cryptid.
body: Loch Ness is 23 miles long, more than 700 feet deep and so full of peat that visibility is a few feet. A new road along its north shore opened in 1933, and that spring a local couple reported a whale-like animal rolling in the water. Nessie mania followed.

The 1934 "Surgeon's Photograph" showed a slender neck rising from the loch; in 1994 it was revealed as a hoax made with a toy submarine. A 2018 environmental DNA survey found no reptile DNA but lots of eel DNA. Sightings still come in every year.
signs: Long neck and small head above the water
One or more humps
Large, unexplained wakes on calm days

name: Ogopogo
region: Okanagan Lake, British Columbia
first: Syilx (Okanagan) traditions of N'ha-a-itk; settler reports from the 1870s
summary: Canada's famous lake serpent of Okanagan Lake, BC.
body: The Syilx people speak of N'ha-a-itk, a powerful spirit of Okanagan Lake who demanded offerings for safe crossing. Settlers reported a long, serpent-like animal from the 1870s, and a 1924 music-hall song gave it the name Ogopogo.
Descriptions are of a dark, 40 to 50 ft serpent with several humps. A statue of Ogopogo stands in Kelowna's City Park.
signs: Several humps in a line
A horse- or goat-like head
Dark green or black skin

name: Champ
region: Lake Champlain, between Vermont, New York and Quebec
first: Abenaki stories of Tatoskok; settler reports from the 1800s
summary: America's Loch Ness: the long-necked creature of Lake Champlain.
body: Lake Champlain is 120 miles long and over 400 feet deep. In 1873 a railway crew reported a huge serpent near Dresden, New York, and P.T. Barnum offered $50,000 for its carcass.

In 1977 Sandra Mansi photographed what looks like a head and neck rising from the lake near St. Albans, Vermont. The Mansi photo is still the centrepiece of the Champ story, and Port Henry, New York keeps a roadside sightings board.
signs: Long neck and humps
Dark, snake-like head
Large wakes

name: Bessie
region: Lake Erie, Ohio, Ontario and Michigan
first: 1793 report from the sloop Felicity
summary: Lake Erie's serpent, reported by sailors since the 1790s.
body: Captain Hiram Bell of the sloop Felicity reported a large serpent near Middle Island in 1793. Over the next two centuries sailors, fishermen and beachgoers described a long, grey, snake-like animal in the western basin.
A cluster of sightings in the early 1990s led a Huron, Ohio company to offer a reward for the capture of "South Bay Bessie" alive.
signs: 30 to 40 ft serpent with humps
Grey or black skin
habitat: Shallow western basin of Lake Erie

name: Cadborosaurus
region: Pacific coast of British Columbia and Washington
first: First Nations art and stories; named after Cadboro Bay, Victoria, in 1933
summary: A horse-headed sea serpent reported off the coast of British Columbia.
body: Coastal First Nations art shows long, serpent-like sea creatures, and settlers around Victoria reported one often enough that a newspaper editor named it Cadborosaurus in 1933, after Cadboro Bay.
In 1937 whalers at Naden Harbour, Haida Gwaii, photographed a strange carcass found in a sperm whale's stomach. It remains a key piece of the Caddy story.
signs: Horse- or camel-like head
Long neck and coils
Moves very fast

name: Bear Lake Monster
region: Bear Lake, on the Utah-Idaho border
first: 1868 newspaper articles by Joseph C. Rich
summary: A serpent of Bear Lake that started with an 1868 newspaper story.
body: In 1868 Joseph C. Rich wrote for the Deseret News about a huge, serpent-like animal in Bear Lake, citing several local witnesses. In 1884 he admitted it had been a tall tale, but sightings kept coming.
Today the monster is a friendly local mascot, with a boat-shaped monster offering lake tours in summer.
signs: Serpent body with small legs
Ears like a cow's
size: Up to 90 ft (in the original story)

name: Flathead Lake Monster
region: Flathead Lake, Montana
first: Steamboat passengers, 1889
summary: Montana's eel-like lake creature, seen by over 100 people since 1889.
body: Flathead Lake is the largest natural freshwater lake west of the Mississippi by surface area. In 1889 passengers on the steamboat U.S. Grant reported a whale-like animal, and more than 100 sightings have followed.
Most describe a dark, eel-like creature 20 to 40 ft long. Some suspect a giant sturgeon; a 7-ft white sturgeon was caught in the lake in 1955.
signs: Dark, eel-like body
Large wakes on calm water

name: Mokele-mbembe
aliases: One who stops the flow of rivers
region: Likouala swamps, Republic of the Congo
first: Reports gathered by German explorers in 1913
summary: A sauropod-like river creature said to live in the Congo Basin.
body: Mokele-mbembe is described by people of the Likouala region as a large, long-necked animal that lives in rivers and kills hippos but eats plants. Since the 1980s many expeditions have searched Lake Tele for it.
It is the most famous "living dinosaur" claim, though no expedition has returned with clear evidence.
signs: Long neck and tail, elephant-sized body
Disturbed river vegetation

name: Bunyip
region: Billabongs, swamps and rivers across southeastern Australia
first: Aboriginal traditions; settler newspaper reports from the 1840s
summary: The fearsome creature of Australia's waterholes.
body: The bunyip comes from Aboriginal traditions of a dangerous creature that lurks in billabongs, creeks and swamps. Descriptions vary widely: dog-like faces, flippers, tusks or a horse-like tail.
Colonial newspapers in the 1840s reported bunyip bones and sightings, and the word became part of Australian English.
signs: Booming calls from the water at night

name: Flatwoods Monster
region: Flatwoods, Braxton County, West Virginia
first: September 12, 1952
summary: A towering figure with a spade-shaped hood seen after a fiery object fell from the sky in 1952.
body: On September 12, 1952, a group of boys in Flatwoods, West Virginia saw a bright object streak across the sky and land on a hillside farm. With their mother and a National Guardsman they climbed up to look and met a 10-foot figure with a glowing face, a spade-shaped hood and a hissing sound, along with a sickening mist.

Investigators later suggested a meteor and a barn owl, but the witnesses held to their story. The town of Sutton now has the Braxton County Monster Museum, and five oversized monster chairs stand around the county.
signs: Bright object landing nearby
Pungent, metallic mist
Glowing eyes in a spade-shaped hood

name: Dover Demon
region: Dover, Massachusetts
first: April 21, 1977
summary: A small, big-headed creature with glowing orange eyes seen over two nights in 1977.
body: On the night of April 21, 1977, 17-year-old Bill Bartlett was driving through Dover, Massachusetts when he saw a thin, pale creature with a huge watermelon-shaped head and glowing orange eyes crawling along a stone wall. Two more teenagers reported the same creature that night and the next.
Bartlett's sketch became one of the most recognisable images in cryptozoology.
signs: Huge head on a thin body
Glowing orange eyes
Long, thin fingers

name: Kelly-Hopkinsville Goblins
region: Kelly, near Hopkinsville, Kentucky
first: August 21, 1955
summary: The night a Kentucky farmhouse was besieged by small, glowing creatures.
body: On the night of August 21, 1955, the Sutton family of Kelly, Kentucky said small, silver-grey creatures with big ears and glowing eyes approached their farmhouse after a bright light landed nearby. The family fired guns at them for hours, then drove to the police station in Hopkinsville.
Police found bullet holes but no creatures. The case helped popularise the phrase "little green men", and Kelly holds a Little Green Men Days festival each August.
signs: Small figures with large ears and long arms
Floating rather than walking
Glowing yellow eyes

name: Loveland Frogman
region: Loveland, Ohio
first: 1955; police sightings in March 1972
summary: A frog-faced humanoid seen by Loveland police officers in 1972.
body: In March 1972 two Loveland, Ohio police officers separately reported a frog- or lizard-like creature about 4 feet tall crossing the road near the Little Miami River. One officer later said it was probably an iguana that had escaped from a home.
The Frogman has become a beloved local legend, with a musical and an annual festival.
signs: Leathery, frog-like face
Walking upright near the riverbank

name: Lizard Man of Scape Ore Swamp
region: Scape Ore Swamp, Lee County, South Carolina
summary: A green, scaly, 7-ft creature that clawed at a teenager's car in 1988.
body: Late on June 29, 1988, 17-year-old Christopher Davis stopped to change a tire near Scape Ore Swamp. He said a 7-ft, green, scaly creature with red eyes and three-fingered hands ran at him and clung to his car's roof as he drove away.
More reports and damaged cars followed that summer, and the Lizard Man became a South Carolina legend.
signs: Green, scaly skin
Red eyes
Three-fingered hands with claws
wiki: Lizard Man of Scape Ore Swamp

name: Mongolian Death Worm
region: Gobi Desert, Mongolia
first: Mongolian nomad tradition; brought west by Roy Chapman Andrews in 1926
summary: A bright red worm of the Gobi, said to kill with venom or electricity.
body: Mongolian herders describe the olgoi-khorkhoi as a fat, red worm 2 to 5 feet long that lives under the sand and comes out after rain. Legend says it can spit acid or kill at a distance with an electric shock.
American explorer Roy Chapman Andrews heard the stories in the 1920s, and several modern expeditions have searched without success.
signs: Red, sausage-like body
Appears after summer rain
habitat: Sand dunes of the southern Gobi

name: Tatzelwurm
region: The Alps: Austria, Switzerland, Bavaria and northern Italy
first: Alpine folklore; a famous 1934 photograph
summary: A stubby, cat-faced lizard of Alpine legend.
body: The Tatzelwurm is a creature of Alpine folklore: a thick, lizard-like body with a cat-like face and only two or four short legs. Farmers reported it from the 1700s.
In 1934 Swiss photographer Balkin said he photographed one; the image was widely printed and later suspected to be a ceramic fish.
signs: Lizard body with a cat's face
Hissing or whistling sound

name: Flying saucer
region: Worldwide
first: Kenneth Arnold's sighting near Mount Rainier, June 24, 1947
summary: The classic disc-shaped UFO that launched the modern era of sightings.
body: On June 24, 1947, pilot Kenneth Arnold reported nine shiny objects flying in formation near Mount Rainier, Washington, moving "like a saucer if you skip it across water". Newspapers coined "flying saucer" within days, and a wave of reports swept the country.
Two weeks later came Roswell. In the decades since, disc shapes have stayed among the most reported UFO types, and the US Air Force set up Project Sign, Grudge and Blue Book to investigate them.
signs: Metallic disc, sometimes with a dome
Silent, very fast or hovering
Lights around the rim
size: Reported from 10 ft to hundreds of feet across

name: Black triangle
region: Worldwide; famous waves over Belgium and Arizona
first: Reports grew through the 1980s
summary: Huge, silent, dark triangles with lights at each corner.
body: Black triangles are large, dark, triangular craft with a light at each corner and often a red light in the centre. They are typically described as silent and slow, sometimes hovering at low altitude.

The Belgian UFO wave of 1989 to 1990 involved thousands of witnesses and F-16 scrambles. On March 13, 1997, thousands of people in Arizona saw the Phoenix Lights, which some described as a vast V or triangle.
signs: Three or more bright lights in a triangle
Dark body blocking out stars
Slow and silent
size: Up to hundreds of feet across

name: Orbs and lights
region: Worldwide; Marfa, Texas and Brown Mountain, North Carolina are famous spots
first: Folklore of will-o'-the-wisps; WWII "foo fighters" in 1944
summary: Glowing balls of light that pace aircraft, dance over deserts or hang in the night sky.
body: Glowing orbs are the most common kind of UFO report. In 1944 and 1945 Allied bomber crews over Europe and the Pacific reported balls of light following their aircraft, which they called foo fighters.
On the ground, the Marfa lights of West Texas and the Brown Mountain lights of North Carolina appear on many nights and draw visitors to official viewing areas.
signs: Glowing spheres, white, orange or red
Split apart or merge
Follow vehicles or aircraft

name: Tic Tac UAP
region: Off the coast of Southern California and the US East Coast
first: November 14, 2004
summary: The white, wingless object that US Navy pilots tracked from the USS Nimitz in 2004.
body: On November 14, 2004, Navy pilots from the USS Nimitz carrier group were sent to intercept an object tracked on radar off San Diego. Commander David Fravor described a smooth, white, 40-ft object shaped like a Tic Tac that moved with no visible means of propulsion.

The New York Times published the FLIR1 video in 2017, along with the Gimbal and GoFast videos from 2015 East Coast encounters. The Pentagon formally released all three in 2020, a turning point that led to the creation of AARO and public congressional hearings.
signs: Smooth white oblong shape
No wings, exhaust or rotors
Sudden acceleration
habitat: Over the ocean, near military training ranges

name: Ohio Grassman
region: Eastern and southeastern Ohio, especially Salt Fork State Park, Stark County and the Hocking Hills
first: Newspaper reports of hairy wild men in Ohio go back to the 1800s; the "Minerva Monster" made headlines in 1978
summary: Ohio's own Bigfoot, named for the flattened grass nests it is said to build.
body: The Grassman is Ohio's regional name for Bigfoot: a tall, dark, hair-covered biped reported in the wooded hills and old strip-mine country of the eastern half of the state. The name comes from lean-tos and beds of flattened grass and bent saplings that some witnesses say they found near sightings.

The best-known case came in August 1978, when a family living near a gravel pit outside Minerva, in Stark County, said a large hairy creature kept returning to their property at night and stared in through a window. Deputies investigated, footprints were reported, and the press dubbed it the Minerva Monster. Some locals suspected a publicity stunt; the family stood by their story.
Since the 1980s Salt Fork State Park near Cambridge has become Ohio's hotspot, with dozens of reports, an annual Bigfoot conference and regular night hikes run by researchers.
signs: Nests or lean-tos of bent saplings and flattened grass
Dark hair, 7 ft or taller, walking upright
Rock throwing and wood knocks near campsites
A rotten, musky smell
Large footprints in creek mud
habitat: Hilly hardwood forest, reclaimed strip mines and state parks

famous.name: Salt Fork reports begin to pile up
famous.place: Salt Fork State Park, Guernsey County, Ohio

name: Mogollon Monster
region: Along the Mogollon Rim of central and eastern Arizona, from Prescott to Alpine
first: An 1903 Arizona Republican story described a wild hairy man near the Grand Canyon
summary: Arizona's red-eyed, foul-smelling wild man of the pine country.
body: The Mogollon Monster is Arizona's Bigfoot, said to roam the ponderosa pine forests along the Mogollon Rim, a 200-mile escarpment that cuts across the middle of the state. Witnesses describe a creature over 7 feet tall with black or reddish-brown hair, glowing red eyes and a smell compared to dead fish, skunk and snapping turtle all at once.

A 1903 story in The Arizona Republican told of a hairy, clawed wild man near the Grand Canyon who screamed at the witness. Cryptozoologist Don Davis said he saw a huge, square-faced creature as a Boy Scout near Payson in the 1940s, and residents of Whiteriver and the Fort Apache reservation have reported sightings in more recent decades.
Campfire tellings add that it mimics birds and coyotes, whistles, throws stones from cover and builds nests of pine needles.
signs: Red or glowing eyes
Long black or reddish hair
A blood-curdling, woman-like scream
Whistles and animal mimicry
Rocks thrown from hiding
Footprints up to 22 inches long
habitat: High pine forest along the Mogollon Rim

name: Old Yellow Top
region: Around the mining town of Cobalt, northern Ontario
first: September 1906, near Cobalt, Ontario
summary: A Bigfoot with a pale blond mane, reported around Ontario's silver mines.
body: Old Yellow Top is the nickname for a sasquatch-like creature reported around Cobalt, a silver-mining town in northern Ontario. What set it apart was a light-coloured, shaggy mane over a dark body, which gave the creature its name.

The first reports date to 1906, during Cobalt's silver rush, and local accounts tell of prospectors in the 1920s who saw a hairy creature feeding in a blueberry patch before it ran off. Sightings were claimed on and off for more than sixty years, making it one of Canada's longest-running regional Bigfoot stories.
signs: A light yellow or blond mane on a dark body
Upright walk, sometimes with a limp
Seen near mine workings and berry patches
habitat: Boreal forest and old mine country

name: Minnesota Iceman
region: Toured US and Canadian fairs; now in Austin, Texas
first: Exhibited from the late 1960s by showman Frank Hansen
summary: A hairy 'missing link' frozen in a block of ice, shown at fairs in the 1960s.
body: The Minnesota Iceman was a carnival exhibit: a hairy, man-like body about 6 feet tall, frozen inside a block of ice in a refrigerated coffin. Showman Frank Hansen toured it around shopping malls and state fairs, hinting it had been found in Siberian ice.

In 1968 naturalist Ivan Sanderson and Belgian zoologist Bernard Heuvelmans examined it through the ice and announced it could be a real, recently killed hominid. The Smithsonian's John Napier looked into it and concluded it was a latex model. Hansen then swapped in what he called a substitute, which muddied the story further.
The figure was sold on eBay in 2013 and now sits in the Museum of the Weird in Austin, Texas, where people can still argue about it in person.
signs: A hairy body frozen in ice
One arm bent over the head
An eye apparently knocked out

famous.name: Sold on eBay to the Museum of the Weird

name: Big Grey Man of Ben Macdui
region: Summit and passes of Ben Macdui, Cairngorms, Scotland
first: Professor J. Norman Collie described his 1891 experience in an 1925 speech
summary: Footsteps in the mist and a towering grey figure on Scotland's second-highest peak.
body: The Big Grey Man, Am Fear Liath Mòr in Gaelic, is said to haunt the summit plateau of Ben Macdui in the Cairngorms. Very few people claim to have seen it clearly. Most describe crunching footsteps in the fog, each step far longer than their own, followed by an overwhelming urge to run.

In 1925 the respected mountaineer and chemist J. Norman Collie told a Cairngorm Club dinner that he had fled the summit in 1891 after hearing giant footsteps behind him in the mist. Other climbers then came forward. Those who say they glimpsed it describe a figure over 10 feet tall, with long arms and broad shoulders.
Skeptics point to the Brocken spectre, where a climber's own shadow is thrown huge onto cloud, plus exhaustion and altitude. Hill walkers still trade Greyman stories in the bothies.
signs: Heavy footsteps in fog, too far apart to be human
A sudden feeling of dread or panic
A huge grey shape in the mist
Strange high singing notes

name: Hibagon
region: Around Mount Hiba, Hiroshima Prefecture, Japan
first: A run of sightings starting in 1970
summary: Japan's ape-man of Mount Hiba, reported in the early 1970s.
body: The Hibagon is a gorilla-like creature reported around Mount Hiba in the mountains of northern Hiroshima Prefecture. Witnesses in the early 1970s described an animal about 5 feet tall with dark bristly hair, a large nose, deep glaring eyes and pale hands and feet.

The sightings drew national press. The town of Saijo set up a Hibagon office to log reports, and local Boy Scouts said they found footprints about 10 inches long. Reports faded by the mid-1970s, but the Hibagon became a local mascot and still appears on signs and souvenirs.
signs: Dark hair with pale hands and feet
Gorilla-like face with deep-set eyes
Footprints about 10 inches long
Shy; flees from people

name: Bukit Timah Monkey Man
region: Bukit Timah Nature Reserve, Singapore
first: Said to date to a Malay elder's report around 1805
summary: A grey, upright 'monkey man' said to live in Singapore's last big forest.
body: The Bukit Timah Monkey Man is a hominid said to live in the Bukit Timah Nature Reserve, a patch of primary rainforest in the middle of Singapore. It is described as grey, about 5 ft 9 in tall, with a monkey's face and a man's upright walk.

Folklore traces the first report to around 1805. Japanese soldiers are said to have reported it during World War II, and The New Paper ran a series of sightings in 2007. A night hiker's report in late 2020 sent the story around local media again.
Reserve staff have pointed to long-tailed macaques, which are common on the hill, though they are far smaller than the creature people describe.
signs: Grey hair and a monkey-like face
Walking upright on two legs
Seen after dark on forest trails

name: Beast of Bray Road
region: Bray Road and the farmland around Elkhorn, Walworth County, Wisconsin
first: Reports from 1989 on; reported in the press in December 1991
summary: A wolf-headed creature seen kneeling by a Wisconsin farm road.
body: The Beast of Bray Road is a wolf-like creature reported along a quiet farm road outside Elkhorn, Wisconsin. Witnesses describe something 6 to 7 feet tall, covered in fur, with a wolf's head, pointed ears and glowing eyes, seen both on all fours and standing upright.

In late 1989 Lori Endrizzi said she saw it crouched by the roadside holding roadkill like a person would. On Halloween night 1991, teenager Doristine Gipson said she hit something on Bray Road and was chased back to her car. Reporter Linda Godfrey began covering the reports for the Walworth County Week that December, and her later books helped spark the wider Dogman craze.
Skeptics suggest wolves, large dogs or a bear with mange. Reports of an upright hairy creature in Walworth County still turn up now and then.
signs: Wolf head with pointed ears on a broad, man-like body
Kneeling or squatting while eating roadkill
Glowing yellow-orange eyes
Switching from four legs to two
Claw marks on cars

famous.name: Godfrey's book The Beast of Bray Road

name: Black Shuck
region: Coast and countryside of Norfolk, Suffolk, Essex and the Cambridgeshire Fens, England
first: The Bungay and Blythburgh church attacks of 4 August 1577
summary: East Anglia's huge, fiery-eyed phantom dog.
body: Black Shuck is the giant black dog of East Anglian folklore, said to pad silently along dark lanes, coast paths and churchyards. Descriptions run from a big shaggy hound to something the size of a calf, often with blazing red eyes, sometimes a single eye in the middle of its head. Meeting it was said to foretell a death, though some stories make it a protective companion.

Its most famous night was 4 August 1577. During a violent thunderstorm, a black dog was said to burst into St Mary's Church in Bungay, killing two worshippers, and then into Holy Trinity Church at Blythburgh, where scorch marks on the north door are still called the devil's fingerprints. Abraham Fleming's pamphlet A Straunge and Terrible Wunder spread the story.
Black dogs appear all over Britain under other names: the Barghest of Yorkshire, the Gurt Dog of Somerset and the Church Grim. Shuck sightings are still reported on the Norfolk and Suffolk coast.
signs: A huge black dog that makes no sound as it walks
Red or fiery eyes, sometimes just one
Seen on coast paths, crossroads and churchyards
Appearing during storms

name: Beast of Gévaudan
region: Former province of Gévaudan (Lozère and Haute-Loire), south-central France
first: 30 June 1764, when 14-year-old Jeanne Boulet was killed near Langogne
summary: A man-eating beast that terrorised rural France for three years in the 1760s.
body: Between 1764 and 1767, something killed and partly ate dozens of people, mostly women and children tending livestock, in the Margeride mountains of south-central France. Witnesses described a wolf-like animal the size of a calf, reddish with a dark stripe down its back, a broad chest and a long tufted tail. It was said to bound across fields at its victims.

King Louis XV sent professional hunters and dragoons. In September 1765 the royal gun-bearer François Antoine shot a very large wolf, which was stuffed and taken to Versailles, but the killings resumed. On 19 June 1767 local hunter Jean Chastel shot another large canine, and the attacks stopped.
One study counted about 210 attacks and 113 deaths. Theories range from one or more large wolves to wolf-dog hybrids, an escaped hyena or a lion. The case is still argued over in France.
signs: A wolf-like animal the size of a calf
Reddish coat with a dark stripe down the back
A long tail ending in a tuft
Attacks aimed at the head and throat

famous.name: François Antoine shoots a large wolf

name: Thylacine sightings
region: Western and northern Tasmania; mainland reports from southern Victoria
first: The last known thylacine died at Hobart Zoo on 7 September 1936
summary: A striped marsupial 'tiger' declared extinct, but still reported in the Tasmanian bush.
body: The thylacine was a real animal: a dog-sized marsupial predator with a stiff tail, a huge gape and dark stripes across its lower back. Hunted with government bounties, it was declared extinct after the last known one died at Hobart's Beaumaris Zoo in 1936.

Sightings never stopped. In 1982 Parks and Wildlife ranger Hans Naarding said he watched one in his spotlight for several minutes in north-west Tasmania, which set off a quiet two-year government search. Ted Turner offered a reward in 1983, The Bulletin offered A$1.25 million in 2005, and trail-camera searches continue today.

Hundreds of reports have been logged since 1936, and a 2023 study argued the species may have lingered into the late 20th century. Most scientists remain unconvinced, but few extinct animals have been searched for this hard.
signs: Dark stripes across the back and rump
A thick, stiff tail held straight out
A stiff, awkward gait
A coughing bark or yap
An enormous yawning gape
size: About 1 m long plus tail, 15 to 30 kg
habitat: Eucalyptus forest, button-grass plains and coastal heath

name: Shunka Warak'in
region: Madison Valley, Montana; mount displayed in Ennis
first: Shot by settler Israel Ammon Hutchins in 1886
summary: A strange wolf-like animal shot in 1886, whose stuffed body still exists.
body: In 1886 Montana settler Israel Ammon Hutchins shot a dark, wolf-like animal that had been prowling around his ranch. It had a sloping back and high shoulders like a hyena. Taxidermist Joseph Sherwood mounted it, named it a ringdocus, and showed it for decades in his store and museum near Henry's Lake, Idaho, until it disappeared from view around 1980.

Hutchins' grandson Jack Kirby tracked the mount down at the Idaho Museum of Natural History in 2007, and it was put on display at the Madison Valley History Museum in Ennis, Montana. Cryptozoologist Loren Coleman linked it to shunka warak'in, an Ioway name usually translated as 'carries off dogs'. Others say that link is a stretch. The animal has never been DNA tested.
signs: A wolf-like animal with a hyena-like sloping back
Dark coat and high shoulders
Prowling near ranches at night

name: Beast of Bodmin Moor
region: Bodmin Moor, Cornwall, England
first: Livestock killings and sightings from 1983
summary: A black panther-like cat blamed for killing sheep on a Cornish moor.
body: The Beast of Bodmin is a large black cat, often described as panther-sized with yellow-green eyes, reported on and around Bodmin Moor in Cornwall since the early 1980s. Farmers blamed it for mauled sheep and calves, and dozens of witnesses reported a big cat crossing roads and fields.

In 1995 the Ministry of Agriculture investigated and concluded there was no verifiable evidence of a big cat, though it could not rule one out. Days later a boy found a leopard skull on the bank of the River Fowey. The Natural History Museum confirmed it was a leopard, but it had been cut from a leopard-skin rug.

Britain's 1976 Dangerous Wild Animals Act made exotic pets expensive to keep, and some owners are thought to have released pumas and leopards. Big cat sightings are reported all over the UK every year.
signs: A long, low black cat much bigger than a house cat
A long curved tail
Sheep killed with throat bites or stripped carcasses
Large rounded paw prints without claw marks
habitat: Open moorland, wooded valleys and farmland

famous.name: Leopard skull found in the River Fowey

name: Beast of Exmoor
region: Exmoor, on the Devon and Somerset border, England
first: Spring 1983, when a South Molton farmer lost dozens of sheep
summary: The big cat that sent Royal Marines snipers onto the moors in 1983.
body: The Beast of Exmoor is a black or tawny big cat reported on Exmoor since the 1970s. It became national news in 1983 when South Molton farmer Eric Ley said he had lost over 100 sheep in three months, all killed with savage throat wounds.
The government took the unusual step of sending Royal Marines snipers to watch the moor. They never got a clear shot, and no cat was ever found.
Sightings continue, and several big cats, including a puma caught in Scotland in 1980, have proven that exotic cats have lived wild in Britain.
signs: A powerful black or tawny cat
Sheep killed by throat bites
Seen at dusk crossing lanes

famous.name: Sheep killings and Royal Marines hunt

name: Beast of Bladenboro
region: Bladenboro and Clarkton, Bladen County, North Carolina
first: 29 December 1953, when a dog was killed near Clarkton
summary: A dog-killing 'vampire beast' that drew hundreds of armed hunters in 1954.
body: Over the winter of 1953 to 1954, something killed dogs and other animals around Bladenboro, a small mill town in North Carolina. Victims were found crushed, with jaws broken and, according to reports, hardly any blood left in them. Newspapers called it the Vampire Beast.

Witnesses described a sleek black animal about 5 feet long with a cat-like face. By early January hundreds of hunters with guns and dogs were roaming the swamps, and the town became a national story. A bobcat was shot and displayed as the culprit, though many locals doubted it.
Bladenboro now holds an annual Beast Fest each fall.
signs: Dogs killed with crushed heads and broken jaws
Carcasses said to be drained of blood
A sleek black cat-like animal about 5 ft long
A scream like a woman or a baby

name: Mngwa
region: Coastal forests of Tanzania
first: Described by colonial officer William Hichens in a 1937 article
summary: A grey, donkey-sized cat said to stalk villages on the Tanzanian coast.
body: The mngwa, Swahili for 'the strange one', is a big cat reported in the coastal forests of Tanzania. It is described as larger than a leopard, as big as a donkey, with grey brindled fur, and it is blamed for night attacks in fishing villages.

British administrator William Hichens wrote about local accounts of the mngwa in 1937, and hunter Patrick Bowen later said he tracked one that had carried off a boy, following prints shaped like a leopard's but as big as a lion's. The same name, nunda, belongs to a giant cat in Swahili folktales. Zoologists suggest unusually large or oddly coloured leopards or lions.
signs: A grey, brindled cat bigger than a leopard
Leopard-shaped prints as big as a lion's
Night attacks on villages

name: Nandi bear
region: Nandi Hills and western Kenya
first: Colonial-era reports from the early 1900s
summary: A ferocious, hyena-shaped 'bear' reported in western Kenya, where no bears live.
body: The Nandi bear is named after the Nandi people of western Kenya, who call it kerit or chemosit. It is described as a powerful carnivore with high shoulders over 4 feet tall, a sloping back like a hyena, and reddish or dark shaggy fur. It is said to attack at night and to go for the head.

Settlers and officers sent in reports in the early 20th century. Charles Hobley published a drawing of a footprint in 1914, and the paleontologist Louis Leakey once wondered whether it could be a surviving chalicothere, an extinct clawed relative of horses. Most zoologists think the stories mix up spotted hyenas, honey badgers and baboons. Reports dropped off as the forests were cleared.
signs: High shoulders and a sloping, hyena-like back
Shaggy reddish or dark fur
Stands up on its hind legs
Night attacks aimed at the head

name: Ozark Howler
region: Ozark Mountains of northern Arkansas, southern Missouri and north-east Oklahoma
first: Mostly 20th-century reports; some tie it to tales from Daniel Boone's day
summary: A bear-sized, horned black cat with a howl that shakes the hollows.
body: The Ozark Howler is a large, dark, shaggy animal said to roam the hills of the Ozarks. Descriptions vary: some say it is bear-shaped, others say it is cat-like with horns on its head, and almost all mention glowing eyes and a terrible howl that mixes a wolf's call with a laugh or an elk's bugle.

In 2014 an emergency call to the Arkansas Game and Fish Commission reported a bear-sized, grey, fast-running animal on a road near Springdale. A year later a TV station received photos claimed to show the Howler, which the commission dismissed as fake.
signs: A deep, eerie howl or laughing call
Glowing red or yellow eyes
Shaggy black or grey fur
Horns or tufted ears on the head

famous.name: Photo hoax sent to TV station

name: Batsquatch
region: Pierce County and the Cascades of Washington state
first: April 1994, near Buckley, Washington
summary: A purple-blue, bat-winged ape that landed in front of a stalled truck.
body: Batsquatch is a hairy, ape-like creature with huge leathery wings, reported in the Washington Cascades. The story starts in April 1994, when 18-year-old Brian Canfield said his truck stalled in Pierce County and a nine-foot creature with bluish fur, a wolf-like face, yellow eyes and bat wings landed on the road in front of him before flying off toward Mount Rainier.

The account ran in the Tacoma News Tribune, and the reporter said Canfield seemed sincere. A few later reports followed, including a pilot who said he saw something similar. The creature is now tied to Mount St. Helens in popular telling, though the original report was nearer Rainier.
signs: Huge leathery bat wings on an ape-like body
Blue or purple-tinged fur
Yellow or red eyes
Vehicles stalling nearby

name: Snallygaster
region: Frederick and Washington counties, Maryland; South Mountain and the Middletown Valley
first: Tales among German settlers from the 1730s; newspaper wave in 1909
summary: Maryland's beaked, tentacled dragon from German settler folklore.
body: The snallygaster comes from the folklore of German immigrants who settled around Frederick, Maryland in the 18th century. Their schneller Geist, or 'quick ghost', was half bird and half reptile, with a metal-like beak full of teeth, and in some versions octopus-like tentacles. It swooped from the sky to carry off people and livestock. Seven-pointed stars painted on barns were said to keep it away.

In February and March 1909 the Middletown Valley Register ran reports of a winged beast with a long beak, hooked claws and one eye in the middle of its forehead, screeching like a train whistle. The story spread nationwide, and the Smithsonian was said to have offered a reward for its hide. It was later revealed as a circulation stunt by the paper's editor and a reporter. A 1932 wave had it dying in a vat of moonshine.
signs: Huge wings and a long hooked beak
A single eye in the forehead
A scream like a locomotive whistle
Seven-pointed hex stars on barns
size: Huge, with a wingspan of many feet (reported)

name: Van Meter Visitor
region: Van Meter, Dallas County, Iowa
first: Late September 1903; first in print in the Des Moines Daily News on 4 October 1903
summary: A bat-winged creature with a glowing horn that visited an Iowa town for five nights in 1903.
body: For several nights in late September and early October 1903, residents of the small town of Van Meter, Iowa reported a huge winged creature, half human and half animal, with bat-like wings and a single blunt horn on its forehead that shone a beam of light.

A farm implement salesman saw the light first on a rooftop. The town doctor said he saw it outside his office window, and a bank cashier fired at it through the bank's front window, leaving only three-toed tracks. Witnesses said bullets did nothing to it. Accounts say townspeople finally drove it and a smaller companion back into an old mine.
Van Meter now holds a Visitor festival each autumn.
signs: Bat-like wings on a part-human body
A single horn that shines a bright beam of light
Three-toed tracks
A strong sulfur smell
Unharmed by gunfire
habitat: Small-town rooftops and an old mine

name: Ahool
region: Mount Salak and the rainforests of western Java, Indonesia
first: Naturalist Ernst Bartels said he saw one on Mount Salak in 1925
summary: A giant bat of Java with a monkey-like face and a 10-foot wingspan.
body: The ahool is a giant bat said to live in the rainforest of western Java. It is named for its call, a long 'a-hoool'. Witnesses describe a grey, furry flier with a wingspan of about 10 feet, a flat monkey-like face, big dark eyes and clawed forearms.

Naturalist Ernst Bartels said one flew right over him while he was exploring Mount Salak in 1925, and that he heard the call again from his home two years later. Ivan Sanderson thought it was an unknown species of bat. Bartels himself later wondered if it might be a large owl. Fruit bats in the region are big, but none come close to the size claimed.
signs: A loud "a-hoool" call at night
A 10-ft wingspan
A monkey-like face and grey fur
Seen skimming over rivers

name: Ropen
region: Umboi Island and nearby islands, Papua New Guinea
first: Local stories; Western expeditions from 1994
summary: A glowing, pterosaur-like flier said to cross the night skies of Papua New Guinea.
body: The ropen is a flying creature from the folklore of Umboi Island and neighbouring islands in Papua New Guinea. It is described as featherless, with leathery wings, a long tail ending in a diamond-shaped flap, and, most strikingly, a body that glows at night.

Since the 1990s a handful of American expeditions, several of them driven by young-earth creationists hoping to find a living pterosaur, have travelled to Umboi to interview witnesses. They reported distant glowing lights but brought back no clear photographs. Scientists point to large fruit bats and frigatebirds, and to bioluminescent fungi or meteors for the lights.
signs: A slow-moving glowing light at night
Leathery wings and a long tail with a flap at the end
Seen over reefs and grave sites

name: Big Bird of the Rio Grande Valley
region: Lower Rio Grande Valley, Texas: Harlingen, Brownsville, Raymondville and San Benito
first: Reports from late December 1975
summary: A flap of giant bird sightings in South Texas in the winter of 1976.
body: Over a few weeks around New Year 1976, people across the Lower Rio Grande Valley in South Texas reported an enormous bird or bat-like flier. Two girls in Harlingen saw a dark bird with a gorilla-like face on New Year's Day, and their family found three-toed tracks.

On 7 January a Brownsville man said something slammed into his trailer home. On 14 January Armando Grimaldo of Raymondville said a creature with a monkey-like face and leathery skin swooped on him in his yard and tore his shirt. A $1,000 reward was offered for its capture. Some sightings were later traced to herons and pelicans, but the flap is still a Valley legend.
signs: A huge dark bird or bat with a wingspan of 10 to 15 ft
A bald, gorilla- or monkey-like face
Three-toed tracks
Attacks from above

name: La Lechuza
region: South Texas and northern Mexico
first: A long-told Mexican and Tejano legend
summary: A witch who turns into a huge owl with a woman's face, from Texas-Mexican folklore.
body: La Lechuza is a figure from Mexican and Tejano folklore: a witch, or a wronged woman, who takes the shape of a huge barn owl, sometimes with the face of an old woman. She is said to perch on rooftops and trees at night, and her whistle or cry is taken as a warning of death or bad luck. Parents in the Rio Grande Valley have long warned children that she snatches kids who stay out late.

Stories say salt, a prayer or a rosary can drive her off, and that a wounded lechuza turns back into a woman with matching wounds. Modern reports from South Texas describe an owl far too large to be real. The legend often blends with the 1976 Big Bird sightings in the same region.
signs: An owl far larger than any real owl
A woman's face on an owl's body
Whistling or a crying baby sound at night
Perching on rooftops

famous.name: Big Bird flap revives the legend

name: Altamaha-ha
region: Mouth of the Altamaha River and the creeks around Darien, McIntosh County, Georgia
first: A local legend; boaters and fishermen have reported it for decades
summary: A long, snouted river monster of coastal Georgia's tidal creeks.
body: Altie is said to live where the Altamaha River spreads into marsh, old rice fields and tidal creeks near Darien on the Georgia coast. Witnesses describe a dark animal 20 to 30 feet long with a long snout, a ridged back and flippers, that swims with up-and-down humps rather than side to side.

The Brunswick News has traced the legend back to Muscogee tradition. Fishermen and boaters have reported it for decades. In 2018 a strange carcass on a beach in the Wolf Island refuge looked like the Altie of local drawings, until performance artist Zardulu said she had built it from a stuffed shark and papier-mâché.
Many think Altie is a very large sturgeon or alligator gar, both of which live in the river. A sculpture of the creature stands at the Darien welcome center.
signs: A long snout like a sturgeon or crocodile
Bony plates or ridges along the back
Up-and-down humps as it swims
Seen in tidal creeks at dawn or dusk
habitat: Brackish river mouth, marsh and tidal creeks

name: Tahoe Tessie
region: Lake Tahoe, on the California and Nevada border
first: A serpent reported by San Francisco visitor I.C. Coggin in 1865
summary: The cold, very deep lake on the California-Nevada line has its own Nessie.
body: Lake Tahoe is over 1,600 feet deep and famously clear, and since the 1800s some visitors have claimed something big swims in it. Tessie is usually described as a dark, humped, serpent-like animal leaving a wake, or a shape moving under the surface.

A San Francisco visitor named I.C. Coggin reported a vast serpent in 1865. In the 1980s hikers, an optician and local police described a dark creature as big as a rowboat. A TV station owner, Mike Conway, said children shouted 'It's Tessie!' during a commercial shoot at Zephyr Cove, though his footage was lost. In 2005 a former sheriff's officer described a big V-shaped wake on calm water.

Stories of water spirits around Cave Rock belong to the Washoe people, who have lived at the lake for thousands of years, but the Tessie legend itself is modern. Large lake trout and sturgeon are the usual suspects.
signs: A V-shaped wake on calm water
A dark humped back
A large shape moving beneath the clear surface

name: Chessie
region: Chesapeake Bay and its rivers, Maryland and Virginia
first: Claims from 1936; a 1943 sighting by perch fishermen near Baltimore
summary: A snake-like sea serpent said to wind through the Chesapeake Bay.
body: Chessie is a long, dark, snake-like animal said to live in the Chesapeake Bay. Witnesses usually describe a body 25 to 40 feet long and about a foot thick, with a football-shaped head and humps that roll along the surface.

In 1943 two fishermen near Baltimore said a black creature about 12 feet long, with a head like a horse, turned its head almost all the way round to look at them. Sightings peaked in the late 1970s and early 1980s. In 1982 Robert and Karen Frew filmed a brown, snake-like shape moving near Kent Island, and Smithsonian scientists who reviewed it could not say what it was.
Some sightings have been traced to manatees, which wander north into the bay in summer. Chessie later became a mascot for keeping the bay clean.
signs: A long, thin, dark body with several humps
A football- or horse-shaped head
Side-to-side serpentine swimming
Seen near the bay shore in summer

name: White River Monster
region: White River near Newport, Jackson County, Arkansas
first: A plantation owner reported it on 1 July 1915
summary: A grey, boxcar-sized river monster so beloved Arkansas gave it a legal refuge.
body: Whitey is a huge grey animal reported in the White River near Newport, Arkansas. In July 1915 a plantation owner described it as wide as a car and three cars long. In 1937 plantation owner Bramlett Bateman said it had skin like an elephant and a face like a catfish, and lay lolling on the surface. Crowds came with cameras, and plans to net it or blast it with dynamite fell through.

In 1971 the creature was back. Witnesses described a peeling grey animal the size of a boxcar with a bony spike on its forehead, making a sound like a cow crossed with a horse, and 14-inch three-toed tracks were found on Towhead Island.
In 1973 the Arkansas legislature created the White River Monster Refuge, where it is illegal to harm the creature. A lost elephant seal or a giant catfish are the favourite explanations.
signs: A huge grey back like an overturned boat
Skin that looks like it is peeling
A bony spike on the forehead
A noise like a cow and a horse mixed
Three-toed tracks on sandbars

name: Memphré
region: Lake Memphremagog, between Magog, Quebec and Newport, Vermont
first: Reports stretch back to the 1800s
summary: The cross-border lake monster of Quebec and Vermont, honoured on a Canadian coin.
body: Memphré is said to live in Lake Memphremagog, a long, deep glacial lake that crosses the border between Quebec and Vermont. It is usually described much like Nessie: a long-necked, humped animal with dark skin.

Local historian Jacques Boisvert founded the International Dracontology Society of Lake Memphremagog in 1986 to collect and study sightings. In 2011 the Royal Canadian Mint put Memphré on a coloured 25-cent coin.
signs: A long neck and small head
Dark humps on calm water
Seen near the deepest stretch of the lake

name: Igopogo
region: Lake Simcoe, Ontario
first: Settler David Soules in 1823
summary: A seal-faced lake animal said to live in Ontario's Lake Simcoe.
body: Igopogo, named as a play on BC's Ogopogo, is said to live in Lake Simcoe north of Toronto. Most witnesses describe a grey, seal-like animal with a dog- or horse-like face, a neck like a stovepipe and dorsal fins, rather than a long-necked dinosaur.

Settler David Soules is credited with the first report in 1823. In 1952 several people, including Georgina Island First Nation chief Wellington Charles, said they saw it. A sonar operator recorded a large target in 1983, and a 1991 video showed a large seal-like animal. Barrie has a sea serpent sculpture on its waterfront.
Some suggest seals or otters, though neither normally lives in the lake.
signs: A grey, seal-like head with a dog-like face
A neck like a stovepipe
Dorsal fins
Seen near Kempenfelt Bay and Beaverton

name: Manipogo
region: Lake Manitoba, Lake Winnipegosis and Lake Winnipeg, Manitoba
first: Fur trader Valentine McKay in September 1909
summary: Manitoba's humped lake serpent, with its own provincial park and festival.
body: Manipogo is a serpent-like animal said to live in Lake Manitoba, with relatives reported in connected lakes. Witnesses describe a brownish-black body 13 to 50 feet long with at least one hump, and a head like a horse, sheep or camel. Some say it lets out a loud cry as it surfaces.

Hudson's Bay Company trader Valentine McKay made the first settler report in 1909. A wave of sightings in 1960 gave it its name, coined by land inspector Tom Locke, who also named Manipogo Provincial Park. In 1962 fishermen Richard Vincent and John Konefell took the only known photograph of it, showing a dark, snake-like shape. First Nations stories of serpents in the lake are much older.
Skeptics suggest swimming moose, sturgeon, otters or floating logs. St. Laurent holds a Manipogo festival every March.
signs: Brownish-black humps on the surface
A flat or horse-like head
A loud cry when it surfaces

famous.name: Name coined after a wave of sightings

name: Lagarfljót Worm
region: Lagarfljót, by Egilsstaðir, east Iceland
first: A "marvel" in the lake recorded in Icelandic annals for 1345
summary: Iceland's many-humped lake serpent, filmed in a viral 2012 video.
body: The Lagarfljót worm is a serpent said to live in Lagarfljót, a long, silty glacial lake in east Iceland. It is a 'many humps' monster, said to be longer than a bus, and in some tales it coils up on the shore.

Icelandic annals record a strange sight in the lake in 1345, and the worm appears on 16th-century maps. A folk tale says it began as a small worm a girl put on a gold ring to make the gold grow, and both grew enormous. In 1963 the head of Iceland's forestry service reported a sighting, and in 1983 contractors said a new phone cable laid across the lake bed was found torn in many places.

In February 2012 a farmer filmed a long shape moving in the icy river, and the video went viral around the world. A local committee later debated whether it showed the worm. Skeptics say it is ice or a fishing net.
signs: Several humps moving in a line
A body longer than a bus
Something coiled on the shore

famous.name: Annals record a marvel in the lake

name: Storsjöodjuret
region: Lake Storsjön, Jämtland, central Sweden
first: First described in a 1635 manuscript
summary: Sweden's lake monster, with a dog- or cat-like head and a protected status.
body: Storsjöodjuret, or Storsie, is said to live in Storsjön, a deep lake in Jämtland in central Sweden. Witnesses describe a dark, serpentine body with humps and a head like a dog or a cat, sometimes with ears or fins.

A 1635 manuscript tells how a rune master bound a sea serpent to the lake bottom with a spell carved on the Frösö Runestone. Hundreds of sightings have been reported since the 1800s. In 1894 a company backed by King Oscar II tried to catch it with giant hooks and failed, and the traps are now in the local museum. From 1986 to 2005 the monster was even listed as a protected animal by the county.
In 2008 a film crew claimed an underwater camera recorded a warm-bodied mass in the lake.
signs: A dog- or cat-like head with ears
A long dark body with humps
A large wake near Frösön island

name: Nahuelito
region: Nahuel Huapi Lake, near San Carlos de Bariloche, Patagonia, Argentina
first: Reports collected by Buenos Aires Zoo director Clemente Onelli from 1897
summary: A plesiosaur-shaped lake monster in the Andes of Patagonia.
body: Nahuelito is said to live in Nahuel Huapi, a huge glacial lake in the Andean foothills of northern Patagonia. It has been described as a giant serpent, a large hump, or a long-necked plesiosaur.

In 1922 George Garret told a Toronto newspaper he had seen a creature in the lake in 1910, with 5 to 7 metres visible above the water. Buenos Aires Zoo director Clemente Onelli then launched an expedition to look for a living plesiosaur in Patagonia, which found nothing. In 1988 a regional newspaper magazine published close-up photos of a hump near Bariloche, sent in anonymously.
Stories of water creatures in the lake predate European settlement.
signs: A long neck or a large dark hump
Turbulent water on a still day
Seen near Bariloche and the lake islands
habitat: Deep glacial lake in the Andes

name: Morag
region: Loch Morar, Lochaber, western Scottish Highlands
first: Reports date back to 1887
summary: Nessie's less famous neighbour, in Britain's deepest freshwater loch.
body: Morag is said to live in Loch Morar, the deepest body of fresh water in the British Isles at over 1,000 feet. After Nessie it is the most written-about Scottish loch monster. Its name is a pun on the loch, and older tradition held that it surfaced before a death in the local MacDonell clan.

Reports go back to 1887, and by 1981 researchers had logged 34, sixteen with several witnesses. The most famous came in August 1969, when Duncan McDonell and William Simpson said their boat struck a brown creature 25 to 30 feet long with three humps. McDonell fended it off with an oar, Simpson fired a rifle at it, and it sank out of sight.
signs: Brown, rough skin and several humps
A snake-like head held above the water
A large wake on a calm loch

name: Lake Tianchi Monster
region: Heaven Lake, in the crater of Changbai (Paektu) Mountain on the China and North Korea border
first: A report of a buffalo-like beast in 1903
summary: Seal-like creatures reported in a volcanic crater lake on the China-North Korea border.
body: Heaven Lake fills the crater of a volcano on the border between China's Jilin Province and North Korea. It is cold, deep and high, yet visitors have reported large animals swimming in it for over a century.

The first report, in 1903, described a buffalo-like creature. In August 1962 a man with a telescope said he watched two chasing each other. More recent descriptions mention a human-like head on a long neck with a white ring around it. In September 2007 a Chinese TV reporter said he filmed six seal-like creatures with long fins swimming in pairs for over an hour.
Scientists doubt anything large could live in the lake. Skeptics suggest floating volcanic rock or swimming bears.
signs: A seal-like head with a white ring around the neck
Several animals swimming together
Long fins or flippers

name: Kappa
region: Rivers, ponds and marshes across Japan
first: A yokai of Japanese folklore, common in Edo-period writings
summary: A turtle-shelled river imp from Japanese folklore with a water-filled dish on its head.
body: The kappa is one of Japan's best-known yokai, a child-sized river creature with green or yellow-green skin, a turtle-like shell, webbed hands, a beak and a dish-shaped hollow on top of its head that holds water. As long as the dish stays full, it is very strong.

Kappa are blamed for drownings and for dragging horses and swimmers into rivers, but they are also polite, love cucumbers and sumo wrestling, and keep their promises. The trick in many stories is to bow: the kappa bows back, spills the water from its dish and loses its strength.
Temples and families around Japan keep so-called mummified kappa hands and bodies. Tōno in Iwate has a famous Kappa-buchi pool, and signs warning about kappa still stand by some rivers.
signs: A child-sized green figure by a river
A shell on its back and a beak
A bowl-shaped dent on top of the head
Cucumbers left as offerings
size: About the size of a child

famous.name: Tōno Monogatari folk tales, including kappa

name: Ningen
region: Antarctic and South Atlantic waters
first: An internet legend from Japanese 2channel posts in the mid-2000s
summary: A ghostly white, whale-sized humanoid said to surface in Antarctic seas.
body: The Ningen, Japanese for 'human', is a modern legend of a huge, pale white creature with a human-like body, arms and sometimes legs or a tail, said to be seen by whaling and research crews in the Southern Ocean. It is described as tens of feet long and smooth-skinned, with small eyes and a slit mouth.

The story spread on the Japanese forum 2channel in the 2000s, where posters claimed whaling crews had seen something they first mistook for a submarine. In 2007 the paranormal magazine Mu ran an article on it, including a Google Earth image off Namibia that seemed to show a white humanoid shape. Skeptics point to icebergs, whales and image glitches, and the Ningen is widely treated as an internet-born legend.
signs: A ghostly white humanoid shape in the water at night
Smooth, hairless skin
Something mistaken for a submarine

name: Emela-ntouka
region: Likouala swamps of the Republic of the Congo and nearby Central Africa
first: In print in 1954 through game inspector Lucien Blancou
summary: A one-horned, elephant-sized swamp beast said to gore elephants in the Congo.
body: The Emela-ntouka, a Lingala name often translated as 'killer of elephants', is a semi-aquatic animal said to live in the swamps of the Likouala region of the Republic of the Congo. Descriptions give it a heavy, rhino-like body the size of an elephant, short legs, a thick tail and a single long horn on its snout.

Former game inspector Lucien Blancou described it in 1954, saying it killed elephants, buffalo and hippos when disturbed, but did not eat them. Biologist Roy Mackal collected accounts on his 1980 and 1981 expeditions looking for the Mokele-mbembe and suggested it might be a surviving horned dinosaur. Most scientists suggest a misremembered rhinoceros.
signs: A single horn on the snout
A heavy, elephant-sized body
A thick crocodile-like tail
Dead elephants found with gore wounds

name: Sea serpent
region: Oceans worldwide; famous waves off Massachusetts and Norway
first: Described by Olaus Magnus in 1555; the Gloucester sightings of 1817 made it a scientific debate
summary: Long, humped serpents reported by sailors in every ocean for centuries.
body: Sea serpents are huge, snake-like animals reported at sea, usually with a horse- or turtle-like head, a long neck and a row of humps behind. Norse sailors told of them, and the Swedish bishop Olaus Magnus drew one wrapping around a ship in 1555.

In August 1817 hundreds of people watched a serpent with a turtle-like head and a humped back swimming in Gloucester Harbor in Massachusetts. Boston's Linnaean Society took sworn statements. On 6 August 1848 Captain Peter M'Quhae and officers of HMS Daedalus reported a 60-foot serpent in the South Atlantic, sparking a debate in The Times. In 1905 two naturalists aboard the yacht Valhalla described a long neck and a large fin off Brazil.
Oarfish, which can top 25 feet, basking sharks, whales and lines of porpoises are the leading explanations.
signs: A row of humps or coils on the surface
A horse- or turtle-like head on a long neck
A mane or crest behind the head
Seen from ships and headlands

name: Beast of Busco
region: Fulk Lake, Churubusco, Whitley County, Indiana
first: Farmer Oscar Fulk reported a giant turtle in 1898
summary: A 500-pound snapping turtle that set off a lake-draining hunt in 1949.
body: The Beast of Busco is a giant snapping turtle said to live in a small lake on a farm outside Churubusco, Indiana. Farmer Oscar Fulk first reported it in 1898. In July 1948 two fishermen said they saw it again, and estimated it at around 500 pounds, with a shell the size of a dining table.

When the story hit the wire services in early 1949, crowds descended on Gale Harris's farm and state police had to direct traffic. Harris tried traps, a diver, and draining the lake with pumps, but a dam broke and the water came back. The turtle, nicknamed Oscar, was never caught.
Churubusco now calls itself Turtle Town USA and holds Turtle Days each June.
signs: A shell the size of a dining table
A huge head breaking the surface
Large drag marks on the bank
size: Shell 4 to 6 ft across, about 500 lb (reported)

name: Dobhar-chú
region: Lakes of Leitrim, Sligo, Mayo and Galway, Ireland
first: Linked to a woman's death at Glenade Lough in 1722
summary: Ireland's giant 'king otter', remembered on an 18th-century gravestone.
body: The Dobhar-chú, Irish for 'water hound', is a giant otter-like creature of Irish lakes, said to be several times the size of a normal otter, with a white or dark pelt and black-tipped ears. It is fiercely territorial and is said to whistle to its mate.

Its best-known story comes from Glenade Lough in County Leitrim. In 1722 Grace Connolly went to the lake to wash clothes and was found dead with the creature lying on her. Her husband killed it, and its mate burst from the water and chased him until it too was killed. A gravestone in Conwall cemetery, said to be hers, is carved with an otter-like animal.
Sightings of large otter-like animals are still reported now and then in the lakes of the west of Ireland.
signs: An otter far larger than normal
A whistling call across the water
Black-tipped ears on a pale pelt

name: Goatman
region: Prince George's County, Maryland, especially Fletchertown Road near Bowie
first: A University of Maryland folklore project in May 1971; in the press that October
summary: A half-man, half-goat said to stalk the back roads of suburban Maryland.
body: Maryland's Goatman is a hairy, man-shaped creature with a goat's horns and legs, said to lurk in the woods of north-east Prince George's County. Stories say he attacks cars with an axe, howls at night and kills dogs.

A University of Maryland student recorded the legend for a folklore project in 1971, and that October the Prince George's County News placed the Goatman on Fletchertown Road near Bowie, linking him to the nearby Beltsville Agricultural Research Center. One popular version says he was a scientist there whose goat experiment went wrong. Another says he was a hermit who lived in the woods.
Teenagers still drive Fletchertown Road at night looking for him. Goatman stories also turn up in Kentucky, Texas and elsewhere, each with its own local twist.
signs: A man-sized figure with horns and a goat's legs
Bleating or screaming in the woods at night
Dogs found dead or missing
An axe-wielding figure near the road
habitat: Wooded back roads and old railway lines

famous.name: Newspaper places him on Fletchertown Road

name: Pope Lick Monster
region: Railroad trestle over Pope Lick Creek, Fisherville, Louisville, Kentucky
first: A long-told Louisville legend; filmed in 1988
summary: A goat-legged figure said to lure people onto a deadly railroad trestle in Louisville.
body: The Pope Lick Monster is a part-man, part-goat (some say part-sheep) creature said to live under a tall railroad trestle over Pope Lick Creek in eastern Louisville. Legends say it hypnotises people or mimics voices to draw them onto the bridge, leaps onto cars passing below, or carries a bloody axe.

Its backstory changes with the teller: a circus performer who escaped when a train derailed, or a farmer who traded goats for dark powers. Local filmmaker Ron Schildknecht made a short film about it in 1988, which upset the railroad.

The real danger is the trestle. It is an active Norfolk Southern main line with freight trains crossing every day, and several people have died or been badly hurt trying to cross it. The railroad warns trespassers will be arrested. Look from the road below, never from the bridge.
signs: A goat- or sheep-legged figure under the trestle
Voices calling from the bridge
Something dropping onto cars below
habitat: A high railroad trestle over a wooded creek

famous.name: Short film The Legend of the Pope Lick Monster

name: Lake Worth Monster
region: Lake Worth and Greer Island, Fort Worth Nature Center and Refuge, Texas
first: July 1969
summary: A furry, scaly 'goat-man' that threw a tire at a crowd in 1969.
body: In July 1969, people around Lake Worth on the edge of Fort Worth, Texas reported a 'half-man, half-goat' with fur, scales and long clawed fingers. Newspapers reported it had jumped from a tree onto a car, leaving a long scratch, and later hurled a spare tire at a group of onlookers from a bluff.

Crowds of armed sightseers came out at night. Local resident Allen Plaster took a blurry photo of a white, furry shape that he later said was probably a prank. In 2005 an anonymous letter to the Star-Telegram claimed three high school friends had staged sightings with a tinfoil mask. Some researchers still think a real animal was involved.
The Fort Worth Nature Center has held a Lake Worth Monster Bash every October since 2009.
signs: A white or grey furry figure with scales
Long claws
Objects thrown from cover
Seen near Greer Island at night

famous.name: Summer of sightings and the tire throw

name: Pukwudgie
aliases: Little wild man of the woods
region: South-eastern Massachusetts (Freetown-Fall River State Forest, the Bridgewater Triangle); also Great Lakes traditions
first: Named in print in 1839; tied to Massachusetts in local histories from 1906
summary: A knee-high forest being from Native American tradition, now part of Bridgewater Triangle lore.
body: The Pukwudgie is a small, human-like forest being from Native American tradition, about knee- to waist-high, with large ears and a grey complexion. In stories it can be mischievous or dangerous, and is said to vanish, shape-shift and lead people astray.
