Similar 'little people' appear in the traditions of many nations, including the Ojibwe, Mohegan, Mi'kmaq and Wampanoag.

The name entered print through Henry Rowe Schoolcraft's Ojibwe stories in 1839 and Longfellow's Song of Hiawatha. Local histories later tied it to Massachusetts, and Wampanoag storytellers retold it in their own way. These are living cultural traditions, and some communities prefer that their beings not be treated as monsters for entertainment, so this page sticks to modern reports.

In recent decades, hikers in Freetown-Fall River State Forest and the swampy Bridgewater Triangle have reported small grey figures, strange lights and a sense of being watched, often credited to Pukwudgies in paranormal books.
signs: A small grey figure, knee- to waist-high
Large ears and long fingers
Glowing lights in the woods
Feeling of being led off the trail
habitat: Deep forest, swamps and rocky ledges

name: Melon heads
region: Ottawa and Allegan counties, Michigan; Kirtland, Ohio; Shelton and Trumbull, Connecticut
first: Teen legend-tripping lore from the mid-20th century
summary: Small, big-headed figures said to live in the woods of Michigan, Ohio and Connecticut.
body: Melon heads are small humanoids with huge, bulbous, hairless heads, said to emerge from the woods at night. The legend turns up in three states, each with its own origin story.

In Michigan they are linked to the area around the Felt Mansion in Laketown Township and said to be children who escaped an asylum, though local historians say no such asylum existed. In Kirtland, Ohio, the story blames a sinister Dr. Crow and his experiments on orphans, and teens drive Wisner Road looking for them. In Connecticut the tales centre on Velvet Street in Trumbull and the woods of Shelton, with origins from a colonial-era family to an escaped asylum.
Folklorists note the stories borrow from real fears and prejudice about disability. They are classic legend-trip tales.
signs: Small figures with oversized bald heads
Glowing eyes along a dark road
Seen in the woods near old buildings
habitat: Woods and back roads near old estates

name: Grafton Monster
region: Riverside Drive and Route 119 along the Tygart Valley River, Grafton, West Virginia
first: 16 June 1964
summary: A tall, pale, headless-looking figure seen by a Grafton newspaperman in 1964.
body: Late on 16 June 1964, Grafton Sentinel reporter Robert Cockrell said he saw a huge, smooth, pale figure, 7 to 9 feet tall and seal-like, standing by the road along the Tygart Valley River. It seemed to have no head. Others later added that it made a strange whistling sound.

Two days later the Sentinel reported groups of teenagers combing the riverbank with flashlights and makeshift weapons. The next day the paper put it down to spring fever. The story lived on in West Virginia folklore, and Grafton launched a Grafton Monster Festival in 2024 for the 60th anniversary. It also appears in the video game Fallout 76.
signs: A tall, pale or white shape with no visible head
Smooth, seal-like skin
A whistling sound

name: Enfield Monster
region: Enfield, White County, Illinois
first: 25 April 1973
summary: A three-legged, pink-eyed creature that scratched at an Illinois front door in 1973.
body: At about 10 pm on 25 April 1973, Henry McDaniel of Enfield, Illinois heard scratching at his door. Outside, he later said, stood a greyish creature about 4.5 feet tall with three legs, a short body, two short arms and two pink eyes as big as flashlights. He fired at it, it hissed like a wildcat, and it bounded off toward the railway embankment, covering 50 feet in three jumps.

Police found odd six-padded tracks. A neighbour boy's claim that it had torn his shoes was later admitted to be a joke. McDaniel reported seeing it again on 6 May, and a radio search party said they heard something in the brush. The case later became a textbook example of how scares spread through a community.
signs: Three legs and two short arms
Large pink, glowing eyes
A wildcat-like hiss
Huge leaps
Dog-like tracks with six toe pads

name: Nain Rouge
region: Detroit, Michigan
first: In print in Marie Hamlin's Legends of Le Détroit, 1883
summary: Detroit's red imp, said to appear before every disaster to hit the city.
body: The Nain Rouge, French for 'red dwarf', is a small, red-faced imp with a glittering eye and a grin full of sharp teeth, said to haunt Detroit. Seeing it is a warning that something bad is coming.

The story says Detroit's founder, Antoine de la Mothe Cadillac, struck the imp with his cane and lost his fortune. Tellers say it danced among the dead after the Battle of Bloody Run in 1763, was seen before the 1805 fire that burned the city, and was spotted by utility workers just before the 1967 riots. The legend first appeared in print in 1883, so how far back it really goes is unclear.
Since 2010 Detroiters have held the Marche du Nain Rouge each spring, a costumed parade that banishes the imp from the city for another year.
signs: A small red figure with a wide, toothy grin
A glittering eye
Seen just before fires, riots or disasters

famous.name: Seen after the Battle of Bloody Run

name: Fresno Nightcrawlers
region: Fresno and Yosemite Lakes Park, California
first: Security camera footage from 2007
summary: Walking pairs of white legs caught on a Fresno security camera.
body: Fresno Nightcrawlers are white, legs-only figures seen on home security footage, often described as a pair of pants out for a walk. They seem to have a tiny head and body sitting directly on long legs, and tend to appear in pairs.

The first clip was recorded in south Fresno in 2007 and shown on Univision. More footage followed from Yosemite Lakes Park in 2011. The TV show Fact or Faked: Paranormal Files gave them their name and could not prove the footage was faked. Skeptic Brian Dunning calls them an urban legend nobody truly believes in, yet they have become a beloved Fresno mascot, with T-shirts, toys and murals.
signs: Two long white legs with almost no body
A slow, swaying walk
Usually seen in pairs on security cameras

name: Black-eyed children
region: Reported across the US and UK; first story from Abilene, Texas
first: Brian Bethel's 1996 Abilene encounter, posted online in 1998
summary: Pale children with solid black eyes who knock at night and insist on being invited in.
body: Black-eyed children look like ordinary kids or teens, usually pale and oddly dressed, until you see their eyes, which are completely black with no whites. They knock on doors or tap on car windows late at night and ask, politely but insistently, to be let in to use the phone or get a ride. Witnesses say they feel a wave of dread they cannot explain. A common thread is that they cannot come in unless you invite them, so they keep asking, more and more insistently.

The legend traces to Brian Bethel, a reporter in Abilene, Texas, who said two black-eyed boys approached his car one night in 1996. He posted the story to a ghost-story mailing list in 1998, and it spread through forums, TV shows and, in 2014, a burst of British tabloid front pages. Bethel still says the encounter happened.

It is a modern, internet-era legend: researchers have found no documented cases beyond first-hand posts and friend-of-a-friend stories, and the tale fits a long line of 'don't let it in' folklore, from vampires to changelings.
signs: Pale children with completely black eyes
Insisting on being invited inside
Stilted, adult-sounding speech
A sudden feeling of fear
habitat: Doorsteps and parked cars at night

name: Shadow people
region: Reported worldwide, often in bedrooms at night
first: Popularised on Coast to Coast AM radio in 2001
summary: Dark, human-shaped silhouettes seen at the edge of vision, including the infamous Hat Man.
body: Shadow people are dark, featureless human silhouettes seen in the corner of the eye, in doorways or standing at the foot of the bed. They are usually solid black, darker than the room around them, and dart away when looked at directly.

The idea took off after Coast to Coast AM devoted a show to them in April 2001 and invited listeners to send drawings. The best-known figure is the Hat Man, a tall shadow in a brimmed hat and sometimes a long coat, often reported during sleep paralysis.

Sleep researchers point out that sleep paralysis often brings vivid sensed presences and figures, and the Hat Man is also widely reported by people who take dangerous overdoses of the antihistamine diphenhydramine.
signs: A solid black human outline
A figure in a brimmed hat watching from the doorway
Being unable to move on waking
Pressure on the chest

famous.name: Coast to Coast AM shadow people show

name: Spring-heeled Jack
region: London and southern England, later the Midlands and Liverpool
first: October 1837, in south London
summary: A fire-breathing, high-leaping figure who terrorised Victorian England.
body: Spring-heeled Jack was a figure of Victorian panic: a tall, thin man in a black cloak with clawed hands and glowing red eyes, who could leap over walls and hedges in a single bound and breathed out blue and white flames.

Reports began in London in 1837. In January 1838 the Lord Mayor of London read out a letter about the attacks at a public session. On 19 February 1838, 18-year-old Jane Alsop answered her door to a man who said he was a policeman, then threw off his cloak, spat flames in her face and tore at her with claws. Lucy Scales reported a similar attack days later.
Sightings went on for decades, including sentries at Aldershot army camp in 1877, until the last widely reported appearance in Liverpool in 1904. He became a star of penny dreadful comics.
signs: Enormous leaps over walls and rooftops
Blue or white flames from the mouth
Clawed hands and glowing eyes
A cloak and tight-fitting oilskin suit

name: Popobawa
region: Pemba and Unguja islands, Zanzibar, and the Tanzanian coast
first: Pemba, around 1965
summary: A shape-shifting night spirit whose name means 'bat wing', behind waves of panic in Zanzibar.
body: Popobawa is a spirit from Zanzibar whose Swahili name means 'bat wing', after the shadow it is said to cast. It is a shapeshifter that can appear as a man or an animal, though it is often pictured as a small, one-eyed creature with bat wings. It visits homes at night, attacks sleepers, and brings a sulfur smell.

Reports began on Pemba around 1965 and returned in waves. In 1995 a major panic spread across Zanzibar and the coast to Dar es Salaam, with families sleeping outdoors around fires to avoid it. Shorter outbreaks followed in 2000 and 2007.
Researchers describe the waves as social panics tied to sleep paralysis, rumour and times of political tension.
signs: Night attacks on sleepers
A shadow like bat wings
A sulfur smell
Families sleeping outside in groups

name: Wendigo
region: Northern forests of Canada and the Great Lakes, in the traditions of Algonquian-speaking peoples
first: In English accounts since at least 1714; popularised by Algernon Blackwood's 1910 story
summary: A being of winter and hunger from Algonquian traditions, far removed from its horror-movie image.
body: The wendigo belongs to the traditions of several Algonquian-speaking peoples, including the Ojibwe, Cree, Saulteaux, Naskapi and Innu. In these teachings it is tied to winter, cold and starvation, and to greed that can never be satisfied. Ojibwe scholar Basil Johnston described it as gaunt, ash-grey and always hungry. It is also a moral idea, a warning about what selfishness does to a person and a community.
These are living spiritual traditions, and many Indigenous people prefer that the wendigo not be treated as a casual campfire monster. We keep this page short for that reason.

The antlered, deer-skulled 'wendigo' seen in films, games and online stories is a recent pop-culture invention that grew from Algernon Blackwood's 1910 story The Wendigo. Most modern 'wendigo sightings' online describe that version, not the being of the traditions.
signs: Modern reports describe a tall, gaunt figure in winter woods
Bitter cold and a sense of dread
Voices or calls deep in the forest

name: Thetis Lake Monster
region: Thetis Lake, near Victoria, British Columbia
first: August 1972
summary: A silver, scaly gill-man two teenagers said chased them from a BC beach in 1972.
body: On 22 August 1972, the Victoria Daily Times reported that two teenage boys said a silver-scaled, man-shaped creature with claws and a sharp, spiked head rose out of Thetis Lake and chased them off the beach. Two other boys fishing on the far shore said they saw it too. The RCMP investigated and found nothing.

Years later skeptic Daniel Loxton tracked down one of the witnesses, who admitted the story was made up. Loxton found the description matched the monster in Monster from the Surf, a film shown on local TV just days earlier.
signs: Silvery scales
A pointed, spiked head with ear-like gills
Clawed hands
Rising out of the water

name: Indrid Cold
region: Interstate 77 near Parkersburg, West Virginia, and the Ohio Valley
first: 2 November 1966
summary: A smiling man in a shiny suit who stepped out of a UFO in West Virginia in 1966.
body: On the evening of 2 November 1966, salesman Woodrow Derenberger said a craft shaped like an old kerosene lamp blocked his truck on Interstate 77 near Parkersburg, West Virginia. A tall man with dark slicked-back hair, a deep tan and a glossy coat stepped out, smiled, and spoke to him without moving his lips. He called himself Cold and said, 'We mean you no harm.'

Derenberger told the story on local TV the next day, and others came forward describing a similar grinning man. Writer John Keel folded the story into his Mothman Prophecies, and Indrid Cold became a fixture of Point Pleasant lore. Derenberger later claimed trips to Cold's home planet, Lanulos.
signs: A tall man with a fixed, too-wide grin
A shiny or glossy coat
Telepathic speech
A lamp-shaped craft blocking the road

name: Grey aliens
region: Reported worldwide, especially in US abduction accounts
first: The 1961 Betty and Barney Hill case made the image famous
summary: Small, grey, big-headed beings with huge black eyes, the classic face of alien encounters.
body: Greys are the beings most often described in alien abduction and close encounter reports: short, slender, hairless humanoids with grey skin, an oversized head, tiny nose and mouth, and large, black, almond-shaped eyes. Tall versions are reported too.

Betty and Barney Hill's 1961 account of being taken aboard a craft in New Hampshire, recalled under hypnosis, set the template. Betty's sketch of a star map led to the idea that greys come from Zeta Reticuli. Later accounts of Roswell bodies and Whitley Strieber's 1987 book Communion, with its famous cover, made the face known everywhere.
Skeptics note that similar big-headed, big-eyed future humans appeared in science fiction long before 1961.
signs: Large black almond-shaped eyes
Grey, hairless skin
Thin body and an oversized head
Telepathic communication
Missing time
habitat: Inside craft, bedrooms and lonely roads

name: Nordic aliens
region: Mostly contactee reports from the US and Europe, especially in the 1950s
first: George Adamski said he met one in the California desert on 20 November 1952
summary: Tall, fair-haired, human-looking visitors from 1950s contactee stories.
body: Nordics are human-looking beings reported in UFO contact stories: tall, often 6 to 7 feet, with long fair hair, pale skin and light eyes. They are usually described as calm and kind, speaking telepathically and warning people about nuclear weapons or the health of the planet.

George Adamski said he met a long-haired visitor named Orthon near Desert Center, California in 1952, who told him he came from Venus. Other 1950s contactees reported similar 'space brothers', and from 1975 the Swiss farmer Billy Meier claimed contact with beings from the Pleiades.
Historians point to the 1951 film The Day the Earth Stood Still as one inspiration. From the 1960s on, greys largely replaced Nordics in encounter reports.
signs: Tall, human-looking people with long fair hair
One-piece suits
Calm, peaceful warnings
Telepathy
habitat: Desert landing sites and contact meetings

name: Men in Black
region: Mostly the United States, following UFO sightings
first: Harold Dahl's 1947 Maury Island story; Albert K. Bender's 1953 visit
summary: Pale, oddly behaved men in black suits who warn UFO witnesses to keep quiet.
body: Men in Black are strangers in dark suits, hats and sunglasses who turn up after a UFO sighting and warn witnesses not to talk. Reports describe them as pale or oddly tanned, stiff, with flat voices, unfamiliar with everyday things like ballpoint pens, and arriving in old but brand-new-looking black cars.

In 1947 Harold Dahl claimed a man in a dark suit warned him about his Maury Island sighting. In 1953 Albert K. Bender shut down his UFO research group, saying three men in black had visited him. Author Gray Barker turned the story into a 1956 book, and John Keel reported MIB visits around Point Pleasant during the Mothman flap.
Folklorists compare them to old tales of meeting the devil on the road. The 1997 film made them comic heroes.
signs: Black suits, hats and sunglasses
Pale skin and stiff, odd movements
Knowing details they could not know
Warnings to stay quiet
Old-model black cars that look new

name: Reptilians
region: Abduction reports worldwide; conspiracy theory spread online
first: Patrolman Herbert Schirmer's 1967 account from Ashland, Nebraska
summary: Scaly, reptile-like humanoids from some abduction reports, and a notorious conspiracy theory.
body: In UFO lore, reptilians are tall, scaly, reptile-like humanoids with slit-pupil eyes, described in a minority of abduction accounts. One of the earliest came from Ashland, Nebraska patrolman Herbert Schirmer, who under hypnosis recalled being taken aboard a craft in 1967 by beings with a slightly reptilian look and a winged-serpent emblem.

From the 1990s the idea was spun into a conspiracy theory claiming shape-shifting reptilians secretly rule the world. Researchers have traced it to pulp fiction of the 1920s, and note it often recycles old antisemitic tropes. This page is about encounter reports only.
signs: Scaly green or grey skin
Vertical slit pupils
Tall, muscular build
A winged-serpent emblem

name: Wampus cat
region: Appalachia, the Ozarks, Tennessee and the Carolinas
first: Appalachian folklore; in newspapers by the 1930s
summary: An Appalachian monster cat with glowing eyes, sometimes said to have six legs.
body: The wampus cat is a big, dark cat of Appalachian and Ozark folklore with glowing green or yellow eyes and a scream like a cougar. Depending on who tells it, it is a spirit cat with strange powers, a six-legged cat that can run forever, or an amphibious panther that swims like a mink.

Some versions draw on older Cherokee stories, while others are plain lumber camp yarns. In the 1930s, newspapers in the North Carolina Piedmont blamed a wampus cat for killing livestock. Today it is a popular school mascot, from the Conway Wampus Cats in Arkansas to schools in Texas and Tennessee.
signs: A dark cat bigger than a panther
Glowing green or yellow eyes
Screams and whistles in the woods at night
Livestock and dogs killed
size: 7 to 20 ft long in tall tales

famous.name: Knoxville paper describes a 15- to 20-foot wampus cat

name: Hodag
region: Rhinelander, Oneida County, Wisconsin
first: Newspaper reports in 1893
summary: Wisconsin's grinning, horned, spiny-backed beast of the logging camps.
body: The hodag is a fearsome critter of the northern Wisconsin logging camps: a dark beast with bull horns, a frog's head, a huge grin full of teeth, a row of spikes along its back and a spear-tipped tail. Lumberjacks said it was born from the ashes of mistreated oxen.

In 1893 surveyor and prankster Eugene Shepard announced that he and some locals had killed a hodag in Rhinelander with dynamite, and released a photo of its charred remains. In 1896 he claimed to have caught one alive and displayed it in a dark tent at the county fair, moving it with wires. When scientists said they would come to see it, he admitted it was a wooden carving.
Rhinelander embraced the beast: its schools are the Hodags, a giant statue stands by the chamber of commerce, and the Hodag Country Festival is held each summer.
signs: Bull horns and a wide, toothy grin
A row of spikes down the back
A long tail with a spear tip
The smell of buzzard meat and skunk

famous.name: Live hodag shown at the fair

name: Tsuchinoko
region: Mountain villages across western Japan; famously Shimokitayama, Nara
first: A yokai in old folklore; a wave of sightings in the late 1980s
summary: A short, fat, jumping snake from Japan with a bounty on its head.
body: The tsuchinoko is a snake-like creature from Japanese folklore, 30 to 80 centimetres long with a fat middle like a beer bottle, a narrow tail and a viper's fangs. It is said to jump a metre or more, sometimes twice in a row, and in some legends it speaks, lies and likes sake. Some say it bites its tail and rolls like a wheel.

In the late 1980s it turned from yokai to cryptid after a burst of sightings. In 1988 the village of Shimokitayama in Nara Prefecture launched a Tsuchinoko Expedition with a reward of a million yen for a live capture. About 200 people joined, and nothing was found. Tsuchinoko hunts are still held as village festivals, and Shimokitayama opened a Tsuchinoko Park in 2023.
Herpetologists suggest it could be a mamushi or blue-tongued skink that has just eaten a big meal.
signs: A short, fat-bodied snake
Jumping leaps of a metre or more
A squeaking or chirping sound
Rolling like a hoop
habitat: Mountain forest and rice paddy edges

name: Hoop snake
region: Rural United States, Canada and Australia
first: Described in a 1784 travel letter
summary: A snake that grabs its tail in its mouth and rolls after you like a wheel.
body: The hoop snake is a staple of American rural tall tales: a snake that takes its tail in its jaws and rolls downhill after its victim like a wagon hoop. At the last moment it straightens out and strikes with a venomous stinger on its tail. The only escape is to jump behind a tree, which takes the hit and dies.

A 1784 travel account from the United States described the rolling snake in detail, and the story later fed into Pecos Bill tales. Snake experts suggest the mud snake and rainbow snake, which have pointed but harmless tail tips, and the habit of some snakes of coiling in a loop.
signs: A snake rolling along in a hoop
A sharp, stinging tail
A tree that withers after being struck

name: Mapinguari
region: Brazilian Amazon, especially Acre, Amazonas and Pará
first: Brazilian folklore; researched by ornithologist David Oren from the 1990s
summary: A foul-smelling Amazon giant, sometimes said to have a mouth on its belly.
body: The Mapinguari is a large, shaggy, upright creature of Amazon folklore, said to stink so badly it dizzies hunters. Folklore gives it backward-turned feet, hooked claws, a single eye and, most strangely, a gaping mouth in its belly. Its roar is said to sound like a human scream or thunder.

Ornithologist David Oren, of the Goeldi Museum in Belém, spent years interviewing rubber tappers, miners and Indigenous people who said they had seen or even shot one. He proposed that the stories could describe a surviving giant ground sloth, a group that died out about 10,000 years ago. His field searches found no animal, and most scientists remain doubtful.
signs: An overwhelming rotten smell
Loud screams in the forest
Twisted palm trees with the hearts eaten
Huge reversed-looking footprints

name: Montauk Monster
region: Ditch Plains beach, Montauk, Long Island, New York
first: Found on 12 July 2008; reported on 23 July 2008
summary: A beaked, hairless carcass on a Long Island beach that broke the internet in 2008.
body: In July 2008, four friends found a strange, bloated carcass on Ditch Plains beach in Montauk, New York. It was hairless, with a beak-like face, sharp teeth and long-fingered paws. A local paper ran the photo as 'The Hound of Bonacville', blogs picked it up, and within days it was a worldwide story.

Rumours linked it to the Plum Island Animal Disease Center just offshore. The carcass vanished before scientists could examine it, but experts who studied the photos concluded it was most likely a raccoon that had been in the water for a while, with its upper jaw bones exposed. Similar 'monsters' have washed up on Long Island and elsewhere since.
signs: A hairless, bloated body
A beak-like face with teeth
Long, finger-like toes
size: About the size of a small dog

name: Sheepsquatch
region: Kanawha, Boone, Putnam and Mason counties, West Virginia
first: A "White Thing" tale in a 1965 folklore collection; sightings in the mid-1990s
summary: A woolly white, horned beast reported in West Virginia hollows in the 1990s.
body: Sheepsquatch is a West Virginia cryptid described as a bear-sized animal covered in long, shaggy white wool, with a sheep- or goat-like head, horns, and the ability to walk on four legs or stand upright. Witnesses also mention a sulfur smell and a scream like a woman.

Mountain folklore had stories of a 'White Thing' long before the name existed, including one in a 1965 collection about a woman who met a white beast riding home from church. A run of sightings in the mid-1990s, many around the Kanawha Valley near Cross Lanes, gave the creature its modern nickname.
signs: Long, dirty white wool
Horns and a sheep-like face
Walking on two legs or four
A sulfur smell
A scream like a woman

name: Cigar-shaped UFO
region: Worldwide
first: Reported since the late 1940s
summary: Long, wingless cylinders, sometimes glowing, sometimes releasing smaller objects.
body: Cigar- or cylinder-shaped UFOs are long, rounded, wingless objects, often metallic by day and glowing by night, sometimes with a row of lit 'windows'. Some witnesses say smaller discs or lights flew out of them, which earned them the nickname 'motherships'.

On 24 July 1948, Eastern Air Lines pilots Clarence Chiles and John Whitted said a glowing, wingless, cigar-shaped craft with two rows of lit windows shot past their DC-3 near Montgomery, Alabama, then pulled up into the clouds. It was one of the cases that convinced Air Force investigators at the time that UFOs deserved study, though Project Blue Book later put it down to a bright meteor. Contactee George Adamski claimed he saw a giant cigar-shaped 'mother ship' over Palomar, California in 1946 and photographed it the next year.
Many cylinder sightings turn out to be blimps, aircraft seen end-on in glare, or rocket and satellite re-entries.
signs: A long, wingless, rounded body
A row of lit windows or portholes
No sound
Smaller objects leaving it
size: From tens of feet to hundreds of feet long

name: Boomerang and V-shaped UFOs
region: Worldwide; famous waves over New York and Arizona
first: The 1951 Lubbock Lights are an early example
summary: Huge V-shaped or chevron formations of lights, gliding silently overhead.
body: Boomerang UFOs are V-shaped or chevron-shaped objects, or formations of lights in a V, often described as enormous, silent and slow. Witnesses often cannot tell whether they are seeing one dark craft with lights on its edges, or separate lights moving together.

In 1951 residents and college professors in Lubbock, Texas saw a V of glowing lights cross the night sky several times. From 1983 to 1984 thousands of people in New York's Hudson Valley and western Connecticut reported a football-field-sized boomerang of coloured lights. Police later found that pilots in light Cessnas were flying in tight formation as a prank, though some witnesses insist that wasn't what they saw. On 13 March 1997 the Phoenix Lights, a mile-wide V of lights, crossed Arizona in front of thousands.
Formations of birds lit by streetlights, aircraft in formation and military flares explain many cases.
signs: Lights arranged in a V or chevron
A dark shape between the lights blocking stars
Silent and slow
Huge apparent size

name: Ghost rockets
region: Sweden, Finland and the rest of Scandinavia
first: 26 February 1946, by Finnish observers
summary: Rocket-shaped objects that streaked across Scandinavian skies in 1946.
body: In 1946, a year before the term 'flying saucer' existed, people across Sweden and Finland began reporting rocket- or cigar-shaped objects streaking through the sky, some trailing fire, some apparently changing course. About 2,000 reports were logged between May and December, with peaks on 9 and 11 August.

On 19 July 1946 a farmer saw an object crash into Lake Kölmjärv in northern Sweden, and the Swedish military searched the lake but found nothing. Officials feared the Soviets were test-firing captured German V-weapons, and the Swedish army told newspapers not to print exact locations.
Investigators concluded that many sightings were meteors, and the August peaks match the Perseid shower. But some reports, including radar returns and recovered fragments, were never fully explained.
signs: A cigar or rocket shape with a fiery tail
Changing direction in flight
Crashing into lakes
No sound

name: Mystery airships
region: Across the United States, starting in California
first: November 1896, over Sacramento, California
summary: Lit-up 'airships' reported across America years before anyone could build one.
body: From late 1896 to mid-1897, thousands of Americans reported airships in the night sky: large, cigar-shaped gas bags with lights, propellers, sometimes wings, and occasionally a crew who spoke to the people below. Reports started over Sacramento in November 1896 and spread east through Texas and the Midwest by spring 1897.

Newspapers of the era printed wild tales, including a story that an airship crashed into a windmill in Aurora, Texas in April 1897 and its pilot was buried in the town cemetery, and a Kansas farmer's claim that an airship lassoed one of his cows. Both are now widely seen as hoaxes. No airship capable of such flights existed yet.
The wave is seen as a forerunner of modern UFO reports, with each era seeing the future technology it imagined.
signs: A lit, cigar-shaped craft at night
Searchlights sweeping the ground
Propellers, fins or wings
Human-looking crews
habitat: Night skies over towns and farms

name: Green fireballs
region: New Mexico and the US Southwest, near Los Alamos and Sandia
first: Pilots reported them over New Mexico on 5 December 1948
summary: Bright green balls of fire over New Mexico's nuclear labs that the military investigated.
body: Starting in late 1948, pilots, scientists and security guards around New Mexico's atomic sites reported brilliant green fireballs crossing the sky. They looked like meteors but were described as flying flat and level, burning a vivid green, and making no sound.

Meteor expert Lincoln LaPaz of the University of New Mexico saw one himself and said it did not behave like an ordinary meteor. The Army worried about foreign weapons, and in 1949 scientists including Edward Teller met at Los Alamos to discuss them. The Air Force ran Project Twinkle to photograph them, with little result.
Today most researchers think they were unusually bright bolide meteors, which can glow green from burning metals.
signs: A bright green ball of light
A flat, level path
No sound
Breaking into fragments at the end

name: UFO crashes
region: Worldwide; best known in New Mexico, Pennsylvania and Nova Scotia
first: The Roswell debris recovery in July 1947
summary: Stories of objects falling from the sky and being quietly taken away.
body: Crash stories are some of the most famous in ufology: something falls from the sky, the military seals off the area, and witnesses say the debris, or bodies, were taken away in secret.

In July 1947 the Roswell Army Air Field announced it had recovered a 'flying disc' on a ranch in New Mexico, then said it was a weather balloon. In the 1990s the Air Force said it was debris from Project Mogul, a secret balloon program. On 9 December 1965 a fireball came down near Kecksburg, Pennsylvania, and residents described an acorn-shaped object hauled away by soldiers. On 4 October 1967 witnesses at Shag Harbour, Nova Scotia saw a lit object hit the sea, and the RCMP and navy searched the water.
Explanations include balloons, meteors and space debris. Each case still has dedicated researchers.
signs: A bright object falling from the sky
Military or police cordons
Unusual metallic debris
Witnesses told to stay quiet

name: Alien abduction
aliases: Close encounter of the fourth kind
region: Reported worldwide, most often in North America
first: Antônio Villas Boas in Brazil in 1957 and the Hills in New Hampshire in 1961
summary: People who say they were taken aboard a craft, often remembering only 'missing time'.
body: Alien abduction reports describe being taken, usually at night from a bedroom or a lonely road, by beings into a craft, examined, and returned with gaps in memory. Common details include a bright light, paralysis, small grey beings, a medical-style exam and an hour or more of missing time.

Brazilian farmer Antônio Villas Boas told of a 1957 abduction, and Betty and Barney Hill's 1961 account from New Hampshire, recalled under hypnosis, became the template. In October 1973 two shipyard workers in Pascagoula, Mississippi, said they were taken aboard a craft by the river. In November 1975 Arizona logger Travis Walton disappeared for five days after his crew said a beam of light struck him.
Psychologists link many reports to sleep paralysis, false memories formed under hypnosis and cultural expectations. Abductees say their experiences are real.
signs: A beam of bright light
Being unable to move
An hour or more of missing time
Grey beings and an exam table
Unexplained marks on the body

name: Crop circles
region: Mostly southern England, especially Wiltshire; also worldwide
first: The term spread in the early 1980s; 1966 "saucer nests" in Australia
summary: Patterns flattened into fields overnight, long linked to UFOs.
body: Crop circles are patterns of flattened grain that appear in fields, often overnight, from simple circles to vast fractal designs. They cluster in southern England, especially Wiltshire near Avebury and Stonehenge, and became linked to UFOs and mysterious energies.

In 1966 a banana farmer at Tully, Queensland said he saw a saucer rise from a swamp and leave a flattened circular 'nest' in the reeds. Circles multiplied in England through the 1980s. In 1991 two men, Doug Bower and Dave Chorley, revealed they had been making circles since 1978 with a plank, rope and a wire loop on a cap to keep their lines straight, and showed reporters how.

Since then artist teams have openly made ever more complex formations, such as the 409-circle design at Milk Hill in 2001. All tested circles have been consistent with human makers, though some visitors still report odd lights and feelings in them.
signs: Flattened crop in precise geometric patterns
Appearing overnight
Bent rather than broken stalks
Lights reported over fields
size: Tens to hundreds of feet across

famous.name: Bower and Chorley reveal their method

name: Cattle mutilations
region: Western United States, especially Colorado, New Mexico and the Plains
first: The death of a horse named Snippy in September 1967
summary: Cattle found dead with neat cuts and no blood, often blamed on UFOs.
body: Cattle mutilation reports describe livestock found dead with parts removed, such as an eye, an ear, the tongue or sex organs, with clean-looking cuts, little blood, and no tracks around the body. Ranchers sometimes reported lights or unmarked helicopters nearby.

The modern story began in September 1967 when a horse called Snippy was found near Alamosa, Colorado with the flesh stripped from its head and neck. Reports surged across the West in the 1970s. In 1979 a federal grant paid for an investigation in New Mexico led by retired FBI agent Kenneth Rommel. His 1980 report concluded that the cases were consistent with normal predators and scavengers.
Veterinarians explain the clean 'surgical' cuts as the work of birds, insects and decomposition. Theories have also blamed cults, secret government projects and the chupacabra.
signs: A carcass with eyes, tongue or ears removed
Smooth-looking cuts
Little or no blood on the ground
No tracks around the body
Lights or helicopters at night

name: Skinwalker Ranch
region: Near Ballard, Uintah Basin, north-eastern Utah
first: The Sherman family's story appeared in the Deseret News in 1996
summary: A Utah ranch famous for claims of UFOs, orbs, strange animals and cattle mutilations.
body: Skinwalker Ranch is a roughly 512-acre property in Utah's Uintah Basin, an area with UFO reports going back to the 1970s. In 1996 the Sherman family told the Deseret News of glowing orbs, mutilated cattle, a huge wolf that bullets could not hurt, and lights in the sky.

That year businessman Robert Bigelow bought the ranch for his National Institute for Discovery Science, and researchers logged around 100 odd incidents. The Defense Intelligence Agency later funded related work through a program called AAWSAP. Today the ranch is the setting of a TV series.

The name comes from the skin-walker of Navajo tradition. Navajo people generally do not discuss skin-walkers with outsiders and many object to the casual use of the word, so this page covers only the ranch.
signs: Glowing orbs over the fields
Cattle found mutilated
Large animals unhurt by gunfire
Electronics failing

name: Bunny Man
region: Colchester Overpass near Clifton, Fairfax County, Virginia
first: Two police reports in Burke, Virginia, October 1970
summary: A man in a rabbit suit with an axe, tied to a railroad overpass near Clifton, Virginia.
body: The Bunny Man is a northern Virginia urban legend about a figure in a rabbit costume who threatens or attacks people with an axe or hatchet. Most retellings place him at the Colchester Overpass, a narrow one-lane railroad bridge near Clifton that locals now call Bunny Man Bridge.

Unlike many legends, this one has a documented starting point. Fairfax County Public Library historian Brian Conley traced it to two police reports from Burke in October 1970. In the first, a young couple parked on Guinea Road said a man in a white suit with long ears shouted about trespassing and threw a hatchet through their car window. Less than two weeks later a security guard said a man in a rabbit costume hacked at a porch post at an unfinished house and threatened him. The Washington Post covered both, and dozens more people called police claiming sightings.

Over the following decades the story grew. A 1973 University of Maryland student paper logged 54 versions, and a widely shared 1999 internet post invented an escaped asylum inmate and a string of murders. Conley found no record of any killings. The overpass is on an active rail line and draws crowds every Halloween, so local police patrol it.
signs: A man in a white or grey rabbit suit with long ears
An axe or hatchet
Shouting about trespassing
Stories centred on a dark one-lane railroad overpass
habitat: Suburban woods and a railroad underpass

famous.name: Hatchet thrown through a parked car's window on Guinea Road
Man in rabbit costume chops at a porch post

name: The Rake
region: Internet legend, mostly set in the north-eastern United States
first: Created on an internet message board in the mid-2000s
summary: A pale, hairless, crouching humanoid with long claws, born as an internet legend in the 2000s.
body: The Rake is a modern internet legend: a pale, thin, hairless humanoid that crawls on all fours, has long claw-like fingers and is said to appear at the foot of people's beds at night. Some tellers say it speaks in a high, rasping voice.

It is widely traced to a mid-2000s thread on an online paranormal board where users set out to invent a new monster together. The supposed historical documents that come with the story, including a 1691 ship's log and later diary entries, were written as part of that fiction. Since then the Rake has spread through creepypasta sites, videos and a low-budget 2018 film.

Some people now describe their own night-time encounters using the Rake's description, often alongside sleep paralysis. There is no record of it before the internet, and it is best treated as an online-era legend.
signs: A pale, hairless figure crouching or crawling on all fours
Very long fingers or claws
Appearing at the foot of a bed at night
A shrill or rasping voice
habitat: Bedrooms and woods at night (in the stories)

name: The Hat Man
region: Reported worldwide, often during sleep paralysis
first: Described online from the late 2000s; tied to older shadow-person reports
summary: A tall shadow figure in a brimmed hat, often seen during sleep paralysis or on certain drugs.
body: The Hat Man is the best-known kind of shadow person: a dark, featureless human outline wearing a fedora or other brimmed hat, sometimes with a long coat. People most often describe him standing in a bedroom doorway or at the foot of the bed, watching, and say they felt him staring even though they could not see a face.

Many accounts come from people waking in sleep paralysis, when the body is still unable to move and the mind can produce vivid dream images. He is also so often reported by people who have taken large overdoses of the antihistamine diphenhydramine (Benadryl) that he has become a well-known warning sign on drug-safety forums.

Descriptions spread widely online from the late 2000s, and many people say they saw him as children. Researchers explain him through sleep paralysis, deliriant drugs and sleep deprivation, while some paranormal writers treat him as a real being.
signs: A dark figure with a brimmed hat and no visible face
Standing in a doorway or at the foot of the bed
Being unable to move while it watches
A strong sense of dread

name: Skinwalker
region: Navajo (Diné) homeland, Arizona, New Mexico and Utah
first: A long-standing Diné belief; recorded by outside ethnographers in the 20th century
summary: A harmful witch figure in Navajo belief; the name has since been taken up widely by outsiders.
body: In Navajo (Diné) culture, a skinwalker is a kind of harmful witch who is believed to take on the form of an animal. It is a living cultural and spiritual belief, not a monster story, and many Diné people prefer not to discuss it, especially with outsiders. This entry does not retell traditional material.

Outside the Navajo Nation, the word has taken on a life of its own. It became the name of Skinwalker Ranch in Utah, a ranch beside the Uintah and Ouray Reservation known for UFO and paranormal claims, and it is now used for a wide range of internet horror stories about pale, long-limbed creatures, mimicked voices and things seen on night roads in the West. Most of these stories have little to do with the original belief.

Native writers have asked non-Native authors to stop borrowing the figure, saying it opens their communities to unwanted questions. If you hear a 'skinwalker' story online, it is usually a modern creature legend that has borrowed the name.
signs: In modern internet stories: a pale, long-limbed figure on four legs
Mimicked voices at night
Animals that seem wrong or move like people
habitat: Deserts and back roads of the Four Corners region

famous.name: Book Hunt for the Skinwalker spreads the name of a Utah ranch

name: Snarly Yow
aliases: Black Dog of the National Road
region: South Mountain and the old National Road, western Maryland
first: Recorded by Madeleine Vinton Dahlgren in South-Mountain Magic, 1882
summary: A huge black phantom dog said to haunt the National Road over South Mountain in Maryland.
body: The Snarly Yow is a ghostly black dog said to haunt South Mountain in western Maryland, especially the old National Road (now Alternate US 40) where it crosses the ridge near Turner's Gap. Travellers said it appeared at night on the road, huge and black, and that bullets and blows passed straight through it.

The best-known source is South-Mountain Magic (1882), a collection of local ghost tales by Madeleine Vinton Dahlgren, who lived on the mountain and gathered stories from her neighbours. The legend later spread across the Potomac, and West Virginia folklore places it near Harpers Ferry as well.
It belongs to the family of black dog legends brought over from Britain, like Black Shuck and the barghest.
signs: A very large black dog on the road at night
Shots or blows that pass through it
Vanishing when approached
Disappearing when someone tries to strike it
size: Large dog, sometimes said to grow (in the stories)
habitat: A mountain road and nearby woods

famous.name: Dahlgren publishes South-Mountain Magic, recording the black dog

name: White Thing
region: Rural West Virginia, especially Kanawha and Mason counties
first: Collected by a folklore student in the 1950s; printed by Ruth Ann Musick in 1965
summary: A white, shaggy, dog-like beast of West Virginia folklore said to scream like a woman.
body: The White Thing is a West Virginia legend of a pale, shaggy animal that moves on all fours and lets out a scream like a woman in pain. Stories place it on lonely roads and hollows at night, where it frightens people walking or riding home.

Its best-known telling comes from a student in Ruth Ann Musick's folklore classes at Fairmont State, which she printed in her 1965 collection The Telltale Lilac Bush and Other West Virginia Ghost Tales. In that story a woman riding home from church hears the cry before a white beast appears.
Later accounts from Mason and Kanawha counties describe a white-furred, dog-headed animal, and many writers treat it as the same creature as, or an ancestor of, the modern Sheepsquatch legend.
signs: A white, shaggy animal on all fours
A scream like a woman in pain
Appearing on dark rural roads

famous.name: Ruth Ann Musick prints the tale from her Fairmont students

name: Tailypo
region: Appalachia and the rural American South
first: An oral folktale from Appalachia and the South; in print by the 20th century
summary: A folktale creature that returns, night after night, to demand its stolen tail back.
body: The Tailypo is the star of a classic Appalachian and Southern 'jump tale', told to make listeners leap at the last line. In the usual version a hungry old hunter living alone in the woods with his hounds chops the tail off a strange animal and eats it. That night the creature comes back again and again, asking for its 'tailypo', and each time one of his dogs chases it off and never returns.

With the dogs gone, the creature reaches the man in his bed. Gentler versions end with only the cabin's chimney left standing. The animal is usually described as dog-sized and dark, with glowing eyes and bobcat-like ears.
It is a folktale rather than a sighting report, and it is well known from storytelling festivals and Joanna Galdone's 1977 picture book.
signs: A dark, dog-sized animal with glowing eyes
Scratching at a cabin at night
A voice asking for its tail
habitat: Deep woods around a lone cabin

name: Jackalope
region: Wyoming and the American West
first: A taxidermy joke from Douglas, Wyoming in the 1930s; older horned-hare tales in Europe
summary: A jackrabbit with antelope horns: a Western tall-tale animal and taxidermy joke, not a real cryptid.
body: The jackalope is a jackrabbit with antlers or horns, and it is a joke rather than a mystery. The American version is usually traced to Douglas Herrick and his brother of Douglas, Wyoming, who in the early 1930s mounted deer antlers on a jackrabbit and sold it to a local hotel. Mounted jackalopes, postcards and souvenirs followed, and Douglas calls itself the home of the jackalope.

Folklorists group it with the fearsome critters, the tall-tale animals of North American lumber camps and ranches that are used to tease newcomers. Tellers say it can mimic cowboys' singing and only breeds during lightning storms.

There is a real-world twist: rabbits infected with the Shope papilloma virus can grow horn-like growths on their heads, and such animals may lie behind older European pictures of horned hares and the Bavarian wolpertinger.
signs: A rabbit or hare with small antlers
Mounted heads in bars and gift shops
Tall tales told to visitors

famous.name: Herrick brothers mount the first jackalope, per the New York Times

name: Wolfman of Defiance
region: Railroad yards of Defiance, north-west Ohio
first: Police reports in Defiance, Ohio, summer 1972
summary: A towering, fanged 'wolfman' that railroad workers said attacked them in Defiance, Ohio in 1972.
body: In the summer of 1972 police in Defiance, Ohio took several reports of a very tall figure with a wolf-like or animal head prowling near the Norfolk and Western railroad tracks on the south side of town. Railroad crewmen working at night said it came at them from behind, and one said he was struck on the shoulder with a club or piece of wood.
Local papers, including the Toledo Blade in early August 1972, picked up the story and set off a brief 'werewolf' scare in the town. A local grocer later said he saw the creature in his headlights.

No one was caught, and the original police reports are no longer on file. A follow-up in the Blade said most locals thought it was a hoax, perhaps someone in a costume. The case is still retold as one of Ohio's best-known dogman stories.
signs: A very tall upright figure with a wolf-like head
Fangs and shaggy hair
Attacks from behind with a club
Seen at night near railroad tracks

famous.name: Railroad crewman reports being struck by a 'wolfman'

name: Ninki Nanka
region: Swamps and creeks of the lower Gambia River and Casamance
first: In a British colonial commissioner's report of 1906
summary: A dragon-like swamp creature of West African folklore whose gaze is said to bring death.
body: The ninki nanka is a feared creature in the folklore of the Gambia and southern Senegal, especially among the Mandinka. It is usually described as a huge reptile or serpent of the swamps and river creeks, with a long neck, a crocodile- or horse-like head with crests or horns, and shining, mirror-like scales.

Seeing it is said to bring illness or death. A 1906 British colonial report described it as a giant crowned serpent of the deep bush and noted that people would not go near places where it was believed to live. The fear kept some fertile swamps unused.

In 2006 a small British cryptozoology expedition travelled to the Gambia to collect accounts, and the trip was covered by the BBC. Witness descriptions varied widely, from a dragon to a large crocodile, and no physical evidence was found.
signs: A long-necked reptile in swamps or creeks
Shining, colour-changing scales
A crest or horns on the head
Sickness said to follow a sighting
habitat: Mangrove swamps, creeks and river forest

name: Grootslang
region: Richtersveld and the Orange River, Northern Cape, South Africa
first: Told among Khoekhoe and settlers; written up by prospectors in the early 1900s
summary: A giant serpent said to guard a cave full of diamonds in South Africa's Richtersveld.
body: The grootslang (Afrikaans for 'big snake') is a huge serpent said to live in a deep cave in the Richtersveld near the Orange River, known as the Wonder Hole or Bottomless Pit. In the stories the cave is filled with diamonds and the snake guards them. Some versions add that the cave connects to the sea or to the river.

Gold prospector F. C. Cornell wrote of a 'groot slang' that local Khoekhoe people and some settlers feared, said to live in a rock in the Orange River and take cattle from the banks. Journalist Lawrence Green later wrote about the Wonder Hole, but explorers who went in reported only bats and bat droppings.

In 1917 English businessman Peter Grayson disappeared while searching for treasure in the Richtersveld after his party was attacked by lions, and rumour blamed the grootslang. Modern online versions give it an elephant's head and tusks, which appears to be a recent invention.
signs: A gigantic snake near a deep cave
Diamonds or treasure nearby
Cattle taken from riverbanks
A strong sense of evil at the cave
habitat: Desert caves and the Orange River gorge

name: Drop bear
region: Eucalyptus bush across Australia (in the joke)
first: In print by 1967 (an Australian Army newspaper); a tall tale for visitors
summary: A meat-eating koala that drops from trees onto tourists: a long-running Australian joke.
body: The drop bear is a hoax. Australians describe it to visitors as a large, vicious relative of the koala that waits in gum trees and drops onto the heads of people walking below. Tourists are told to protect themselves with forks in their hair, Vegemite behind the ears, or by speaking with an Australian accent.

Its origin is unknown, but an Australian Army newspaper mentioned 'a dreaded Drop Bear' in 1967, and it turns up in later service papers and newspaper jokes. The Australian Museum has run a straight-faced spoof entry giving it the scientific name Thylarctos plummetus, and Australian Geographic once published an April Fool's piece on it.

It is the Australian cousin of the American jackalope and fearsome critters. Fans like to point out that a real predatory marsupial, the 'marsupial lion' Thylacoleo, did live in Australia until the late Pleistocene.
signs: A koala-like animal staring down from a gum tree
Something heavy dropping onto your head
Locals warning you with a straight face

name: Barghest
region: Yorkshire, County Durham and northern England
first: In northern English folklore; a ballad was printed by William Hone in 1830
summary: A monstrous black dog of northern England, said to be an omen of death.
body: The barghest is a monstrous black dog of northern English folklore, with huge teeth and claws and fiery eyes. In some places the name means a shape-shifting ghost that can also appear as a headless man, a white cat or a rabbit. The name may come from 'burh-ghest' (town ghost) or a German phrase meaning mountain ghost.

Its most famous haunt is Troller's Gill, a narrow limestone gorge in the Yorkshire Dales. A ballad printed by William Hone tells of a man who went there to summon the barghest and was found dead with strange marks on his chest. Stories also place it in the snickelways of York, around Whitby, near Leeds, and near Darlington in County Durham.

Like other black dogs, the barghest is said to foretell a death, sometimes leading a howling procession of local dogs when an important person dies. It cannot cross running water. It is a close relative of East Anglia's Black Shuck.
signs: A huge black dog with saucer-like, fiery eyes
Rattling chains with nothing visible
Howling before a death
A wound from its paw that never heals
habitat: Gorges, lanes and old town streets

famous.name: Ballad of the Troller's Gill barghest printed by William Hone

name: Bukavac
region: Lakes and ponds of Syrmia (Srem), Serbia
first: A belief recorded in Serbian folklore of the Srem region
summary: A six-legged, horned lake demon of Serbian folklore that bellows at night and strangles prey.
body: The bukavac is a demon of Serbian folklore, known especially in Syrmia (Srem), the flat farmland between the Danube and Sava rivers. It was imagined as a six-legged beast with gnarled horns and bright eyes that lived in lakes and ponds.
At night it came out of the water making a loud bellowing roar, which gives it its name (buka means noise). It was said to leap onto people or animals near the water and strangle them.
It is a folklore being rather than a modern sighting report. One down-to-earth idea links the noise to the booming call of the bittern, a marsh bird that is called 'bukavac' in Serbian.
signs: A loud bellowing from a pond at night
A horned, many-legged shape leaving the water
Animals found strangled near water

name: Inkanyamba
region: Howick Falls and the Umgeni and Umkomazi rivers, KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa
first: A long-held Zulu and Xhosa belief; modern sightings from 1962
summary: A storm serpent of Zulu and Xhosa belief, said to live in the pool below Howick Falls.
body: The inkanyamba is a giant serpent in Zulu and Xhosa belief, linked to tornadoes and summer storms. Its Xhosa name roughly means 'snake cloud'. It is especially associated with the deep pool below Howick Falls on the Umgeni River, which has earned it the local nickname 'Howie'.

In traditional belief it is a powerful being of storm, water and hail rather than an ordinary animal, and angering it is said to bring destructive winds. Shiny metal roofs are said to attract it because it mistakes them for water.

Modern sighting reports describe a long serpent with a horse-like head and a mane or fin. A game ranger named Buthelezi said he saw such an animal basking on a sandbank of the Umgeni in 1962, and more local reports followed in the 1970s to 1990s. Sceptics suggest large eels, crocodiles or tourism stories.
signs: A long serpent with a horse-like head
A mane or row of fins along the back
Seen in deep river pools and below waterfalls
Linked with violent storms

famous.name: Game ranger reports a horse-headed serpent on the Umgeni River

name: Lukwata
region: Lake Victoria, Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania
first: Recorded by colonial administrator C. W. Hobley in 1913
summary: A great serpent of Lake Victoria in Baganda folklore, said to attack fishermen and canoes.
body: The lukwata is a water creature of Baganda folklore, said to live in Lake Victoria. Its Luganda name comes from a word meaning 'to seize'. It is described as 20 to 30 feet long, with smooth dark skin and a rounded head, and it was blamed for attacks on fishermen and their canoes.

British administrator C. W. Hobley wrote in 1913 that people on both sides of the lake, including the Luo, told stories of it overturning fishing boats. He was unsure whether the tales came from big pythons or an unknown animal. A 1937 article on 'African mystery beasts' kept the idea of an unknown animal alive.
There is no scientific evidence for such an animal, and most modern writers treat the lukwata as part of the lake's cultural history rather than a zoological mystery.
signs: A long, dark, smooth-skinned body in the water
A rounded head
Canoes attacked or overturned

famous.name: C. W. Hobley records Lukwata stories around the lake

name: Dingonek
region: Rivers flowing into Lake Victoria, western Kenya
first: Reported by hunter John Alfred Jordan in 1907; published in 1910
summary: A scaly, tusked water beast a hunter said he shot at in a Kenyan river in 1907.
body: The dingonek is a strange water animal that big-game hunter John Alfred Jordan said he saw in 1907 on the Migori (then 'Maggori') River, which flows into Lake Victoria. His friend Edgar Beecher Bronson told the story in his 1910 memoir In Closed Territory.

Jordan described it as about 14 or 15 feet long, with a broad head, spotted leopard-like markings, scales and two long downward fangs or tusks. He said he fired a .303 rifle at it, the animal leapt from the water, and he ran. He searched the river banks for two days but never saw it again.

Colonial official C. W. Hobley mentioned the account in a 1913 natural history article alongside other Lake Victoria monster stories, and Jordan later wrote it up himself. Suggestions range from a misread crocodile or hippo to pure exaggeration.
signs: A long, scaly body in a river
Leopard-like spots
Two large tusks or fangs
Unaffected by a rifle shot

famous.name: John Alfred Jordan fires at the dingonek

name: Mbielu-mbielu-mbielu
aliases: Animal with planks growing out of its back
region: Likouala swamps, northern Republic of the Congo
first: Collected by biologist Roy Mackal around 1980
summary: A Congo river animal said to have planks growing from its back, sometimes called a living stegosaur.
body: Mbielu-mbielu-mbielu means 'the animal with planks growing out of its back'. It is said to live in the rivers and lakes of the Likouala swamp region of the northern Republic of the Congo, the same area linked with mokele-mbembe and emela-ntouka.
It is described as staying mostly underwater with only its back showing, and the 'planks' are often said to be green with algae. The first reported sighting is placed near Epena.

Biologist Roy Mackal gathered descriptions on his Congo trips around 1980. One local woman picked out a picture of a Stegosaurus, though she said she had never seen the animal and was repeating what her elders told her. Mackal himself leaned towards a large monitor lizard, and others suggest a crocodile with a ridged back.
signs: A ridged or plated back just above the water
Plates green with algae
Mostly active in the afternoon

famous.name: Roy Mackal's expedition collects descriptions
famous.place: Epena, Likouala, Republic of the Congo

name: Mamlambo
region: Mzintlava River near Mount Ayliff, Eastern Cape, South Africa
first: A river being of Zulu and Xhosa belief; news reports in 1997
summary: A river serpent of southern African belief, blamed for drownings on the Mzintlava River in 1997.
body: Mamlambo is a powerful river being in Zulu and other southern African traditions, often described as a huge snake-like creature and sometimes linked to wealth and its dangers.

In early 1997 South African newspapers reported that villagers near Mount Ayliff blamed a 'giant reptile' in the Mzintlava River for several deaths. They described a creature about 20 metres long with a horse-like head, a snake's neck, short legs and a fish-like tail, glowing green at night. Police said the injuries on the bodies came from crabs after drowning.
The panic earned the creature the nickname 'the brain sucker'. A later TV expedition found nothing.
signs: A long serpent with a horse-like head
A green glow in the river at night
Drownings blamed on the creature

famous.name: Villagers blame drownings on a giant river reptile
famous.place: Mount Ayliff, Eastern Cape, South Africa

name: Tokoloshe
region: South Africa, Lesotho, Eswatini and neighbouring countries
first: A long-standing belief among Nguni-speaking peoples
summary: A small, mischievous or harmful spirit of southern African belief; beds are raised on bricks against it.
body: The tokoloshe is a small, dwarf-like spirit in the beliefs of Zulu, Xhosa and other Nguni-speaking peoples. It is said to be summoned by people who wish others harm, to make itself invisible, and to cause trouble, illness or worse. It is a living belief for many families, and it is also joked about and used in satire in South Africa.

The best-known protection is raising a bed on bricks so the short tokoloshe cannot reach the sleeper. One explanation for this custom is that people sleeping on the floor beside indoor fires were at risk from carbon monoxide, which pools low, while those on raised beds survived.
Stories of tokoloshe scares still turn up in South African news. Traditional healers and church ministers are called on to drive it away.
signs: A small, hairy figure seen at night
Noises and attacks blamed on an invisible presence
Beds raised on bricks for protection

name: Barmanou
region: Chitral and the Hindu Kush, northern Pakistan and Afghanistan
first: Local tradition; researched by Jordi Magraner from 1987
summary: A hairy wild man said to live in the mountains of northern Pakistan, between Yeti and Almas country.
body: The barmanou is an upright, hairy wild man reported by shepherds in the mountains of northern Pakistan and Afghanistan, especially the Chitral district. Its range sits between the Himalaya of the Yeti and the Central Asian home of the Almas.

Local stories describe it as part human and part ape, sometimes draped in animal skins, and say it has tried to carry off women. The name comes from the Khowar language and is used across several regional languages.

Spanish-born zoologist Jordi Magraner searched for it from 1987 and said he collected more than 50 eyewitness accounts. In 1994 he and colleagues reported hearing deep guttural calls one evening in the Shishikoh valley. Magraner was murdered in the region in 2002, and no physical evidence has been confirmed.
signs: A hairy, upright figure in high valleys
Animal skins worn on the back or head
Deep guttural calls at dusk
Said to carry off women

famous.name: Magraner's team hears unexplained guttural calls in the Shishikoh valley

name: Mande Barung
aliases: Forest man of the Garo Hills
region: Garo Hills, Meghalaya, north-east India
first: Local Garo tradition; reported in the press from the 2000s
summary: A large, hairy, upright 'forest man' reported from the Garo Hills of north-east India.
body: Mande Barung means 'forest man' in the Garo language. It is described as a large, hairy, upright ape-like creature living in the subtropical forests of the remote Garo Hills in Meghalaya.

Local hunters and villagers tell of seeing it in thick forest and of finding big footprints and broken branches. Similar 'wild man' stories exist next door in Bangladesh (ban manush) and across the Himalaya.
No physical evidence has been confirmed, and sceptics point to bears, which live in the region.
signs: A tall, hairy figure walking upright
Large footprints
Branches broken at a height

name: Nittaewo
region: Mahalenama area, south-east Sri Lanka
first: Recorded by Hugh Nevill in 1887 from Vedda oral history
summary: Small, hairy, clawed wild people of Vedda tradition in Sri Lanka, said to have been wiped out about 1800.
body: In the traditions of Sri Lanka's Vedda people, the nittaewo were a tribe of small, hairy, upright beings about 3 to 4 feet tall, with short powerful arms and long claws. They were said to live in caves or nests in trees, hunt small animals, and speak in a twittering language.

The best-known story says the Veddas trapped the last of them in a cave and smoked them out, sometime around the late 1700s. Explorer Hugh Nevill wrote this down in 1887 from a chain of tellers, and colonial official Frederick Lewis heard the same story from older Veddas in 1915.

In 1963 an army captain searched caves at Kudumbigala and found shells and turtle bones. Odd reports have surfaced since, including a wave of village scares in 2019, but those described a very different creature. Primatologists have suggested the legend may reflect gibbons, bears or even memories of another human group.
signs: Small, hairy upright figures
Long claws on short arms
Twittering, bird-like speech
Nests in trees or caves

famous.name: Army captain searches the Kudumbigala caves

name: Chuchuna
region: Yakutia (Sakha Republic), north-east Siberia
first: Told among Yakut (Sakha) and Evenk (Tungus) peoples; studied by Soviet researchers in the 20th century
summary: A tall, dark-haired wild man of Siberian folklore, said to wear animal skins.
body: The chuchuna is a wild man of north-east Siberia, described in stories told by the Yakut (Sakha) and Evenk (Tungus) peoples. It is said to be six to seven feet tall, covered in dark hair, powerfully built and dressed in animal skins, sometimes with a pale patch of fur on its arms.

Some stories make it dangerous and say it would steal food or attack people, and it is sometimes counted as a northern cousin of Central Asia's Almas. Soviet-era 'snowman' researchers collected Siberian accounts in the 20th century.
No physical evidence has been found. It is mostly known through folklore collections and cryptozoology books.
signs: A tall, dark-haired man-like figure
Animal skins worn as clothing
A white patch on the forearms
Food taken from camps

name: Amomongo
region: Foot of Mount Kanlaon, La Castellana, Negros Occidental, Philippines
first: A Negros folktale creature; a widely reported attack scare in June 2008
summary: A hairy, long-nailed ape said to live in caves on Mount Kanlaon, blamed for a 2008 scare.
body: The amomongo is an ape-like creature in the folklore of Negros island in the Philippines, said to live in caves near the foot of the volcano Mount Kanlaon. Its name likely comes from the Hiligaynon word for ape or monkey.

In June 2008, residents of La Castellana said an amomongo clawed two men, leaving them with scratches, and killed goats and chickens over two nights. Witnesses described a hairy ape with long sharp nails, about the height of a person.
Local people describe it as a wild animal rather than a supernatural being. Officials and scientists suggested a misidentified animal, such as a large monkey or wild cat, and nothing was caught.
signs: A hairy, man-sized ape
Long, sharp nails
Livestock killed and entrails eaten
Coming from caves

famous.name: Two men clawed and livestock killed in a two-night scare

name: Orang Mawas
region: Endau-Rompin forests of Johor, Malaysia
first: Claims recorded from 1871
summary: A tall, black-furred wild man said to roam the jungles of Johor in southern Malaysia.
body: The orang mawas, or simply mawas, is a hairy, upright creature reported in the jungles of Johor in southern Malaysia, and sometimes in Singapore. It is described as tall, covered in black fur, and seen catching fish and raiding fruit orchards.
Local Orang Asli people call it hantu jarang gigi, the 'snaggle-toothed ghost'. Claimed sightings go back to 1871, and a burst of reports in the mid-2000s drew national news coverage in Malaysia.
Some fans link it to the extinct giant ape Gigantopithecus. Scientists point to misidentified sun bears or orangutan stories, as 'mawas' is also a Sumatran name for the orangutan.
signs: A tall figure with black fur walking upright
Large footprints near rivers
Fruit orchards raided
Fish taken from rivers

name: Issie
region: Lake Ikeda, Ibusuki, Kagoshima, Kyushu, Japan
first: Local legend; a wave of sightings in 1978
summary: A humped lake monster said to live in Lake Ikeda, the largest lake on Japan's Kyushu island.
body: Issie is Japan's best-known lake monster, said to live in Lake Ikeda, a deep volcanic caldera lake near Ibusuki at the southern tip of Kyushu. The name copies Nessie of Loch Ness.

A local tale says Issie was once a white mare who lost her foal and threw herself into the lake in grief, becoming a giant beast that still surfaces looking for it. In 1978 about twenty people said they saw a dark animal with two humps swimming in the lake, and a man named Matsubara took a photograph.
Lake Ikeda is home to very large eels, some around six feet long, which are the most common explanation. Issie is now a local mascot.
signs: Two dark humps moving across the lake
A large wake on calm water
Something long just below the surface

famous.name: About twenty people see a two-humped creature; a photo is taken

name: Labynkyr Devil
region: Lake Labynkyr, Oymyakon district, Yakutia, Russia
first: Local tales; first written about by geologist Viktor Tverdokhlebov in 1953
summary: A lake monster said to lurk in a remote, ice-bound lake near the coldest inhabited place on Earth.
body: The Labynkyr Devil is a creature said to live in Lake Labynkyr, a deep, remote lake in Yakutia near Oymyakon, one of the coldest inhabited places in the world. Local stories tell of a large dark animal living in the lake.

The earliest written mention is from geologist Viktor Tverdokhlebov, who wrote in 1953 about the lake and the ideas people had about it, from a giant pike to a surviving reptile. Later visitors reported large objects on sonar.

In 2013 a Russian expedition dived under the winter ice and set a record for depth under ice. Divers saw nothing larger than fish, though some press reports claimed a scan had picked up bones. A giant pike is the usual explanation.
signs: A dark shape surfacing in a cold lake
Large objects on sonar
Strange waves on calm water

famous.name: Geologist Viktor Tverdokhlebov writes about the lake creature
Expedition makes a record dive under the lake's ice

name: Lake Van Monster
region: Lake Van, eastern Turkey
first: Armenian dragon (vishap) lore; an Ottoman newspaper report in 1889; modern sightings from 1995
summary: A lake monster in Turkey's huge soda lake, made famous by a disputed 1997 video.
body: Lake Van in eastern Turkey has two kinds of monster story. Old Armenian writers told of vishaps, water dragons living in the lake, and of the god Vahagn hauling them out. In 1889 the Ottoman newspaper Saadet reported a creature dragging a man into the lake, and a government team went to look but found nothing.
The modern legend began with sightings in the mid-1990s. In 1997 a local man, Ünal Kozak, released video he said showed the animal swimming, and a local academic wrote a book about it.

Critics noted the video seemed framed to hide a boat and that the 'breathing' looked like a steady release of air. Many locals saw the story as a tourism ploy. Lake Van is very salty and alkaline, and only one kind of fish, the pearl mullet, is common in it.
signs: A dark animal swimming at the surface
A spout or spray as it breathes
Seen near the shore

famous.name: Saadet newspaper says a creature dragged a man into the lake
Ünal Kozak films an alleged monster

name: Monkey-man of Delhi
region: East Delhi and nearby towns, India
first: A panic in May 2001
summary: A clawed, monkey-like attacker reported hundreds of times in Delhi in 2001, now seen as mass panic.
body: In May 2001 people in New Delhi began reporting night attacks by a monkey-like creature. Descriptions varied wildly: some said it was about four feet tall with black hair, a metal helmet, metal claws, glowing red eyes and buttons on its chest; others described an eight-foot muscular figure that leapt between rooftops.

More than 350 sightings were reported and about 60 people said they were injured. Police released sketches, and at least two people died after falling from roofs or stairwells in panic. The scare faded after a few weeks.

Researchers treat it as a case of mass hysteria fuelled by summer power cuts, people sleeping on rooftops in the heat, and news coverage. A similar scare, the 'muhnochwa', hit Uttar Pradesh the next year.
signs: A small, hairy, monkey-like attacker at night
Metal claws or a helmet
Leaping from roof to roof
Scratches on victims
size: 4 ft, sometimes said up to 8 ft (reported)
habitat: Rooftops and streets of a crowded city

name: Queensland tiger
region: Coastal ranges of north and south-east Queensland, Australia
first: Witness reports from 1871; an earlier Aboriginal tradition of the yarri
summary: A dog-sized, striped, tree-climbing cat reported in Queensland's forests since the 1870s.
body: The Queensland tiger is a striped, cat-like predator reported in the forests of Queensland. Witnesses describe an animal about the size of a dog, with stripes, a long tail, big front teeth and a fierce temper, and say it can climb trees.

The earliest written witness reports date from 1871. Norwegian naturalist Carl Lumholtz, exploring around the Herbert River in the 1880s, heard Aboriginal people describe a savage, dingo-sized, long-tailed animal they called the yarri. Australian Museum curator Ellis Troughton later included a 'striped marsupial cat' in his book on Australian mammals.
Some suggest a surviving marsupial lion (Thylacoleo) or a mainland thylacine. Modern sightings that have been checked, such as the 'Beast of Buderim', have usually turned out to be large feral cats.
signs: A dog-sized, striped cat
A long tail
Climbing trees when chased
Prominent front teeth

famous.name: Carl Lumholtz's Among Cannibals describes the yarri

name: Tantanoola Tiger
region: Tantanoola, Limestone Coast, South Australia
first: Livestock attacks in the 1880s and 1890s
summary: A 'tiger' blamed for sheep kills in South Australia in the 1890s; the animal shot was a wolf.
body: In the late 19th century farmers around Tantanoola in South Australia lost sheep to a mysterious predator that locals called the Tantanoola Tiger. Search parties were organised and the story spread widely in colonial newspapers.

In August 1895 a local man, Thomas Donovan, shot an animal believed to be the culprit. It turned out to be a wolf, later identified as an Arabian wolf. How it reached Australia has never been settled; theories include an escape from a ship.
The stuffed animal is still on display at the Tantanoola Hotel, and the local football club is called the Tigers. It is a rare case where a 'phantom cat' story ended with a body.
signs: Sheep killed at night
A large, striped or dog-like predator
Tracks bigger than a fox's

famous.name: Thomas Donovan shoots the 'tiger', which proves to be a wolf

name: Moehau monster
region: Moehau Range, Coromandel Peninsula, New Zealand
first: Linked to older Māori stories of the maero; 20th-century sighting stories
summary: A hairy wild man said to live in the bush of the Moehau Range on New Zealand's Coromandel Peninsula.
body: The Moehau monster is a hairy, man-like creature said to live in the bush of the Moehau Range at the tip of the Coromandel Peninsula. Some Māori link it to the maero, wild giants or 'wild men of the woods' in older stories.
One popular explanation was an escaped pet baboon from a ship anchored in the bay, but Auckland Zoo's director said such an animal could not survive in the New Zealand bush.

In 1970 local people told researcher Robyn Gosset that the 'hairy Moehau' started as a joke, and that the name 'Moehau Monster' had once been the nickname of an American steam log hauler. New Zealand has no native apes, and no evidence has been found.
signs: A tall, hairy figure in thick bush
Large tracks
Screams in the forest

name: Waitoreke
region: Rivers and lakes of New Zealand's South Island
first: A four-footed animal seen by Captain Cook's crew at Dusky Sound in 1773
summary: A small, otter-like animal reported from New Zealand's South Island, where no such mammal is known.
body: The waitoreke is a small, otter- or beaver-like animal reported in New Zealand's South Island for over 200 years. New Zealand's only native land mammals are bats, so any furry swimmer would be a real mystery.

On Captain Cook's second voyage, crew members at Dusky Sound saw a cat-sized, short-legged, mouse-coloured animal in 1773. Geologist Julius von Haast reportedly obtained a brown pelt with white spots in 1868, which sounds more like a quoll. Reports clustered around Otautau in Southland.
Suggested explanations include seals, escaped or introduced animals, or stories that grew in the telling. Nothing has been confirmed.
signs: A cat-sized, brown, furry animal near water
Short legs and a long tail
Swimming like an otter

famous.name: Cook's crew see a cat-sized four-footed animal

name: Mono Grande
region: Forests of Venezuela, Colombia and the Guianas
first: Wild-man tales heard by Alexander von Humboldt around 1800; de Loys photo published 1929
summary: A large, tailless ape said to live in South American forests, famous for the de Loys photo.
body: Mono Grande means 'big monkey'. It refers to reports of a large, tailless, ape-like animal in the forests of northern South America, where no apes are known to live. Explorer Alexander von Humboldt heard stories around 1800 of hairy wild people called salvajes on the Orinoco, though he did not believe them.

The most famous piece of evidence is a photograph taken by Swiss geologist François de Loys during an expedition near the Colombia-Venezuela border around 1920. It shows a dead, upright-propped animal his party had shot. Anthropologist George Montandon published it in 1929 and named it a new species.
Experts quickly identified the animal as a spider monkey with its tail hidden or removed, and the photo is now widely considered a hoax. Similar photos appeared in the 1950s.
signs: A large, tailless monkey walking upright
Aggressive behaviour, throwing branches
Seen in riverside forest

name: Minhocão
