region: Southern Brazil, including Santa Catarina and Paraná
first: Described to naturalist Auguste de Saint-Hilaire in the 1840s; Fritz Müller wrote about it in 1878
summary: A colossal worm of Brazilian folklore blamed for trenches, toppled trees and lost cattle.
body: The minhocão (Portuguese for 'big earthworm') is a giant burrowing creature of Brazilian folklore. Nineteenth-century accounts describe a worm-like animal up to 50 yards long, with a hard, scaly or armoured skin, sometimes with horns or a pig-like snout, that ploughs deep trenches, uproots trees and pulls animals into water.

French naturalist Auguste de Saint-Hilaire recorded stories of it dragging horses and cattle under the water in lakes. In 1878 German naturalist Fritz Müller published accounts gathered in the southern highlands, including from a resident of Curitibanos, and the journal Nature summarised them.

Suggested explanations include large lungfish, a giant caecilian, or a folk memory of the giant armadillos that once lived in the region. The trenches it was blamed for may simply have been erosion after heavy rain.
signs: Long, deep trenches appearing after rain
Uprooted trees and diverted streams
Rumbling like thunder underground
Livestock dragged into water

famous.name: Fritz Müller publishes highland accounts of the minhocão

name: Cadejo
region: Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica and southern Mexico
first: A long-standing Central American folk belief with Maya and Nahua roots
summary: A spectral dog of Central American folklore: a white one protects night travellers, a black one hunts them.
body: The cadejo is a ghostly dog that appears to people walking lonely roads at night in Central America and parts of Mexico. It is usually described as a large, shaggy dog, sometimes as big as a cow, with glowing eyes, sometimes with goat hooves, and dragging chains.

In many places there are two: a white cadejo that guards travellers, and a black cadejo that tries to kill them and is linked to the devil. In Guatemala and El Salvador the cadejo is also said to protect drunk people on their way home. In Costa Rica it is a single black dog that is frightening but usually harmless.
Folklorists trace it to Maya and Nahua beliefs about animal companions and dogs that guide the dead, blended with European black dog stories.
signs: A huge shaggy dog following you at night
Glowing red or blue eyes
The sound of chains or goat-like hooves
A strong goat-like smell
size: Large dog, up to calf- or cow-sized (in folklore)
habitat: Rural roads and village lanes at night

name: Huay Chivo
region: Yucatán Peninsula, Mexico, and Guatemala
first: A Maya folk belief; reported in the regional press
summary: A Maya sorcerer said to turn into a red-eyed goat or dog to prey on livestock in the Yucatán.
body: The huay chivo is a figure of Maya folklore in the Yucatán Peninsula and Guatemala: a sorcerer who can turn into an animal, usually a goat, dog or deer, to raid livestock at night. Its name mixes the Yucatec Maya word for sorcerer or animal spirit with the Spanish word for goat.
Witnesses describe a half-man, half-beast with burning red eyes. In recent decades livestock killings in the region have sometimes been blamed on it, and it is often linked with the chupacabra.
It is a local version of the wider Mesoamerican nahual, a person who takes animal form.
signs: A goat- or dog-like animal with glowing red eyes
Livestock found dead at night
A figure that seems part man, part beast

name: Moca Vampire
region: Moca and other towns in Puerto Rico
first: Newspaper reports from Moca, February 1975
summary: Unknown attacker blamed for blood-drained livestock in Puerto Rico in 1975, a forerunner of the chupacabra.
body: In February 1975 newspapers in Puerto Rico reported that farm animals in the Rocha neighbourhood of Moca had been found dead with puncture wounds and their blood apparently drained. The toll included fifteen cows, three goats, two geese and a pig. The unknown killer was dubbed the Vampiro de Moca.

Similar reports followed during 1975 in Corozal, Fajardo and rural San Juan, and some residents linked the deaths to UFO sightings. No culprit was ever identified, though feral dogs and other predators were suggested.
When livestock killings were reported again in Canóvanas in the 1990s, the attacker got a new name: the chupacabra. Moca's vampire is often seen as its direct ancestor.
signs: Livestock with puncture wounds
Bodies that appear drained of blood
Strange lights reported nearby

name: Lusca
region: Blue holes around Andros, The Bahamas
first: Local lore reported by visiting scientists in the mid-20th century; a large dead octopus reported in 1872
summary: A giant octopus-like monster said to lurk in the blue holes of Andros in the Bahamas.
body: The lusca is a sea monster of Bahamian lore said to live in the blue holes around Andros, the deep underwater caves and sinkholes that dot the island and its shallows. It is described as a giant octopus, a giant cuttlefish, or half shark and half octopus, said to grab swimmers and fishing boats and drag them down.

Divers and scientists who explored the blue holes heard the stories from local guides. One diver, George Benjamin, wrote in a 1970 National Geographic article that a guide warned him the lusca, 'Him of the Hands', would kill him if he went in. In 1872 a resident of Nassau reported a large dead octopus on a beach.
Strong tidal currents in the blue holes create whirlpools that can pull down debris and small boats, which may explain the legend.
signs: Long tentacles rising from a blue hole
Whirlpools and sudden sucking currents
Boats or swimmers pulled under

famous.name: Diver George Benjamin's National Geographic article on the blue holes

name: Morgawr
region: Falmouth Bay and the Helford River, Cornwall, England
first: A wave of reports in 1975 and 1976
summary: A long-necked sea serpent reported in Falmouth Bay in the 1970s, now widely thought to be a hoax.
body: Morgawr (Cornish for 'sea giant') is a long-necked sea serpent said to live in Falmouth Bay, Cornwall. The first reports came in 1975, describing a humped animal with a long neck and dark skin like a sea lion's near Pendennis Point.

In 1976 the local Falmouth Packet newspaper received photographs said to be from an anonymous 'Mary F', and that July two fishermen said they saw it off Lizard Point. Local showman and magician Tony 'Doc' Shiels, who coined the name, also claimed to photograph it near Mawnan.

A 2022 academic article concluded the whole story began as a hoax, with Shiels at the centre. Sightings are still claimed along the stretch of coast between Rosemullion Head and Toll Point, nicknamed Morgawr's Mile. Owlman, also linked to Shiels, was reported nearby in the same year.
signs: A long neck and small head above the water
Humps on the back
Dark, sea-lion-like skin

famous.name: 'Mary F' photographs sent to the Falmouth Packet
Two fishermen report the creature off Lizard Point

name: Selma
region: Lake Seljordsvatnet, Seljord, Telemark, Norway
first: Earliest written account from 1750
summary: A serpent said to live in Lake Seljord in Norway since at least 1750, now on the town's coat of arms.
body: Selma is a lake serpent said to live in Seljordsvatnet, a long, narrow lake in Telemark, southern Norway. Sightings tend to cluster in hot, calm summers, and witnesses describe a long, dark, humped animal, sometimes with a horse-like or crocodile-like head.

The oldest written account dates from 1750, when a man rowing across the lake said the creature circled his boat. Reports have continued since, and several sonar and camera searches were made from the 1970s onwards, with no conclusive result.
Selma has been on Seljord's municipal coat of arms since 1989, shown in gold on a red background.
signs: A long dark body with humps
A head like a horse or crocodile
Boats bumped or circled
Seen in hot, still summer weather

famous.name: Oldest written account of the serpent

name: Gwyllgi
region: Wales, especially the Nant y Garth Pass, Denbighshire
first: A traditional Welsh black dog legend
summary: A ghostly black mastiff of Welsh folklore with red eyes and foul breath, seen on lonely roads.
body: The gwyllgi, roughly 'dog of darkness' or 'wild dog', is the Welsh version of the phantom black dog. It is described as a huge mastiff or black wolf with blazing red eyes and terrible breath, appearing to travellers on lonely roads at night.

It is linked to the Cŵn Annwn, the hounds of the Otherworld in Welsh tradition, and to the 'corpse dog' that foretells a death. The Nant y Garth Pass near Llandegla in Denbighshire is its best-known haunt, and reports also come from around Marchwiel near Wrexham.
It is one of many black dog legends found across Britain, including the barghest, Black Shuck and the Isle of Man's Moddey Dhoo.
signs: A huge black dog with red eyes on a dark road
Foul breath
Following travellers silently

name: Moddey Dhoo
region: Peel Castle and the Isle of Man
first: Described by George Waldron in an account published in 1731
summary: A phantom black dog said to haunt Peel Castle on the Isle of Man.
body: The Moddey Dhoo (Manx for 'black dog') is a phantom hound said to haunt Peel Castle on the west coast of the Isle of Man. English writer George Waldron recorded the story in the early 1700s: a large, shaggy black dog used to come into the guardroom at dusk and lie by the fire until morning.

In Waldron's telling, a drunken soldier insisted on carrying the keys alone through the passage the dog used. He came back speechless with fear and died three days later, and the passage was sealed. Sir Walter Scott later used the tale in his 1823 novel Peveril of the Peak.

Folklorist William Walter Gill collected more modern Manx sightings. In one, a doctor driving near Milntown, outside Ramsey, in 1931 met a black dog-like creature nearly the size of a calf with staring eyes.
signs: A large, shaggy black dog
Eyes like burning coals
Appearing at dusk and leaving at dawn
Linked to a death soon after

famous.name: George Waldron's description of the Isle of Man is published
Doctor meets a calf-sized black dog near Milntown

name: Wulver
region: Shetland Islands, Scotland
first: Described by Shetland writer Jessie Saxby in the early 20th century
summary: A gentle wolf-headed man of Shetland folklore said to leave fish for poor families.
body: The wulver is a wolf-headed, hairy man from Shetland folklore. Unlike most werewolves, it was said to be harmless if left alone. Shetland writer Jessie Saxby described it fishing from a rock and leaving some of its catch on the windowsills of poor families.
Some later writers say it was never human at all but a separate kind of being, and some versions say it could turn dangerous if provoked.

There is a twist: Shetland Museum archivist Brian Smith has argued that the wulver may never have been a real island tradition. He suggests Saxby misread a place name, Wulvers Hool, which earlier scholars had translated as a fairy hill.
signs: A man-like figure with a wolf's head
Short brown hair all over
Fish left on windowsills

name: Wolpertinger
region: Forests of Bavaria and Baden-Württemberg, Germany
first: Horned-hare images in 17th-century engravings; taxidermy jokes from the 1800s
summary: A Bavarian joke animal stitched from rabbit, antlers and wings; a cousin of the jackalope.
body: The wolpertinger is a mock creature of Bavarian folklore, said to live in the Alpine forests of southern Germany. It is usually shown as a rabbit or squirrel with deer antlers, bird wings and fangs, and no two are alike.

Bavarian taxidermists began making stuffed wolpertingers from real animal parts in the 1800s, both for fun and to sell to visitors. They still hang in inns and souvenir shops, and the German Hunting and Fishing Museum in Munich has a display of them. Tradition says only beautiful young women can see one, at full moon, if led to the right spot by the right man.
Like the jackalope, the idea may draw on real rabbits with horn-like growths caused by the Shope papilloma virus. Neighbouring regions have their own versions, such as Thuringia's rasselbock.
signs: A small furry animal with antlers and wings
Stuffed specimens in country inns
Stories told to tourists

name: Gef the talking mongoose
region: Cashen's Gap, near Dalby, Isle of Man
first: Reported by the Irving family from September 1931
summary: A talking 'mongoose' an Isle of Man family said lived in their farmhouse walls in the 1930s.
body: In 1931 the Irving family, who farmed at Cashen's Gap near Dalby on the Isle of Man, said a small animal living behind the wooden panelling of their house had begun talking to them. It called itself Gef, said it was a mongoose born in India in 1852, and chatted, sang, swore and reported local gossip. The Irvings' teenage daughter Voirrey described it as rat-sized and yellowish with a bushy tail.

The story became a sensation in the British press. Ghost hunter Harry Price and journalist Richard Lambert visited in 1935 and wrote a book about it. Hair samples said to be Gef's turned out to be from the family's sheepdog, and an expert said prints in plasticine were not a mongoose's.
Most investigators concluded it was a hoax, perhaps using ventriloquism. The family left in 1945. Voirrey, who died in 2005, always said she did not invent Gef.
signs: A voice speaking from inside walls
A small yellowish animal glimpsed briefly
Scratching and rustling in panelling

famous.name: Irving family report a talking animal in their walls
Harry Price and Richard Lambert investigate

name: Steller's sea ape
region: Shumagin Islands and the Aleutians, Alaska
first: Seen by naturalist Georg Steller on 10 August 1741
summary: A playful, whiskered, dog-headed sea animal a naturalist watched off Alaska in 1741 and never identified.
body: On 10 August 1741, naturalist Georg Steller, sailing with Vitus Bering's expedition, watched a strange animal swimming near the ship off the Shumagin Islands in Alaska for about two hours. He described it as about five feet long, with a dog-like head, pointed ears, large eyes and drooping whiskers, a thick grey and reddish fur coat, no visible front limbs and a tail with two fins like a shark's.

It rose upright in the water, dived under the ship again and again, and played with a long piece of seaweed. Steller fired at it to get a specimen but missed, and it swam away. In 1965 sailor Miles Smeeton and two companions reported a similar animal off Atka Island.
Several naturalists later gave it scientific names, but most experts think Steller saw a young northern fur seal behaving unusually.
signs: A dog-like head with long whiskers
Rising upright in the water
Playful, curious behaviour around a boat
Thick grey and reddish fur

famous.name: Georg Steller watches the 'sea ape' for two hours
Miles Smeeton reports a similar animal

name: Turtle Lake Monster
region: Turtle Lake, west-central Saskatchewan, Canada
first: Older Cree stories; regular sighting reports from the 20th century
summary: A large, dog- or pig-headed lake creature reported about once a year in a Saskatchewan lake.
body: The Turtle Lake Monster is said to live in Turtle Lake in west-central Saskatchewan. Witnesses describe a long animal with no back fin, scaly or smooth skin, and a head like a dog's, a pig's or a seahorse's. Someone reports seeing it roughly once a year.

Local Cree tradition is said to include stories of people who went into its waters and vanished. In one well-known report, a man fishing with his daughter and grandson said its head and back came up and it rolled over, and its head looked like a seahorse's.
Fisheries biologists suggest a very large lake sturgeon, which can grow huge and live for a century.
signs: A long back rolling at the surface
A dog-, pig- or seahorse-like head
No dorsal fin

name: Mussie
region: Muskrat Lake, Cobden, Ontario, Canada
first: Anecdotes from about 1916
summary: A friendly lake monster of Muskrat Lake, Ontario, sometimes said to have three eyes.
body: Mussie is the monster of Muskrat Lake, a long, deep lake beside the village of Cobden, about 75 miles north-west of Ottawa. Descriptions vary: a walrus-like animal, a big sturgeon, or a Nessie-type creature with three eyes and sharp teeth.

Stories go back to around 1916, when it was called Hapyxelor. A local claim that Samuel de Champlain wrote about it in the 1600s has no evidence behind it. A sonar search by author Michael Bradley picked up two large shapes he thought could be marine mammals.
Mussie is now a cheerful local mascot on welcome signs, sometimes wearing a Santa hat. A 1990s tourism campaign offered a million dollars for a live capture, which no one claimed.
signs: A walrus-like or long-necked animal
Three eyes (in some stories)
Large shapes on sonar

famous.name: First anecdotes of the lake creature

name: Old Ned
region: Lake Utopia, Charlotte County, New Brunswick, Canada
first: An old local story said to come from the Maliseet; reported through the 19th and 20th centuries
summary: A whale-like creature said to live in Lake Utopia, New Brunswick, near the Bay of Fundy.
body: Old Ned is the monster of Lake Utopia, a lake in southern New Brunswick near St. George and the Bay of Fundy. Local legend says that long ago two Maliseet men canoeing on the lake were chased from one end to the other by the creature.

It is described as long and bulky, more like a whale than a serpent, and is sometimes said to travel between the lake and the sea. A 1908 report by a schooner crew of a sea serpent in the Bay of Fundy near Cutler, Maine is often linked to it.
Other explanations include large fish, floating logs and waves.
signs: A long, bulky, whale-like body
A large wake
Something chasing a boat

famous.name: Schooner crew reports a sea serpent in the Bay of Fundy

name: Sharlie
region: Payette Lake, McCall, Idaho
first: First settler sighting in 1920; named in a 1954 contest
summary: A 30 to 40 ft humped serpent reported in Idaho's Payette Lake since 1920.
body: Sharlie is the lake monster of Payette Lake, a deep mountain lake at McCall in central Idaho. The first settler report came in 1920, when workers cutting railroad ties saw what looked like a log start to move.

In August 1944 several groups described a 30 to 35 foot animal with a dinosaur-like head, humps like a camel and shell-like skin. In September 1946 about twenty people, including a doctor from Nampa, said they saw something 30 to 40 feet long diving repeatedly and leaving a wake like a small motorboat.
In 1954 the local newspaper ran a contest to name it, and the winning entry, 'Sharlie', came from a radio catchphrase, 'Vas you der, Sharlie?' Sightings were reported until at least 1997.
signs: A moving 'log' on the water
Camel-like humps
A dinosaur-like head
A boat-sized wake

famous.name: Tie cutters see a 'log' start to move
About twenty people watch a 30 to 40 ft creature diving
Newspaper contest names the serpent Sharlie

name: Wild Man of the Navidad
region: Navidad River bottoms, Lavaca and Jackson counties, Texas
first: Settler reports from about 1836; capture in 1851
summary: A 'wild man' stealing food along a Texas river in the 1830s-1850s, later identified as an escaped enslaved man.
body: From about 1836, settlers along the Navidad River in south-east Texas, near present-day Sublime, reported food and tools going missing at night. Tools were sometimes returned polished, and only half the food was taken. Some described hair-covered wild people, and enslaved people on nearby farms called the visitor 'the thing that comes'.

In 1851 residents captured a man living in the woods who spoke no English. A former Lavaca County historical marker said he was an African-born man, the son of a chief, who had escaped slavery with a companion who died. He was sold back into slavery and died in 1884. The story was collected by folklorist J. Frank Dobie in 1928.
In recent times the tale has been retold as a Bigfoot story, and a 2008 horror film borrowed its name. The historical record points to a real person surviving alone in the wild.
signs: Food taken at night, with half left behind
Tools borrowed and returned polished
A hairy figure glimpsed in river woods

famous.name: Settlers report night thefts along the Navidad bottoms

name: Kushtaka
region: South-east Alaska and the northern British Columbia coast
first: A Tlingit belief; recorded by ethnographers by the early 1900s
summary: A shape-shifting 'land otter man' of Tlingit belief; the name is now used widely in Alaskan monster stories.
body: Kóoshdaa káa, often written kushtaka, means 'land otter man' in Tlingit. In Tlingit belief it is a being that can take human or otter form, linked to people lost at sea or in the woods. It is part of a living culture, and this entry does not retell traditional stories.

Outside Tlingit communities, the kushtaka has become a popular monster in Alaskan horror fiction, TV shows and online stories, where it is described as luring people to rivers with the sound of a crying baby or a woman's scream. Similar beings appear in the traditions of other Alaska Native and Northwest Coast peoples.
A well-known non-Native tale by Harry Colp, about miners at Thomas Bay near Petersburg, describes hairy, man-like creatures that some later writers identify as kushtaka.
signs: In modern stories: a crying baby or scream near water
An otter-like figure on land
A three-part whistle

name: Vegetable Man
region: Grant Town, Marion County, West Virginia
first: Claimed encounter in July 1968; first printed by Gray Barker in 1976
summary: A thin, plant-like humanoid a West Virginia man said grabbed him in 1968; only told by a known hoaxer.
body: The Vegetable Man is a West Virginia creature based on one man's story. Jennings Frederick said that in July 1968, while hunting groundhogs near Grant Town, he heard high-pitched jabbering, received a message asking for help, and was grabbed by a seven-foot humanoid with very thin, plant-like arms and long fingers tipped with needles and suction cups that drew his blood.

He said its yellow eyes turned red and it bounded away in huge leaps, after which he heard humming from the woods. The account was first published in 1976 by Gray Barker, a writer known for promoting and inventing UFO stories, including the Men in Black.
A Skeptical Inquirer investigation found the story rests entirely on a single witness reported by a known hoaxer. Fairmont now holds an annual Veggie Man Day celebrating West Virginia cryptids.
signs: A thin, green, plant-like humanoid
Long fingers with needle tips
High-pitched jabbering
Yellow eyes turning red

name: Piasa
region: Mississippi River bluffs at Alton, Illinois
first: Rock paintings described by Marquette and Jolliet in 1673
summary: A monster painted on Mississippi River bluffs, seen by French explorers in 1673; later retold as a giant bird.
body: The Piasa takes its name from a Native American rock painting high on the limestone bluffs above the Mississippi River at present-day Alton, Illinois. French explorers Jacques Marquette and Louis Jolliet saw paintings of two monsters there in 1673 and described a creature as big as a calf, with horns, red eyes, a man-like face, scales and a very long tail ending in a fish's fin. Scholars now see it as an underwater panther, a powerful water being in the region's Native traditions.

In 1836 writer John Russell published a dramatic story of a man-eating 'Piasa bird' defeated by a chief, and later pictures gave the creature wings. Many folklorists regard Russell's tale as invented.
The original painting was destroyed by quarrying in the 19th century. A large modern replica now stands on the bluff at Alton.
signs: In the old painting: horns, a bearded man-like face and red eyes
Scales and a very long tail
Wings in later retellings

famous.name: Marquette and Jolliet see the painted monsters

name: Fairies
region: Ireland and Britain, with relatives across Europe
first: Medieval Irish and British tales; Robert Kirk's Secret Commonwealth, 1691
summary: The hidden people of Irish and British folklore, still reported in gardens, woods and old forts.
body: Fairies are the 'Good People' or 'Gentry' of Irish and British folklore, a hidden race said to live alongside us in a world just out of sight. In Ireland they are the aos sí or daoine sídhe, the people of the fairy mounds. People used polite names for them on purpose, so as not to give offence. In the older stories they can be human-sized, beautiful and dangerous: they steal children and leave changelings, lead travellers astray and take offence at anyone who damages a fairy fort or lone hawthorn.

The tiny winged fairy of Victorian picture books came later. In 1691 Robert Kirk, minister of Aberfoyle in Scotland, wrote The Secret Commonwealth, a sober account of what his parishioners believed about fairies. The belief could have tragic results: in 1895 Bridget Cleary of County Tipperary was killed by her husband, who said he believed she had been replaced by a changeling.

Fairy experiences are still reported today. The Fairy Investigation Society, founded in Britain in 1927 and revived online by historian Simon Young in 2013, ran a Fairy Census from 2014 that gathered hundreds of first-hand accounts. People describe small figures in gardens and woods, lights, music and lost time. The most famous 'evidence', the Cottingley Fairies photographs of 1917, was a hoax: the two cousins who took them admitted in 1983 that they used cardboard cut-outs.
signs: Small human-like figures in gardens or woods
Music or voices with no source
Lights dancing near old forts or hawthorns
Getting lost on a familiar path
Time passing strangely
size: A few inches to human height (about 6 in to 5 ft)
habitat: Fairy forts (ringforts), lone hawthorns, hills, woods and gardens

famous.name: Robert Kirk writes The Secret Commonwealth
Murder of Bridget Cleary, said to be a changeling
Latoon fairy bush saved from the Ennis bypass

name: Tylwyth Teg
region: Wales
first: A 14th-century poem attributed to Dafydd ap Gwilym
summary: The 'Fair Family', the fairy people of Welsh folklore, known for fairy rings and lake maidens.
body: Tylwyth Teg means 'Fair Family' in Welsh, and it is the usual Welsh name for the fairy folk. In southern Wales they were also called Bendith y Mamau, 'the Mothers' Blessing', a polite name meant to keep them friendly. The name first turns up in a 14th-century poem attributed to Dafydd ap Gwilym.

In the stories they are fair-haired and love golden-haired human children, whom they may swap for changelings. They dance in fairy rings, ride in night-time processions, live underground or under lakes, and give gifts that vanish if spoken of. Households left out bowls of milk for them. They cannot bear iron.

The 19th-century folklorist Wirt Sikes sorted them into elves of the groves, mine fairies (coblynau), household fairies like brownies (bwbachod), lake maidens (gwragedd annwn) and hag-like mountain fairies (gwyllion). The best-known lake maiden rose from Llyn y Fan Fach in the Black Mountains, married a local farmer, and left when he struck her a third time. Her sons were said to become the Physicians of Myddfai.
signs: Rings of trampled or darker grass
Music and dancing at night
Night processions of riders
A child who suddenly seems changed
size: Human-sized or smaller; no fixed height
habitat: Hills, lakes, groves and underground halls

famous.name: Lady of Llyn y Fan Fach legend printed in Meddygon Myddvai

name: Pixies
region: Cornwall, Devon and Somerset, England
first: West Country folklore, recorded in the 18th and 19th centuries
summary: The small, mischievous little people of Cornwall and Devon, blamed for leading travellers astray.
body: Pixies (or piskies in Cornwall) are the little people of England's West Country, especially the moors of Cornwall and Devon. They are said to live in stone circles, barrows and caves, and to dance and wrestle through the night. The older stories describe them in ragged clothes; the pointed ears, green suits and pointy hats are Victorian additions.

Their best-known trick is being 'pixy-led': a walker loses the way on a familiar path and wanders in circles until they turn their coat inside out. Pixies also ride moorland ponies at night, leaving knots in their manes, and may help a poor widow with her housework.

Ottery St Mary in East Devon has a Pixie Day each June, re-enacting a legend that pixies were banished to a cave called the Pixies' Parlour. Samuel Taylor Coleridge, born in the town, wrote 'Songs of the Pixies' after visiting the cave in 1793. By 1824 the Cornish writer Samuel Drew was already saying that 'the age of pixies, like that of chivalry, is gone.'
signs: Getting lost on a path you know well
Tangled knots in a pony's mane
Laughter or music on the moor at night
Small figures in ragged clothes
size: Small; often described as knee-high or less
habitat: Moors, stone circles, barrows and caves

famous.name: Coleridge visits the Pixies' Parlour and writes Songs of the Pixies
Earliest Three Little Pigs tale, with pixies instead of pigs

name: Brownies
region: Scotland and northern England, with Welsh and Manx relatives
first: Scottish Lowlands, early 16th century
summary: A shaggy household spirit that does farm work at night in return for a bowl of cream.
body: The brownie is a household spirit from Scotland and the English border country. It comes out at night while the family sleeps and threshes grain, churns butter, sweeps and tends the animals. In return, the household leaves it a bowl of cream, milk or porridge by the hearth. The name comes from its colouring: brownies are described as brown-skinned, hairy and dressed in rags or nothing at all.

Brownies are easily offended. Criticise their work, watch them at it, or give them a gift of clothes, and they leave forever, sometimes wrecking things on the way out. Reginald Scot noted the clothing rule in 1584. In 1597 King James VI called the brownie a demon that appeared 'like a rough-man', though, he admitted, people believed it made the house luckier.

In the oldest stories brownies are human-sized or larger; later they became small and wizened. Juliana Horatia Ewing's 1865 story 'The Brownies' inspired the name of the youngest Girl Guides, and Palmer Cox's cartoon brownies of the 1880s made them a children's favourite. The Kodak Brownie camera took its name from them.
signs: Chores done overnight
Cream or porridge left out and found eaten
Things tidied, or thrown about if already tidy
Pinches for lazy servants
size: Small and wizened in later tales; human-sized in the oldest
habitat: Farmhouses, mills, barns and nearby caves or streams

name: Hob
region: Yorkshire, northern England and the Midlands
first: Northern English folklore; 'hob' recorded as a name for these spirits by the 16th century
summary: A small, hairy northern English farm spirit that helps out, but leaves if given new clothes.
body: A hob is a small household or farm spirit of northern England, especially Yorkshire. 'Hob' is a short form of Robin, and calling the spirit by a homely nickname was a way of making it less frightening. Hobs are described as small, hairy, wizened men who work at night in the farmyard or the house.

Like brownies, hobs are touchy. Speak badly of one and it may break dishes or let the cattle out. Give it a new shirt or hood and it vanishes, often with a rhyme such as 'Ha! a cap and a hood, Hob'll never do mair good.' A Farndale story tells of a farmer so plagued by his hob that he packed up to move, only to hear the hob say it was coming too.

Some hobs had their own homes in the landscape. The Hob Holes, sea caves at Runswick Bay on the North Yorkshire coast, were said to house a hob who could cure children of whooping cough. Mothers brought their children at low tide and called, 'Hob Hole hob, my child has the kin cough, take it off, take it off!'
signs: Farm work done overnight
Broken crockery after an insult
Livestock let loose
A spirit that follows a family when they move
habitat: Farms, caves, hills and burial mounds

name: Leprechaun
region: Ireland
first: Echtra Fergus mac Léti, an Irish tale dated to the 8th century
summary: Ireland's solitary little shoemaker, said to hide a crock of gold and grant wishes when caught.
body: The leprechaun is a small, solitary fairy of Irish folklore, usually pictured as a little old bearded man mending a single shoe. Catch him and keep your eyes on him, the stories say, and he must lead you to his hidden gold; look away for a second and he is gone. The earliest version appears in an 8th-century tale in which three lúchorpáin drag King Fergus mac Léti into the sea and grant him three wishes to let them go.

Before the 20th century, leprechauns were said to wear red, not green. Writing in 1888, David Russell McAnally described one as 'about three feet high' in a red jacket and cocked hat. The green suit, buckled hat and rainbow came later, partly through tourism and St Patrick's Day imagery. Irish folklorists see the leprechaun as separate from the aos sí, the more dangerous fairy host.

The Cooley Mountains above Carlingford in County Louth have become Ireland's best-known leprechaun country. Locals campaigned for years and, in 2010, newspapers reported that the area had become a protected zone for 'little people'. In fact the legal protection covers the mountain's wildlife habitat, but the annual leprechaun hunt goes on.
signs: A tapping sound like a tiny hammer
A small man in red or green, working on a shoe
Glint of gold that disappears
Gone the moment you look away
habitat: Fields, hedges, ringforts and remote hillsides

famous.name: Cooley Mountains 'protected zone' for little people reported

name: Púca
region: Ireland, with relatives in Wales, Cornwall and the Channel Islands
first: Irish and British folklore; strongly tied to Samhain
summary: An Irish shape-shifter that takes riders on wild night gallops, most often as a black horse.
body: The púca is a shape-shifting spirit of Irish folklore. It can appear as a horse, goat, cat, dog, hare or eagle, or as a person with animal ears or a tail, but it is usually dark-furred. Its favourite form is a sleek black horse with glowing eyes that tempts a traveller onto its back, then gallops off on a terrifying ride before dumping them back where they started.

The púca can help as well as frighten. Lady Wilde told of a púca that ground a farmer's corn every night until the farmer's son gave it a silk suit. It is closely tied to Samhain: crops left in the field after November 1st were 'púca' and not to be eaten, and some reapers left a 'púca's share' behind. In parts of County Down it is a small, misshapen goblin who wants his share of the harvest.

Wearing sharp spurs was said to protect a rider, since the púca feared 'the sharp things'. The name survives in places such as Poulaphouca, 'the púca's hole', in County Wicklow. Since 2019 a Púca Festival in County Meath has marked Halloween around Trim and Athboy.
signs: A black horse that appears on a lonely road
A wild ride you can't stop
Spoiled blackberries after November 1st
An animal that speaks
size: Horse-sized as a black horse; small goblin form in some counties
habitat: Mountains, hills, bogs and lonely roads

famous.name: First Púca Festival held for Halloween

name: Gnomes
region: German-speaking Europe; now worldwide as garden figures
first: Paracelsus, published 1566
summary: Paracelsus' earth spirits that swim through rock, later reborn as the garden gnome.
body: The word 'gnome' was coined, or at least first printed, by the Swiss physician and alchemist Paracelsus in a book published after his death in 1566. He described gnomes as earth elementals, about two spans (18 inches) tall, that move through solid rock as easily as we move through air. He borrowed the idea from German miners' stories of the Bergmännlein, little mountain men who haunted the mines.

From there gnomes spread into fairy tales and fantasy. In the 19th century German potters began making small clay gnome figures for gardens. Sir Charles Isham brought a group of them to his rockery at Lamport Hall in Northamptonshire from 1847; the one survivor, nicknamed Lampy, is often called the oldest garden gnome in England.

Today's red-hatted gnome owes a lot to the Scandinavian tomte and the Dutch kabouter. Modern sighting reports of small bearded figures in gardens and woods often use the word gnome, even when the witness describes something closer to a dwarf or brownie.
signs: A small bearded figure in a pointed red cap
Glimpsed in gardens or at the edge of woods
Movement in rocks or underground
Knocks in mines

famous.name: Sir Charles Isham begins the gnome rockery at Lamport Hall

name: Dwarves
region: Germanic and Norse Europe
first: Old Norse poems and the Prose Edda (13th century)
summary: Germanic master smiths of rock and mountain, from Norse myth to Snow White.
body: Dwarfs (or dwarves) are supernatural beings of Germanic folklore. In the Old Norse poems and the Prose Edda they are master smiths who live in rocks and mountains and forge the gods' greatest treasures, including Thor's hammer Mjölnir and Odin's spear Gungnir. Oddly, the earliest Norse sources never say they are short; their small size becomes a fixed feature only in later sagas and folk tales.

In medieval German stories dwarf kings such as Alberich guard hoards of treasure and can be as strong as twelve men. In later folklore dwarfs live inside hills, borrow and lend tools, and reward or punish people depending on how they are treated. Some, like Alvíss in the Norse poems, turn to stone in daylight.

The Brothers Grimm's Snow White, first printed in 1812, fixed the image of dwarfs as small, bearded miners for the modern world. Iceland still has named dwarf rocks; information boards at Dverghamrar say the local dwarfs are 20 to 30 cm tall.
signs: Hammering inside a hill
Small bearded figures near rocks or caves
Tools or treasures that appear or vanish
Voices from under the ground
size: Usually short; some German tales say knee-high

name: Huldufólk
region: Iceland and the Faroe Islands; related beliefs across the Nordic countries
first: Icelandic sources become plentiful around 1600
summary: Iceland's hidden people, who live in rocks and lava fields and still shape road-building debates.
body: Huldufólk means 'hidden people'. In Icelandic tradition they look and live much like people, farming and fishing in a parallel world inside rocks, hills and lava fields, and they show themselves only when they choose. Many Icelanders use 'elves' and 'hidden people' for the same beings. One old story says they are the unwashed children Eve hid from God.

The tradition is still alive. Icelanders leave food out at Christmas, light candles on New Year's Eve when the hidden people move house, and hold elf bonfires on Twelfth Night. Surveys suggest most Icelanders will not rule the hidden people out, though few say they are certain. Folklorists note that the stories also teach respect for a harsh landscape.

Road works have repeatedly run into this belief. In 1971 a bulldozer kept breaking down on Álfhólsvegur ('Elf Hill Road') in Kópavogur, and newspapers blamed elves in a large rock. In 2013 protesters, some citing elves and many citing the lava itself, halted a road through the Gálgahraun lava field near Garðabær; in 2015 the road authority moved a rock said to be an elf church, Ófeigskirkja, rather than destroy it.
signs: Machinery breaking down near a particular rock
People in old-fashioned clothes who vanish
Lights or voices in lava fields
Dreams of grey- or green-clad visitors
habitat: Rocks, cliffs, hillocks and lava fields

famous.name: Bulldozer trouble blamed on elves at Álfhólsvegur
Group searches for elves at the NATO base
Rockfall on residential streets blamed by some on hidden people
Road through the Gálgahraun lava field halted by protests

name: Tomte
region: Sweden, Norway, Denmark and Finland
first: Old Swedish mentions of 'tomte gods' (14th century)
summary: The small grey-clad farm guardian of Scandinavia, who expects porridge with butter at Christmas.
body: The tomte (Swedish) or nisse (Danish and Norwegian) is a small household spirit of the Nordic farm. He is described as about the size of a child, with an old man's face, a red cap and grey woollen clothes. He lives under the floorboards or in the barn, looks after the animals and the farm at night, and is attached to the place rather than the family.

A tomte is a good friend but a dangerous enemy. He is strong for his size and hates swearing, laziness, carelessness and change. His yearly wage is a bowl of Christmas porridge with a pat of butter on top. In a much-told tale, a farmer hid the butter at the bottom; the furious tomte killed the cow, then found the butter and went off in shame to find a replacement.

In the 19th century the farm spirit turned into the Christmas gift-bringer. Danish artists drew julenisser in the 1840s, and Jenny Nyström's pictures for Viktor Rydberg's 1881 poem 'Tomten' shaped the Swedish jultomte. Garden gnomes are still called trädgårdstomte in Swedish and havenisse in Danish.
signs: A small grey figure in a red cap near the barn
A horse groomed overnight
Braided manes (nisse-plaits)
Milk spilled or animals upset after a slight

name: Domovoi
region: Russia, Ukraine, Belarus and other Slavic lands
first: Slavic household beliefs, recorded by 19th-century folklorists
summary: The Slavic house spirit, an old grey man behind the stove who guards the family and its animals.
body: The domovoi, 'the one of the house', is the household spirit of Slavic tradition. He is usually pictured as a small, grey-haired old man with bright eyes, sometimes with a tail or little horns, living behind the stove or under the threshold. He can also appear as a cat or dog, or take the look of the master of the house or a departed ancestor.

A domovoi protects the family, its children and its animals, and may warn of coming deaths, wars or disasters. If the family quarrels or swears, he can turn against them or leave. People kept him happy with leftovers from supper or bread and salt, and when a family moved, they invited him to come too, sometimes carrying embers from the old stove to the new one.

Many related spirits watch other parts of the homestead: the dvorovoi in the courtyard, the bannik in the bathhouse and the ovinnik in the threshing barn. Some English writers call the domovoi a 'house elf'.
signs: Footsteps or sighs at night
Feeling pressed on in bed
Animals unsettled in the stable
Small things moved or hidden
habitat: Behind the stove, under the threshold, in barns and courtyards

name: Kobold
region: Germany
first: German household-spirit tales from the Middle Ages; Hödeken of Hildesheim, recorded c. 1500
summary: Germany's household sprite, helpful when fed and vicious when mocked, and the root of the word cobalt.
body: A kobold is a household sprite of German folklore. Like the brownie or tomte, it lives by the hearth or in the barn or cellar, does chores at night, and expects a bowl of milk or porridge in return. Kobolds are often invisible, but when seen they may look like a child, a small man in a red pointed cap, an animal, or a streak of fire.

Kobolds can be dangerous. In a chronicle of Hildesheim, the sprite Hödeken took terrible revenge on a kitchen boy who kept throwing slops at it. The Heinzelmännchen of Cologne, written down by Ernst Weyden in 1826, baked bread for the city's bakers each night until a curious tailor's wife scattered peas to trip them, and they left for good.
Miners had their own kobolds. They blamed troublesome ore, which gave off poison fumes and yielded no silver, on these sprites, and the name stuck: the metal cobalt is named after the kobold.
signs: Chores done overnight
Knocks and bangs in the house
Milk or porridge left out and eaten
Pranks after an insult
size: Child-sized; about 1 ft in one East Frisian tale
habitat: Hearths, kitchens, barns, cellars and mines

famous.name: Ernst Weyden writes down the Heinzelmännchen legend

name: Knockers
region: Cornwall and Devon, England; mining towns of the American West
first: Cornish mining folklore; carried to US mines from the 1820s
summary: Little mine spirits whose knocking warned Cornish and American miners of rich ore and cave-ins.
body: Knockers are the mine spirits of Cornwall and Devon. Miners described them as about two feet tall, with big heads, long arms, wrinkled skin and white whiskers, dressed in tiny miners' clothes. Their knocking in the rock was said to lead miners to rich veins of tin, and later to warn them of a coming collapse. Miners threw the last bite of their pasty down the shaft for them.

Cornish and Welsh miners, nicknamed 'Cousin Jacks', took the knockers with them to the mines of Pennsylvania, California, Nevada and Colorado, where they became tommyknockers. Some Cousin Jacks would not enter a new mine until they were sure the tommyknockers were already there. In the American West they came to seem more like the ghosts of dead miners than little elves.

Belief lasted well into the 20th century. In 1963 the organisers of Grass Valley's Fourth of July celebration in California asked Herbert Hoover, who had begun his career in a local mine, to explain tommyknockers to them; he wrote back describing them as gnomes that warned miners of rock falls.
signs: Knocking in the rock with no one there
Tools or food going missing
Candles blown out underground
Warning raps before a collapse
habitat: Tin, copper, gold and silver mines

famous.name: Herbert Hoover writes to Grass Valley about tommyknockers
Tommyknocker Brewery named after the mine spirits

name: Spriggans
region: West Penwith, Cornwall, England
first: Cornish folklore collected by Robert Hunt and William Bottrell in the 1860s and 1870s
summary: Cornwall's grim little treasure guards, said to be the ghosts of giants and able to swell to giant size.
body: Spriggans are among the least friendly of Cornwall's little people. The name comes from the Cornish word for 'spirits'. They are described as ugly, wizened old men with large heads, found at ruins, cairns, barrows and hillforts, where they guard buried treasure. Though small, they were said to be the ghosts of giants and kept a giant's strength; in one story they swell to enormous size.

Spriggans were blamed for sudden whirlwinds, storms that ruined crops, stolen cattle and robbed houses, and for taking human children and leaving changelings. In one tale an old woman beat a band of them by turning her clothes inside out. The folklorist Katharine Briggs called them the fairies' bodyguards.

Robert Hunt tied them to Trencrom Hill, a hillfort near St Ives. They are distinct from the friendlier pixies and from the knockers of the tin mines. A spriggan sculpture by Marilyn Collins has peered out of an arch on the Parkland Walk in north London since 1993.
signs: Sudden whirlwinds on a still day
Small grotesque figures near cairns or barrows
A figure that seems to grow larger
Bad luck after digging for treasure
size: Small, but said to swell to giant size
habitat: Hillforts, cairns, barrows and old ruins

famous.name: Robert Hunt links spriggans to Trencrom Hill in Popular Romances of the West of England
Spriggan sculpture installed on the Parkland Walk

name: Hobyahs
region: Scotland, via a tale printed in the United States; later popular in Australian schools
first: Printed in the Journal of American Folklore, 1891
summary: Night-time goblins from a grim folk tale who shout 'Hobyah!' and carry off a little girl in a sack.
body: The Hobyahs are goblin-like creatures from a short and scary folk tale. A family living in a house of hemp stalks is visited night after night by Hobyahs shouting, 'Hobyah! Hobyah! Hobyah! Tear down the hempstalks, eat up the old man and woman, and carry off the little girl!' Each night the little dog barks them away, and each night the old man punishes the dog, until it can bark no more.

The Hobyahs then tear down the house and carry the girl off in a sack. They sleep by day, which is their undoing: a passer-by rescues her and leaves his big dog in the sack instead. The tale was collected by S. V. Proudfit of Washington, D.C., from a family from Perth, Scotland, and Joseph Jacobs reprinted it in More English Fairy Tales.

The story became a schoolroom classic in Victoria, Australia, after it appeared in The School Paper in 1926 and later in the Victorian Readers, and it inspired the dark Australian film Celia (1989). The Hobyahs exist only in this tale, not in reported sightings.
signs: Voices shouting 'Hobyah!' in the dark
Visits only at night
Fear of dogs
habitat: Dark places; they sleep by day

famous.name: Tale from a Perth family printed in the Journal of American Folklore

name: Menehune
region: Hawaiian Islands, especially Kauaʻi
first: Hawaiian oral tradition; written down in the 19th century
summary: In Hawaiian tradition, a people of master builders said to finish great stone works in a single night.
body: In Hawaiian tradition the Menehune are a people who lived in the islands' forests and hidden valleys, away from human settlements. They are known above all as superb builders: fishponds, temples (heiau), roads, canoes and houses are credited to them, often said to have been finished in a single night. If a job was not done by dawn, they left it unfinished. They are said to love bananas and fish.

Several real structures are still linked to them, including the ʻAlekoko (Menehune) Fishpond near Līhuʻe on Kauaʻi and the Kīkīaola ditch at Waimea. In Martha Warren Beckwith's account of Hawaiian mythology, the Menehune are about two feet tall and live in caves.

Scholars disagree about the history behind the stories. Some link the name to the Tahitian word manahune, meaning commoners, and point to an 1820 census of Kauaʻi that counted 65 people as menehune. Folklorist Katharine Luomala argued the small-people image grew after contact with Europeans. For many Hawaiians the Menehune remain part of a living cultural heritage rather than a curiosity.
signs: Stonework finished overnight
Voices or work sounds in the forest at night
Small figures seen only by those they choose
habitat: Deep forests, hidden valleys and caves

famous.name: Census of Kauaʻi lists 65 people as menehune
ʻAlekoko (Menehune) Fishpond listed on the National Register

name: Duwende
region: Philippines
first: Spanish-era borrowing of 'duende', joined to older Filipino nature-spirit beliefs
summary: Small house and nature spirits of the Philippines, greeted with 'tabi tabi po' when passing their mounds.
body: Duwende (from the Spanish duende) are small spirits in Filipino folk belief. They are said to live in rocks and caves, old trees, dark corners of houses, anthills and termite mounds. They are often sorted by colour: white duwende are good and black ones are bad. Children are said to see them more easily than adults and sometimes play with them.

The nuno sa punso, 'old man of the mound', is a related but more easily angered spirit of the ancestors who lives in an anthill or termite mound. Kicking or urinating on a mound is said to bring a curse such as a swollen foot or sudden illness. When modern medicine fails, families may consult an albularyo, a traditional healer, who may advise an offering to the offended spirit.
Many Filipinos still say 'tabi tabi po' ('excuse me, please step aside') when passing a mound, a big tree or a dark field at night. It is a living custom of respect, not just a ghost story.
signs: Unexplained illness or swelling after disturbing a mound
Small figures seen by children
Things moved or hidden in the house
Laughter or voices from a dark corner
habitat: Anthills, termite mounds, old trees, rocks and quiet corners of houses

name: Orang Bunian
region: Malaysia, Indonesia (Sumatra, Borneo), Brunei and Singapore
first: Malay and Indonesian oral tradition
summary: The hidden people of Malay tradition, who live unseen in deep forests and mountains.
body: Orang bunian means roughly 'hidden people' or 'whistling people' in Malay. In Malaysian, Indonesian, Bruneian and Singaporean tradition they are beings almost identical to humans, often beautiful and dressed in old-fashioned Southeast Asian clothing, who are invisible to most people. Only those with 'spiritual sight' can see them. Some accounts say they have no groove above the upper lip.

They are said to live in deep forests and on high mountains in Sumatra, Borneo and the Malay Peninsula, in communities with families, clans and royalty much like human society. They are generally regarded as kindly and may help healers and shamans, but people entering their places should show respect and observe the right customs first.

Many stories tell of people who go missing in the forest and are said to have been taken in by the bunian, or of men who married bunian women and returned home to find that many years had passed. These tales are compared to Rip Van Winkle and the Japanese Urashima Tarō.
signs: Faint music or voices deep in the forest
Someone lost for days who says they were looked after
Time passing strangely
Whistling with no source

name: Korpokkur
region: Hokkaido, Sakhalin and the Kuril Islands, Japan
first: Ainu oral tradition; discussed by anthropologists from the 1880s
summary: In Ainu tradition, a little people who lived in the land before the Ainu and traded with them by night.
body: The Korpokkur are a little people in the oral tradition of the Ainu, the Indigenous people of northern Japan. The Ainu tell that the Korpokkur lived in the land before them. They were short, quick and skilled at fishing, and lived in pit houses roofed with butterbur (coltsfoot) leaves. The name is popularly explained as 'people under the butterbur leaves', though the missionary-linguist John Batchelor argued it really means 'people who dwell below', with no idea of small size.

Long ago the Korpokkur were on good terms with the Ainu and brought them deer and fish, but they hated to be seen and left their gifts at night. One day a young man grabbed a Korpokkur by the hand as she left a gift at his window and pulled her inside. She was so angry at his rudeness that her people left and have not been seen since. Their pits, pottery and stone tools are said to remain in the landscape.

In the late 19th century some Japanese scholars argued the Korpokkur were a real people the Ainu had displaced. Later research showed the pit houses and artefacts belonged to earlier cultures of Hokkaido and to the Ainu themselves. The story is best understood as part of Ainu tradition, not as evidence of a lost race.
signs: Small figures under large leaves
Gifts left at a window overnight
Old pit-house hollows and pottery
size: Small; said to shelter under butterbur leaves
habitat: Pit houses, riverbanks and fishing grounds

name: Alux
region: Yucatán Peninsula (Mexico), Belize and Guatemala
first: Maya oral tradition; possibly pre-Columbian
summary: Knee-high Maya guardian spirits who watch over fields and forests and expect offerings and respect.
body: Aluxo'ob (singular alux) are small spirits in the tradition of Maya peoples of the Yucatán Peninsula, Belize and Guatemala. They are about knee-high and look like tiny Maya people in traditional dress. They are usually invisible but can take physical form to talk to people, frighten them or gather together. They are linked to forests, caves, stones and fields. Some Maya say they are ancestral spirits or spirits of the land itself.

In one living custom, a farmer builds a little house for an alux in his maize field (milpa). For seven years the alux helps the corn grow, calls the rain and whistles at night to scare off animals and thieves. Treated with respect and given offerings, an alux brings protection and luck; ignored, it plays tricks or brings sickness. It is said to be unwise to speak their name aloud.

Construction crews in the Yucatán often hold ceremonies at new sites so as not to offend the aluxo'ob. In February 2023 Mexico's president Andrés Manuel López Obrador posted, alongside photos of Tren Maya progress, a dark picture said to show a small elf-like figure. News outlets compared it to the alux, and social media users soon found the photo was older than claimed.
signs: Whistling in the fields at night
Small stones thrown with no one in sight
Tools or pots moved or thrown
Illness after refusing an offering
habitat: Maize fields, forests, caves and stone shrines

name: Duendes
region: Spain and Portugal; Mexico, Central and South America
first: Spanish folklore; discussed by Fray Antonio de Fuentelapeña in 1676
summary: The small house and forest spirits of Spanish-speaking lands, from Spanish trasgos to Belize's Tata Duende.
body: Duende probably comes from dueño de casa, 'master of the house'. In Spain a duende is a small spirit that lives in a home, moves and hides things, makes noises in cupboards and plays tricks, much like a brownie or kobold. Spain has many regional cousins: trasgos in Asturias, trasnos in Galicia, follets in Catalonia and the big-headed martinicos of Castile.

The belief crossed the Atlantic. In Mexico and the American Southwest, duendes are small gnome-like beings said to live in the walls of houses, sometimes in children's bedrooms, and to trim the toenails of children who don't wash. Among the Mixtec and Zapotec of Oaxaca they are linked to the mossy cloud forests. In Belize, Tata Duende is a thumbless forest spirit who guards the woods and may lead people astray.

In 1676 the Spanish friar Antonio de Fuentelapeña wrote a whole book, El ente dilucidado, arguing that duendes were real, invisible creatures. The flamenco sense of duende, a mysterious power in music, comes from the same word.
signs: Objects moved or hidden around the house
Noises inside walls or cupboards
A small figure in a big hat in the woods
Children who say they have a little friend
habitat: Houses, walls, cupboards, forests and mountains

name: Nimerigar
aliases: Little people of the Rocky Mountains
region: Wyoming and the Rocky Mountains, United States
first: Shoshone oral tradition
summary: A little people in Shoshone tradition, said to shoot poisoned arrows from tiny bows.
body: The Nimerigar are a little people in the traditions of the Shoshone of the Rocky Mountains. In the stories they are fierce and warlike and shoot poisoned arrows from tiny bows. The name is often translated as 'people eaters'. Some tellings say they ended the life of any of their own who became too sick to take part in their society.

In the 1930s gold prospectors in Wyoming's Pedro Mountains found a tiny mummy, nicknamed 'Pedro', in a cave. Newspapers called it an adult 'pygmy', and it soon became linked to the Nimerigar. Later examination of it, and of a similar mummy in the 1990s, showed these were the remains of Native American infants born with anencephaly. Pedro itself has since been lost.

These are the traditions of a living people, and the mummy story says more about how outsiders used them than about the Nimerigar. Similar little-people traditions exist among many other nations of the region.
signs: Small arrows or tiny tracks
Being shot at from the rocks with no one seen
Small figures in mountain caves
size: Small (no fixed height in the stories)
habitat: Mountains and caves of the Rockies

name: Yunwi Tsunsdi
region: Southern Appalachians, especially western North Carolina; also Oklahoma
first: Cherokee oral tradition; recorded by James Mooney in 1900
summary: The Little People of Cherokee tradition, knee-high helpers who love music and want to be left alone.
body: Yunwi Tsunsdi means 'Little People' in Cherokee. In Cherokee tradition they are well-shaped, handsome people who stand about knee-high, with long hair reaching almost to the ground. They live in rock caves on the mountainsides, love music and drumming, and are often heard but seldom seen. They are distinct from the Nunnehi, the 'people who live anywhere', who look like full-sized Cherokee.

The Little People are generally helpful, especially to lost children and travellers, but they do not like to be disturbed, and people who follow them can come back confused. Cherokee tradition holds that if you find something in the woods, such as a knife, you should say 'Little People, I want to take this' first, because it may belong to them.

The ethnologist James Mooney recorded many of these traditions among the Eastern Band of Cherokee in western North Carolina and published them in Myths of the Cherokee in 1900. The Little People remain part of living Cherokee culture and storytelling, and many families still speak of them with respect.
signs: Drumming or singing in the hills with no source
Small figures at the edge of sight
A lost child who says little people helped them
Objects left in the woods
habitat: Rock caves, mountainsides and laurel thickets

famous.name: James Mooney publishes Myths of the Cherokee

name: Memekwesiw
region: Cree lands across northern Canada
first: Cree oral tradition
summary: Small river-dwelling little people of Cree tradition, playful tricksters who may tip over canoes.
body: Memekwesiw (plural memekwesiwak) are little people in the traditions of the Cree. They are described as small water spirits about the size of young children, living among river rocks and rapids, and are often said to have no noses. They are tricksters who like to play pranks, but they are not usually dangerous unless treated without respect, when they might capsize a canoe.

The name is pronounced differently across Cree dialects, and English books often spell it Mannegishi. In some Cree communities the word apiscinis, 'little person', is used for the same beings. They are closely related to the memegwesi of the Anishinaabe (Ojibwe), who are also said to live by the water.

Care is needed with popular accounts. The widely repeated description of Mannegishi with huge heads, spindly limbs and six fingers does not seem to come from Cree sources, and it is often borrowed to explain modern sightings like the Dover Demon. This page follows the Cree descriptions.
signs: Splashing or laughter near rapids
A canoe tipped without cause
Small, child-sized figures on river rocks

name: Makiawisug
region: Mohegan Hill, Uncasville, Connecticut; also southern New England
first: Mohegan oral tradition; recorded by Frank Speck from Fidelia Fielding in 1903
summary: The Little People of Mohegan tradition, led by Granny Squannit and honoured with baskets of food.
body: The Makiawisug are the Little People of the Mohegan (and Pequot) people of Connecticut. The name is linked to the Mohegan-Pequot word for the whippoorwill, the bird they are associated with. They are described as about knee-high, living among the rocks of Mohegan Hill and in the woods, and walking the border between this world and the spirit world, which is why they are rarely seen.

Their leader is Granny Squannit, a powerful healer and the wife of the giant Moshup, who also appears in Wampanoag stories. Mohegans traditionally leave baskets of cornbread, berries or meat in the woods for the Makiawisug as a mark of respect, and it is said to be rude to stare at them. In one Mohegan story a medicine woman nursed Granny Squannit back to health and was rewarded with gifts of herbs and crystals.

Mohegan language speaker Fidelia Fielding shared these traditions with the anthropologist Frank Speck, who published 'Mohegan Traditions of Muhkeahweesug, the Little Men' in 1903. Her grand-niece Gladys Tantaquidgeon, later Mohegan medicine woman, was trusted with tribal knowledge partly because she did not laugh at the Little People. They remain part of living Mohegan tradition.
signs: Small figures among rocks in the woods
A whippoorwill calling nearby
Food offerings left in the woods
Symbols carved on rocks
habitat: Woodlands and rock outcrops of southern New England

famous.name: Frank Speck publishes the Muhkeahweesug traditions told by Fidelia Fielding

name: Ebu Gogo
region: Central Flores, Indonesia
first: Nage oral tradition, central Flores
summary: Small, hairy forest people of Flores folklore, now linked by some to the extinct 'hobbit' human.
body: The Ebu Gogo are human-like beings in the folklore of the Nage people of central Flores, Indonesia. In the Nage language the name means roughly 'grandparent who eats anything', something like 'old glutton'. They are described as about 5 ft tall, hairy, fast runners with wide flat noses and large mouths, who murmured in their own language and could repeat words back like parrots.

In the stories they were greedy and stole food, and even children. One tale says that in the 18th century villagers gave the Ebu Gogo palm fibre to make clothes, then set it alight once it was in their cave, killing all but perhaps one pair who fled into the forest.

The legend gained worldwide attention in 2003, when archaeologists at Liang Bua cave in western Flores found the remains of Homo floresiensis, a tiny human species nicknamed the 'hobbit'. Anthropologist Gregory Forth suggested such tales may preserve memories of real encounters. Most scientists are doubtful, because H. floresiensis now appears to have died out around 50,000 years ago.
signs: Murmuring voices in the forest
Food stolen from fields
Small, hairy upright figures
Words repeated back
habitat: Forest and caves of central Flores

famous.name: Homo floresiensis fossils found at Liang Bua

name: Agogwe
region: East Africa (Tanzania and Mozambique)
first: Capt. William Hichens' account in Discovery, 1937
summary: Small, upright, russet-haired 'little men' reported by colonial hunters in East Africa.
body: The agogwe is a small, human-like creature reported from East Africa. Witnesses describe it as about 4 to 5 ft tall, walking upright and covered in brown or russet hair. It is known almost entirely from two colonial-era accounts.

In December 1937 Captain William Hichens wrote in the journal Discovery that, years earlier, while waiting for a man-eating lion in the Ussure and Simibit forests west of the Wembere plains in Tanganyika, he saw two 'little men, about 4 feet high, walking upright, but clad in russet hair' cross a forest glade. His local guide called them agogwe, 'the little furry men whom one does not see once in a lifetime.' The next year Cuthbert Burgoyne wrote that in 1927 he and his wife had seen two small brown upright figures walk among baboons on a beach in Portuguese East Africa.
There is no physical evidence and no further well-documented sightings. Both men allowed that they might have seen some kind of monkey.
signs: Small upright figures with reddish-brown hair
Walking on two legs in forest glades
Moving among baboons without alarming them

famous.name: Capt. William Hichens' account of two agogwe published

name: Goblins
region: Western Europe, especially France and Britain
first: The demon Gobelinus of Évreux, in Orderic Vitalis' 12th-century history
summary: The grotesque, mischievous little creatures of European folklore, and a catch-all name for small fae.
body: A goblin is a small, grotesque and usually ill-natured creature of European folklore. The word came into English from Old French gobelin, and earlier from a Latin gobelinus: the 12th-century monk Orderic Vitalis wrote of a demon called Gobelinus driven out of a church at Évreux in Normandy. Goblins are said to live underground or in houses, and to do everything from playing pranks to doing real harm.

'Goblin' is used loosely for many small, troublesome fae: Yorkshire's boggarts, French lutins that knot horses' manes, Scottish redcaps, and even the household brownie. Christina Rossetti's poem Goblin Market (1862) gave the goblin men selling enchanted fruit a lasting place in English literature.

Writers also use 'goblin' for similar beings from other cultures, such as the Korean dokkaebi or the Zulu tokoloshe, and for modern encounters. The most famous is the 1955 Kelly-Hopkinsville case in Kentucky, where a family said small, glowing 'goblins' besieged their farmhouse all night.
signs: Small grotesque figures in the dark
Pranks, breakages and lost items
Knots in horses' manes
Sounds under floors or in cellars
size: Small; about 1 ft in some traditions
habitat: Caves, underground places, old houses and cellars

name: Hobgoblin
region: England, with Scottish and Welsh relatives
first: The word is recorded from about 1530
summary: A homely English household goblin, helpful but fond of practical jokes, like Shakespeare's Puck.
body: A hobgoblin is a household spirit of English folklore, a 'hob' that is also a goblin. Hobgoblins are said to be small, hairy little men who, like their close relatives the brownies, do odd jobs around the house while the family sleeps, in return for food. Shakespeare's Puck in A Midsummer Night's Dream is called a hobgoblin, and Robin Goodfellow is the best known of the kind.

Hobgoblins are more fond of practical jokes than brownies, and can shape-shift. Robin Roundcap of Spaldington Hall in East Yorkshire threshed the corn but, in a bad mood, mixed the wheat back with the chaff and kicked over the milk pail; three clergymen are said to have confined him in a well. In Somerset, Blue Burches haunted a shoemaker's home as an old man in blue breeches, a white horse or a puff of blue smoke.
Over time 'hobgoblin' also came to mean an imagined fear or bugbear, as in Emerson's line 'a foolish consistency is the hobgoblin of little minds.'
signs: Chores done overnight
Practical jokes such as spilled milk or scattered grain
A spirit that changes shape
A family that moves and finds the spirit has followed

name: Redcap
region: The Anglo-Scottish Border
first: Border folklore; in Walter Scott's Minstrelsy of the Scottish Border, 1802
summary: A murderous Border goblin that haunts ruined castles and dyes its cap in travellers' blood.
body: The redcap is the most violent goblin of the Anglo-Scottish Border. It is said to haunt ruined peel towers and castles, especially those with a history of cruelty. It is described as a short, thickset old man with long teeth, talons, fiery red eyes, iron boots, a pikestaff and a red cap. It throws stones at travellers who shelter in its ruin and, if it kills them, dips its cap in their blood to keep it red.

Human strength is useless against it, but words of scripture or a cross are said to drive it off with a yell, leaving behind a large tooth. The most famous redcap, Robin Redcap, was said to be the familiar of the cruel lord William de Soulis of Hermitage Castle in Liddesdale. Walter Scott printed John Leyden's ballad 'Lord Soulis' in Minstrelsy of the Scottish Border in 1802, and wrote that every ruined tower in the south of Scotland was supposed to have such a spirit.
Not every redcap is cruel. One at Grantully Castle in Perthshire was a kindly little man who brought luck to those who saw him.
signs: A squat figure in a red cap at a ruined tower
Stones thrown from the ruins
Iron footsteps
A large tooth left behind

famous.name: Ballad of Lord Soulis and his redcap printed in Scott's Minstrelsy

name: Hinzelmann
region: Hudemühlen Castle, Lower Saxony, Germany
first: 1584, from the diary of Pastor Feldmann; book published 1701 and 1704
summary: A talkative kobold that haunted Hudemühlen Castle in Lower Saxony from 1584 to 1588.
body: Hinzelmann was a kobold, or household spirit, said to have haunted Hudemühlen Castle near today's Hodenhagen in Lower Saxony. The story comes from a book, Der vielförmige Hintzelmann (1701, second edition 1704), based on the diary of Pastor Feldmann of Eickeloh, who lived through the events. The Brothers Grimm later retold it.

It began in 1584 with banging noises. Then the spirit began to talk to the servants. It said its name was Lüring and that it came from the Bohemian Forest. It washed dishes, scrubbed pots, groomed horses, found lost things and gave advice, and demanded a bowl of sweet milk with white bread each day, a place at the table and its own room. It thrashed anyone who mocked it, tore up an exorcist's book, and followed the lord to Hanover in the form of a white feather when he tried to escape.

Hinzelmann was rarely seen. Children said it looked like a little boy in a red silk jacket with curly blond hair; Feldmann, as a teenager, saw something more like a 'transparent shadow'. It left of its own accord in 1588. The castle was abandoned after the Thirty Years' War.
signs: A voice that talks but no one is seen
Chores done in the kitchen and stable
A white feather that seems to follow someone
Beatings for those who mock it
size: Like a small child; usually invisible
habitat: A castle kitchen, stables and its own room

famous.name: Hinzelmann's haunting begins at Hudemühlen Castle

name: Mermaid
region: Coasts and seas worldwide
first: Fish-tailed 'sea girls' appear in the Liber Monstrorum (7th to 8th century); Columbus logged three 'sirens' in 1493
summary: Half-human, half-fish beings reported by sailors and coast dwellers for centuries, and still seen today.
body: Mermaids are sea beings with a human upper body and a fish's tail. Fish-tailed versions appear in European writing from the 7th or 8th century, as the singing sirens of Greek myth, first pictured as bird-women, merged with older sea maidens. That is why Spanish and Italian still call a mermaid a sirena and French a sirène. Nearly every coastal culture has its own merfolk, from the Irish merrow and the Scottish selkie to the Japanese ningyo.

On 8 January 1493, near the mouth of the river he called the Río del Oro (the Yaque del Norte, by Monte Cristi in today's Dominican Republic), Christopher Columbus saw three 'sirens' and wrote that they were not as beautiful as they are painted, with rather masculine faces. Historians agree he saw manatees. On 15 June 1608, two of Henry Hudson's crew reported a mermaid in Arctic waters, in either the Norwegian or the Barents Sea. Around 1830, seaweed cutters on Benbecula in the Outer Hebrides saw a small, woman-like creature in the water; a boy hit it with a stone, and a few days later a small body washed up at Culla Bay, where the local sheriff is said to have had it buried in a coffin and shroud.

Hoaxes have always followed. The 'Feejee mermaid' that P. T. Barnum showed in New York in 1842 was a monkey's upper body sewn to a fish's tail, one of many made for sale in Japan. In August 2009, after dozens of people reported a mermaid leaping out of Haifa Bay, the Israeli town of Kiryat Yam offered a $1 million reward for proof. In February 2012 Zimbabwe's water minister told a parliamentary committee that workers at dam projects near Gokwe and Mutare had refused to carry on because of mermaids, and traditional ceremonies were held to appease the water spirits.

In May 2012 Animal Planet aired 'Mermaids: The Body Found', a fictional mockumentary with actors playing scientists. So many viewers took it as real that NOAA, the US ocean agency, published a statement that no evidence of aquatic humanoids has ever been found. Manatees and dugongs, whose order Sirenia is named after the sirens, are the usual explanation for real sightings, along with seals.
signs: A human-like head and shoulders above the water, then a tail as it dives
Long hair, often combed on a rock
Singing or calls heard over the water
A shape that turns out to be a manatee, dugong or seal
size: About 3 to 6 ft (reported); Barnum's fake was about 3 ft
habitat: Coastal seas, bays, rocky shores and river mouths
